title: Sparse tensor networks for individual tree diameter estimation in mixed forests
summary: Measurements of tree diameter at breast height (DBH) are fundamental to forest inventories, but manual surveys across entire stands or regions are impractical. UAV-borne laser scanning (ULS) enables scalable automated forest surveys, yet canopy occlusion makes accurate DBH estimation from ULS point clouds non-trivial. Limited stem-level point density of ULS data constrains approaches relying on detailed stem reconstruction, such as Quantitative Structure Models (QSMs) and circle fitting. Empirical machine learning methods based on predefined point cloud metrics are an alternative. New deep learning approaches offer an even more principled solution, allowing models to learn directly from point clouds. Sparse tensor networks have shown particular promise, transforming forestry tasks such as tree species classification. We investigate whether these strengths can be extended to estimate individual tree DBH from ULS data across four mixed-species temperate forest plots in Germany. We further advance existing sparse tensor networks by introducing TreeNext, a lightweight deep learning architecture for direct individual tree parameter estimation from voxelized LiDAR point clouds. We present a fully automated forest inventory pipeline from individual tree instance segmentation to DBH regression, and quantify the impact of segmentation errors by comparing performance on automatically segmented and ground truth instances. TreeNext achieves an $R^2$ of 0.8355 on automatically segmented trees and 0.9380 on ground truth segments, outperforming strong tabular baselines including Random Forest and XGBoost. Segmentation quality emerges as the dominant error source in the automated pipeline. TreeNext proves highly data-efficient, performing well even in small data scenarios. Our findings establish sparse tensor networks as a practical foundation for automated individual tree DBH estimation from ULS.

We further advance existing sparse tensor networks by introducing TreeNext, a lightweight deep learning architecture for direct individual tree parameter estimation from voxelized LiDAR point clouds. Data and code are openly available. Introduction section:introduction Forests are essential for climate regulation, biodiversity, and human well-being, providing a large and persistent global carbon sink and a wide range of ecosystem services watson2018exceptional,pan2011large . Accurate measurement and estimation of individual tree parameters underpins modern forest inventories, enabling operational assessment of stand structure, management, and biodiversity indicators oettel2021linking . Among these parameters, diameter at breast height (DBH) is fundamental. DBH is the standard, non-destructive, and repeatable measure of tree size that supports efficient data collection and long-term monitoring across diverse forest types liang2022close . Critically, DBH is the strongest single predictor in allometric models and often suffices by itself to estimate many key forest attributes with high accuracy, most notably above-ground biomass brede2022nondestructive,kuyah2012allometric . Traditionally, DBH is measured manually using tools like diameter tapes, calipers, or dendrometers liang2022close . While accurate, these field-based methods are widely understood as labor-intensive, time-consuming, and costly, limiting their application for large-scale inventories liang2022close, sun2022predicting, du2023lidar . Remote sensing technologies offer efficient alternatives for estimating forest attributes ozturk2026barriers, chave2019ground . In particular, Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) technology enables the acquisition of high-density three-dimensional (3D) point clouds, allowing for the detailed characterization of complex forest structures due to its ability to penetrate the canopy brede2017comparing, sun2022predicting, du2023lidar . This canopy penetration provides key advantages over photogrammetric methods (e.g., Structure from Motion), enabling more accurate tree measurements hartley2025uav . Various laser scanning platforms have been developed to address different operational requirements and trade-offs between coverage, resolution, and deployment effort. Ground-based platforms, such as terrestrial laser scanning (TLS) and mobile laser scanning (MLS), provide highly detailed point clouds holvoet2025terrestrial, bekkers2014improving, brede2017comparing . However, both TLS and MLS are labor-intensive for large plots, requiring multiple scan positions brede2022nondestructive, wilkes2017data or narrow trajectories kuzelka2025trajectory to mitigate occlusion, and face limitations in efficiently covering large areas and capturing the upper tree canopy dhont2024evaluating, liang2022close, brede2017comparing . Airborne laser scanning (ALS) systems efficiently cover larger areas vezeteu2025direct , with UAV-borne laser scanning (ULS) emerging as a particularly effective modern approach for smaller continuous forest areas brede2017comparing, du2023lidar . ULS combines flexible deployment with the ability to acquire point clouds with point density substantially exceeding that of conventional manned ALS dersch2023towards,brede2022nondestructive,brede2017comparing , enabling detailed tree analysis even in complex, mixed forests sun2022predicting, brede2022nondestructive . The capacity of ULS for rapid acquisition of high-quality 3D data opens a direct path to characterizing forests at large spatial scales with substantially reduced field effort. The resulting point clouds represent forest structure in high detail, and translating them into quantitative inventory measurements is a critical step toward highly automated forest inventories at single tree level. Such measurements underpin complex silvicultural decision-making, from selective thinning, fertilization, and herbicide application to the modeling of biomass and carbon storage at scales relevant for climate reporting oettel2021linking , and emerging carbon-crediting markets, where forest owners may benefit from documenting actual biomass stocks at high spatial detail wheeler2026path . Multiple approaches have been developed to translate point cloud data into operational forest inventory products. Area-based approaches, among the earliest to reach operational maturity, rely on statistical models that predict average attributes for entire plots coops2021modelling, xu2021lidar . While well suited for large-area monitoring and strategic planning coops2021modelling , these methods inherently aggregate data, obscuring the fine-scale structural details of individual trees. The richness of modern LiDAR-derived point clouds, however, provides the opportunity to move beyond plot-level summaries to the scale of individual trees. Consequently, recent research has increasingly focused on individual tree approaches shao2024largescale , which more closely resemble classical forest inventory and can yield detailed structural and demographic information, enabling practitioners to quantify competitive interactions within stands, assess growth trajectories, and inform tree-level management prescriptions xu2021lidar, rodrigues2024applications . Achieving this level of detail from point cloud data is, however, a substantially more complex task, for which machine learning methods have become a common methodological solution. Automating single-tree inventory with machine learning typically consists of two stages: individual tree segmentation and per-tree parameter estimation. The latter is commonly framed as a supervised machine learning task on structured, tabular data derived from the point cloud. For extremely high-density ground-based acquisitions such as TLS, this structured data can contain direct geometric proxies of the target parameter estimated from stem geometry, for example by circle fitting liang2022close , or through quantitative structure models (QSMs) and related approaches that reconstruct woody tree structure demol2022estimating . ULS, while offering the key advantages of rapid and flexible large-area coverage, does not generally permit such direct measurements due to canopy occlusion and lower stem-level point density brede2017comparing . Instead, the principled approach for ULS-based tree parameter estimation relies on computing comprehensive sets of per-tree point cloud metrics (e.g., height percentiles, distribution statistics, return ratios) that describe overall tree structure rather than being limited to the geometry of a parameter of interest alone. These metrics then serve as input to common machine learning regressors such as Linear Regression, Random Forest, and gradient boosted decision trees (GBDT) ye2025estimating,xu2025improving,hartley2025uav,zhang2022estimation,sun2022predicting,du2023lidar . While effective and widely adopted, incorporating only features that practitioners explicitly define can overlook further valuable 3D spatial context present in the raw point cloud, and can be especially sensitive to segmentation artifacts and varying data acquisition conditions rodrigues2024applications . These limitations raise the question whether a model capable of learning directly from the raw 3D point cloud structure, bypassing explicit metric definition, could extract richer geometric and structural information and ultimately yield a more principled, resilient, and accurate approach to automated forest inventory. To realize this potential in the complex operational environments characteristic of forest ecosystems, modern deep learning represents a highly promising direction. Deep learning has transformed classification and segmentation of forest point clouds [] puliti2025benchmarking,murray2025individual,wielgosz2024segmentanytree , yet direct regression of tree parameters from LiDAR-derived 3D point cloud data remains underexplored. Recent work explored dense 3D convolutional neural networks for plot-level above-ground biomass estimation from ALS data, achieving performance comparable to tabular baselines such as Random Forest but without consistently outperforming them schaefer2024cnn . Advancements in data representation, particularly sparse tensor networks that exploit the inherent sparsity of point cloud data choy2019minkowskiengine,graham2018submanifold , have since led to stronger performance, as demonstrated by oehmcke2024deep for estimating plot-level biomass from ALS. However, whether these advantages extend to estimating individual tree parameters from ULS point clouds remains an open question, as this setting differs fundamentally in spatial scale, point density, and structural complexity. To date, sparse tensor networks have not been applied to single-tree DBH estimation, nor has deep learning been systematically evaluated for per-tree parameter regression from ULS point clouds, a need highlighted as one of the logical next steps toward improving single-tree inventory in precision forestry rodrigues2024applications . Here, we aim to address this need in several ways. First, we investigate whether sparse tensor networks, which have demonstrated strong performance for plot-level regression from ALS, can transfer to the complex domain of ULS data and the fine spatial scale of individual trees. title: GOFish: Full Field-of-View Gaussian Splatting and Mesh Extraction
summary: Robots, autonomous vehicles, and consumer 360° cameras use fisheye lenses for wide fields of view (FoVs). Simulation-ready digital twins require photorealistic rendering across the full FoV and an aligned collision mesh. However, prior fisheye Gaussian Splatting methods only rasterize up to 180° and do not produce meshes, while Gaussian surface reconstruction methods assume pinhole training images. We present GOFish, the first 3D Gaussian Splatting surface reconstruction method to train directly on fisheye images, rasterize FoVs beyond 180°, and extract an aligned mesh from the same scene. Calibrated densification recovers the surface across the entire FoV, while Calibrated Mip Filtering and Wide-Angle Appearance Modeling keep pixel blur and lens falloff out of the scene and mesh. Across the 200° FIORD and 205° FullCircle benchmarks, GOFish improves PSNR over the best prior method by 2.28 and 1.97 dB, respectively. It also outperforms fisheye rendering baselines within their own FoVs and achieves the highest mesh F-score on FIORD and the main ScanNet++ set. Together, the Gaussian scene and mesh form a LiDAR-free, simulation-ready digital twin that renders in real time, ray traces the full FoV, and provides collision geometry.

Introduction sec:intro Digital twins are virtual replicas of real environments used for robot simulation and training. To support visual perception and physical interaction, they must combine photorealistic appearance with aligned collision geometry. Fisheye cameras are commonly used for robotic perception and mapping~ yogamani2019woodscape,liao2022kitti360 , while consumer cameras pair back-to-back fisheye lenses for omnidirectional scene capture~ foroutan2026fullcircle . LiDAR scans are expensive to collect at scale, motivating recovery of both appearance and geometry directly from calibrated fisheye images over their full field of view (FoV). No prior 3D Gaussian Splatting~ kerbl3Dgaussians method delivers both. Fisheye Gaussian Splatting rasterizers~ liao2024fisheyegs,wu20253dgut,yang2025directfisheye,deng2025self,huang20253dgeer cover at most , while 3DGRT~ moenne20243d ray traces the full FoV but bakes pixel blur into the scene; neither produces a mesh. Conversely, Gaussian Opacity Fields (GOF)~ Yu2024GOF and other Gaussian surface methods~ radl2025sof,radl2026come,chen2024pgsr,guedon2025milo extract aligned meshes but assume pinhole training images. Using fisheye captures therefore requires rectification, which discards peripheral rays and prevents rendering the native FoV required for accurate sensor simulation. We present GOFish, the first 3D Gaussian Splatting surface reconstruction method to train directly on fisheye images, rasterize calibrated FoVs beyond , and extract an aligned mesh from the same Gaussian scene. A calibration-defined domain and complete admission cover every valid ray, while calibrated densification recovers the surface across the FoV. We further introduce Calibrated Mip Filtering and Wide-Angle Appearance Modeling to keep view-specific sampling and camera response outside the shared scene representation used for meshing. Figure~ fig:teaser illustrates GOFish's full-FoV rendering and aligned mesh on a FIORD capture~ gunes2025fiord , while Figure~ fig:capabilities demonstrates full-FoV ray tracing and mesh-based physics simulation. GOFish leads every rendering metric across the FIORD, FullCircle, ScanNet++, and pinhole Tanks~ ~Temples benchmarks~ foroutan2026fullcircle,yeshwanth2023scannet++,Knapitsch2017tanks . On average, it also outperforms all fisheye baselines within their respective fields of view, confirming higher rendering quality even without its coverage advantage. Furthermore, its meshes achieve the highest F-score on FIORD and the main ScanNet++ set. Beyond these gains, GOFish renders in real time, ray traces the full FoV, and provides collision geometry, turning native fisheye captures into LiDAR-free, simulation-ready digital twins. In summary, our contributions are: Full Field-of-View Rasterization: Calibration-defined domains and complete admission extend Gaussian rasterization beyond for the first time, with a 2.28\,dB PSNR lead over the best prior baseline on FIORD. Wide-Angle Appearance Modeling: Camera-fixed attenuation captures steep rim falloff outside the 3D scene, improving FIORD PSNR by 3.17\,dB over PPISP~ deutsch2026ppispphysicallyplausiblecompensationcontrol . Full Field-of-View Mesh Extraction: Calibrated densification and filtering enable an aligned full-FoV opacity-field mesh, achieving the highest mean F-score and recall among Gaussian surface methods on FIORD. Related Work sec:related Gaussian surface methods extract meshes from 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes~ kerbl3Dgaussians . Gaussian Opacity Fields (GOF)~ Yu2024GOF constructs a 3D opacity field by compositing per-view Gaussian responses and taking the minimum across views. SOF~ radl2025sof adds per-pixel sorting, geometry losses, and fast extraction, while CoMe~ radl2026come adds confidence-driven optimization. PGSR~ chen2024pgsr uses planar Gaussians with geometric consistency. MiLo~ guedon2025milo jointly refines a Gaussian scene and its extracted mesh. Other approaches use surface-oriented primitives or explicit mesh connectivity~ huang20242dgs,guedon2024sugar,zhang2025qgs,held2025meshsplatting . Existing Gaussian surface methods assume pinhole or rectified inputs, precluding direct mesh reconstruction from fisheye imagery. Fisheye Gaussian Splatting methods train directly on distorted images. Fisheye-GS~ liao2024fisheyegs and DirectFisheye-GS~ yang2025directfisheye modify the splatting projection, while Self-Calibrating GS~ deng2025self learns a lens deformation. 3DGUT~ wu20253dgut supports arbitrary camera models, and 3DGEER~ huang20253dgeer evaluates Gaussians exactly along rays up to . However, their rasterizers stop short of the full per-lens FoVs of the dual-fisheye cameras used to capture FIORD and FullCircle~ gunes2025fiord,foroutan2026fullcircle . 3DGRT~ moenne20243d ray traces the full field of view with one ray per pixel, baking pixel blur into the Gaussian scene while rendering substantially more slowly than rasterized methods. Omnidirectional methods~ lee2024odgs,li2025omnigs,foroutan2026fullcircle target panoramas and casual captures. None of these methods includes mesh extraction. GOFish instead trains directly on fisheye images, rasterizes the full field of view, and extracts a mesh from the same Gaussian scene. When unmodeled, sampling and appearance effects are absorbed into the Gaussian scene, degrading rendering and mesh extraction. Mip-Splatting~ yu2024mip suppresses aliasing in pinhole Gaussian Splatting with 3D and screen-space filters. Gaussian surface methods use VastGaussian's appearance model~ lin2024vastgaussian to keep photometric inconsistencies from creating spurious geometry~ Yu2024GOF,radl2025sof . PPISP~ deutsch2026ppispphysicallyplausiblecompensationcontrol instead limits corrections to camera effects, but its low-order vignetting misses steep rim falloff in wide-FoV fisheye images. GOFish adapts Mip-Splatting's filters to calibrated fisheye cameras and extends PPISP to model this falloff. title: What Actually Matters? A Paired Evaluation of Inference Settings for $π_{0.5}$ on BEHAVIOR-1K
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models offer a promising paradigm for general-purpose household robotics. However, inference and data-collection strategies that have been deployed in smaller-scale settings do not necessarily generalize to large-scale, diverse task suites. To address this gap, we conduct a systematic, paired evaluation of previously proposed inference and data-collection strategies across all 100 tasks. Our evaluation uses a fine-tuned $π_{0.5}$ model based on the 2025 BEHAVIOR Challenge winner, which achieves a Q-score of 0.39 on the public test set. These results show that proposed strategies do not transfer uniformly to new environments and tasks. Project page, videos, and detailed analysis: https://rubenhammele.github.io/behavior2026
full_text: * Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models offer a promising paradigm for general-purpose household robotics. However, inference and data-collection strategies that have been deployed in smaller-scale settings do not necessarily generalize to large-scale, diverse task suites. To address this gap, we conduct a systematic, paired evaluation of previously proposed inference and data-collection strategies across all 100 tasks. Our evaluation uses a fine-tuned model based on the 2025 BEHAVIOR Challenge winner, which achieves a Q-score of 0.39 on the public test set. These results show that proposed strategies do not transfer uniformly to new environments and tasks. Project page, videos, and detailed analysis: rubenhammele.github.io/behavior2026 Introduction VLA performance depends not only on learned parameters but also on inference and data-collection strategies. Inference strategies are often adopted from prior fine-tuning pipelines, yet their effectiveness beyond the original evaluation settings remains unclear. The inference strategies of the winner of the BEHAVIOR Challenge 2025~ li2024behavior1k , larchenko2025taskadaptation , remain understudied. Other approaches investigate advantage guidance and rollout optimization in the context of garment folding larchenko2026learningfold , while industrial reports evaluate fine-tuning and inference settings on a single real-world manufacturing task dreammachines2026pi05 . The extent to which these strategies generalize across diverse household tasks therefore remains an open question. We systematically evaluate proposed inference and data-collection strategies using a fine-tuned model across 4 instances of all 100 tasks of BEHAVIOR-1K~ li2024behavior1k . Halving the number of actions executed per prediction decreases Q-score by 0.16, potentially causing consecutive chunks to pursue different strategies. The inherited playback speed-up remains beneficial, likely because it fits more of each task into the time budget. Reducing denoising from twenty steps to one causes no detectable loss, suggesting that a single step already lands close to its mode. For data collection, snapshot-based restarts reduce simulation-step consumption by 29--43 , since retries resume near the failure point instead of re-simulating already completed stages from the initial state. Experimental Setup sec:setup Training Our policy is initialized from the pre-trained checkpoint introduced by~ larchenko2025taskadaptation . The policy is fully fine-tuned on the BEHAVIOR-1K dataset. Training then continues in a loop in which the current checkpoint collects rollouts on training instances, and the (partial) successful rollouts are mixed with the demonstrations for further training. Each training frame carries a binary advantage label for RECAP-style conditioning~ intelligence2025pi06 . Benchmark and Statistical Analysis. We evaluate all 100 BEHAVIOR-1K tasks on public test instances under official constraints~ behavior2026eval . For each cell, the control is the mean of two independent baseline runs. We assess paired score differences ( ) using task-clustered bootstrap 95 confidence intervals (CIs), classifying effects as helpful or harmful when the CI excludes zero. Experiments Results Inference Ablations Action-Chunk Execution Horizons: Prior work adopts different action-chunk execution horizons~ black2026pi0,chi2024diffusionpolicy , while findings on the benefits of longer execution horizons remain task- and policy-dependent~ larchenko2025taskadaptation,bai2025openpicomet . Consistent with this trade-off, halving the executed prefix from 26 to 13 actions substantially reduced Q-score and success rate while increasing episode length~(Tab.~ tab:inference ). Playback Speed-Up: The playback speed-up used by~ larchenko2025taskadaptation also outperformed standard-speed execution, whereas increasing the speed-up to leaned worse without reaching significance. Denoising Steps: Prior work uses different numbers of flow-matching inference steps, from 4 in GR00T~N1~ nvidia2025gr00tn1 to 10 in ~ black2026pi0 . Starting from the 20-step configuration of larchenko2025taskadaptation , reducing denoising to 10 or one step produced no detectable performance change. Overlap Inpainting: Real-Time Chunking (RTC) uses inpainting to maintain chunk continuity during asynchronous inference~ black2025actionchunking . larchenko2025taskadaptation also uses overlap inpainting but does not ablate it. Disabling it had no detectable effect on Q-score. Advantage-Guidance Strength: Increasing advantage-guidance strength to was worse, while matched . Rendering: Motivated by the gains from high-resolution rendering reported by bai2025openpicomet , we compare downsampling with direct rendering at 224 × 224. Data Collection To maximize the number of successful rollouts collected for training, we evaluate strategies to reduce data-collection costs and improve recovery from failed episodes~(Tab.~ tab:collection ). Restart Points: Prior work replays failure states~ larchenko2026learningfold , revisits promising states~ DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2004-12919 , and expands start states outward from the goal~ DBLP:journals/corr/FlorensaHWA17 . Among the tested restart points, restarting before the first drop in predicted task progress earned more progress than restarting at the last progress point. Simulation Cost: Restarts reduced simulation cost but did not significantly improve successes per simulation step. Stage-Belief Restoration: Since the policy feeds back its predicted stage~ larchenko2025taskadaptation , omitting this state during restoration reduced Q-score and task progress, supporting the preservation of policy-side state. Conclusion We have evaluated inference and data-collection strategies across all 100 BEHAVIOR-1K tasks. Shorter action chunks significantly reduced Q-score and a playback speed of 1.3 improved performance. Fewer denoising steps and disabling overlap inpainting maintained performance, whereas stronger advantage guidance offered no benefit. Snapshot restarts reduced simulation cost but not success, and required restoring the policy’s stage belief. These results suggest that inference and data-collection strategies do not necessarily scale uniformly across task complexity.

title: Self-Labeled Preference Transfer for Steerable Robot Manipulation
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies can learn to follow execution preferences, such as where to grasp an object or how to move around an obstacle, from demonstrations annotated with preference labels. Providing these annotations for every new task, however, is costly. We study whether learned preference control can transfer to new tasks whose demonstrations contain the desired behaviors but lack preference annotations. We find that a policy trained with preference annotations can follow preferences on a new task before adaptation but achieves limited task success. Fine-tuning on target demonstrations without these annotations improves task success while weakening preference control. Motivated by this finding, we introduce Self-Labeled Preference Transfer (SPT). SPT jointly trains a shared vision-language backbone for preference-conditioned action prediction and preference recognition on annotated source demonstrations. It then freezes the recognizer to preserve its cross-task preference recognition capability and uses it to self-label target demonstrations for policy fine-tuning. Across five types of execution preferences in simulation, the recognizer achieves 96.4% accuracy, and SPT reaches 84.8% preference following and 89.2% task success, compared with 59.4% and 88.0% for naive finetuning. We further extend to multiple preferences, achieving 93.8% preference following compared with 42.5% of baselines. In real-world experiments, SPT increases preference following from 52.5% to 92.5% relative to naive finetuning across two task transfers. These results show that SPT can support preference adaptation across tasks and objects while maintaining success, without additional manual preference annotations.

Providing these annotations for every new task, however, is costly. We study whether learned preference control can transfer to new tasks whose demonstrations contain the desired behaviors but lack preference annotations. We find that a policy trained with preference annotations can follow preferences on a new task before adaptation but achieves limited task success. Fine-tuning on target demonstrations without these annotations improves task success while weakening preference control. Motivated by this finding, we introduce Self-Labeled Preference Transfer (SPT). SPT jointly trains a shared vision-language backbone for preference-conditioned action prediction and preference recognition on annotated source demonstrations. It then freezes the recognizer to preserve its cross-task preference recognition capability and uses it to self-label target demonstrations for policy fine-tuning. Across five types of execution preferences in simulation, the recognizer achieves 96.4 accuracy, and SPT reaches 84.8 preference following and 89.2 task success, compared with 59.4 and 88.0 for naive finetuning. We further extend to multiple preferences, achieving 93.8 preference following compared with 42.5 of baselines. In real-world experiments, SPT increases preference following from 52.5 to 92.5 relative to naive finetuning across two task transfers. These results show that SPT can support preference adaptation across tasks and objects while maintaining success, without additional manual preference annotations. Introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) models trained on large multi-task datasets can now follow language instructions across scenes, objects, and embodiments~ o2024open,kim2024openvla,black2024pi0,libero,nasiriany2024robocasa,mees2022calvin . Demonstrations in these datasets usually show one way to complete a task, or follow whatever pattern the operator found natural. In reality, a task has several acceptable executions, and which one is wanted depends on the context and on the user. A mug can be grasped near its rim or near its base; an object can be placed at the center of a tray or in a corner; a path can pass close to an obstacle or give it a wide berth. We call such choices execution preferences: they concern how a task is performed rather than what is accomplished, and the desired choice may depend on the user or context. Standard task-level instructions do not specify this choice, leaving the user without explicit control over it. This paper studies how a VLA can follow a stated execution preference on a new task when its target demonstrations do not contain preference labels. Existing work approaches execution-level control from two directions. One line makes VLAs steerable by enriching training prompts with descriptions of how each demonstration was performed, produced by human annotators or automated pipelines~ steer,finevla,demian,pi07 . These works show that VLAs can follow execution-level instructions once such annotations are available, but a new task still has to be annotated before the policy can be steered on it. The other line is preference learning, which infers a reward or policy from comparisons between executions~ Sadigh2017ActivePL,cpl,zhang2024grape,moletta2026rko . The output of preference learning is a policy aligned to a user's preference (often through ranking executions~ Peng2025UUPL ) rather than one that switches on command to a named style. Preference learning is typically used to adapt a policy toward preferred behavior on a particular task, rather than to provide command-conditioned switching among named execution preferences across tasks. Neither line asks whether preference control learned on labeled source tasks can be preserved when adapting to a new task whose demonstrations lack preference labels. This setting introduces two challenges. First, the source supervision must teach preference semantics that transfer across tasks, so that the behavior shown in a target demonstration can still be recognized. Second, the policy must adapt to the target task without losing its response to the preference command. Finetuning on target demonstrations with the task instruction alone provides no signal tying the demonstrated motion to a preference, so the control learned on the source can be weakened during adaptation. We study preference transfer without target preference annotations. We assume preference-labeled demonstrations for a set of source tasks and demonstrations with varied execution behaviors, but no preference labels, for a set of target tasks. Our approach, Self-Labeled Preference Transfer (SPT), addresses this setting in two stages. In Stage~A, a shared vision-language backbone learns both to execute a stated preference and to recognize the preference expressed in a demonstration. In Stage~B, we freeze the Stage-A recognizer and use it to label the target demonstrations, then finetune a trainable copy of the policy on the target actions paired with these inferred preference prompts. These labels associate each target behavior with the corresponding preference command during adaptation. At deployment, only the policy runs, and the user selects a behavior using the same preference vocabulary learned on the source tasks. We evaluate SPT in simulation and on a real robot. In RoboTwin~2.0~ robotwin , we synthesize pick-and-place demonstrations along five preference axes and transfer to held-out object and receptacle combinations. On a real robot experiment, we transfer across task types: from pick-and-place to pushing and from air hockey to billiards. The Stage-A recognizer labels target demonstrations with 96.4 average accuracy, and SPT raises average preference following from 59.4 to 83.8 in simulation and from 52.5 to 92.5 on the robot, with similar average task success. Ablations on placement and contact height isolate the roles of source preference transfer and target self-labeling. Before target adaptation, the Stage-A policy reaches 80 and 88 preference following on the two target tasks, but with lower target-task success. Finetuning the same Stage-A checkpoint with bare target instructions reduces preference following to 52 and 50 , whereas SPT retains 83 and 90 while adapting to the target tasks. Shuffling the inferred target labels gives similarly poor preference following, indicating that the benefit depends on correctly associating each target behavior with its preference rather than on adding preference text alone. In summary, this paper makes three contributions. (1)~We formulate transfer of a named execution-preference vocabulary to target tasks whose demonstrations lack preference annotations. (2)~We introduce SPT, which jointly learns preference-conditioned action prediction and preference recognition, then reuses a frozen recognizer to label target demonstrations before policy adaptation. (3) We evaluate this approach across five simulated preference axes and two real-robot task transfers, with controls for source initialization and target label assignment, comparisons to target-labeled reference conditions, and an extension to two simultaneous preferences. Related Work sec:related Steerable VLAs. Large multi-task datasets have produced policies that condition on language and generalize across tasks, scenes, objects, and embodiments~ o2024open,kim2024openvla,black2024pi0 , usually by attaching an action head to a pretrained VLM and finetuning on demonstrations~ kim2024openvla,kim2025oft . Their language conditioning is not always robust~ liberoplus , and the goal-level instructions in most datasets say nothing about execution. A recent line of work addresses this by writing execution details into the training language. STEER grounds modular skills in dense attribute annotations~ steer ; DeMiAn and FineVLA re-annotate existing datasets with fine-grained process descriptions, through a VLM pipeline in one case and human-verified labels plus a trained robotics VLM annotator in the other~ demian,finevla ; and trains a generalist on prompts that carry strategy and metadata alongside the goal~ pi07 . These works establish that a VLA follows how-level instructions once its training data contains them, and each obtains that data by annotating it. SPT differs in what it asks and where the labels come from. We assume a labeled source set and ask whether preference recognition learned jointly with the source policy can transfer to a new task, so that its demonstrations can be labeled without additional preference annotation and the adapted policy can still respond to the source vocabulary. Preference learning and personalization. Preference learning typically learns rewards or policies from comparisons between executions~ Sadigh2017ActivePL,cpl,Peng2025UUPL . In manipulation, GRAPE, APO, and RKO apply preference optimization to VLAs and diffusion policies~ zhang2024grape,xia2025hapo,moletta2026rko , and Preference VLM, VARP, and VLP replace human comparisons with VLM judgments, the last training an annotator that transfers to downstream tasks~ ghosh2025prefvlm,singh2025varp,vlp . Personalization work asks how a robot should choose among several valid behaviors for a given user: COMMET resolves human-induced conflicts by selecting among options according to stored user preferences~ li2025commethumaninducedconflictsmobile , TacStyle has an LLM pick a point in a learned style latent from a handful of labels~ tacstyle , and Freeform Preference Learning trains a policy that responds to several language-defined preference axes~ fpl . Our setting shares the premise that the user, not the task, decides the execution, but the supervision differs. A label such as ``grasp low'' describes a style without ranking it above ``grasp high''; both are correct when requested. Rather than aligning a policy separately on each task, we ask whether preference following learned on labeled source tasks can be transferred to target tasks whose demonstrations lack preference labels. Self-labeling and auxiliary supervision in VLAs. Using a model's own predictions as labels for unlabeled data is standard in semi-supervised learning~ fixmatch , and foundation models have been used to label robot data with task instructions~ blank2024nils and process descriptions~ demian . In VLAs, auxiliary language objectives are usually added to improve representations: LAP co-trains action prediction with visual question answering~ zha2026lap , SG-VLA adds spatial grounding~ tu2026sgvla , and TwinBrainVLA keeps a generalist pathway beside the action pathway~ yu2026twinbrainvla . SPT combines these two ideas but uses them differently. The recognition objective is not only an auxiliary training signal: the resulting recognizer is reused to label demonstrations from a different task. The preference axis is a finite vocabulary set that captures preferred behaviors that modify aspects of the task (e.g., low grasp contact height or high placement location). title: Embodied at Sea: Imitation Learning for Multi-Task Underwater Manipulation
comment: 8 pages, 8 figures. For associated files, see https://lair-research-nyu.github.io/Embodied-at-Sea/
summary: Behavior Cloning has demonstrated promising generalization capabilities for robotic manipulation in terrestrial environments. However, marine visual distortions and dynamic currents create a severe domain shift that remains a key bottleneck in adapting generalist architectures to underwater field manipulation. To address this, 1616 episodes of underwater manipulation data were collected in calm and turbulent waters and were used to train 14 generalist Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models (DynamicVLA) with varying proprioception observation configurations. Across three tasks on 1260 gradable on-hardware rollouts in a pool, 10 models outperformed the baseline, with the highest-performing model achieving a 93.3% overall success rate, including partial successes. Results are also introduced from a case study evaluating the performance of a single-task Action Chunking Transformer (ACT) and a generalist VLA (SmolVLA) policy for two tasks in marine archaeology and conservation: grasping and mooring. Experiments are performed on an ROV on and around the WWII wreck Coralita X127 and at Manoel Island Marina, Malta. Across 748 collected episodes and 508 gradable on-hardware rollouts, the ACT policy substantially outperformed SmolVLA (47.9% vs. 7.9% pooled success rate), earning a 66.7% success rate on the most successful task at the marine archaeological site. To enable further contributions to embodied intelligence in marine field robotics, the BLUEMBODIED KIT used to collect data, train models, and deploy policies on the ROV has been open sourced.

However, marine visual distortions and dynamic currents create a severe domain shift that remains a key bottleneck in adapting generalist architectures to underwater field manipulation. To address this, 1616 episodes of underwater manipulation data were collected in calm and turbulent waters and were used to train 14 generalist Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models (DynamicVLA) with varying proprioception observation configurations. Introduction Marine conservationists and archaeologists routinely perform tasks such as environmental monitoring and specimen retrieval, constrained by poor visibility, dynamic currents, and the physiological limits of human divers. At deeper depths, monitoring requires repeated dives that are slow, costly, and risky due to lengthy decompression procedures deepdives . Automating these operations, e.g. via robots, could accelerate scientific research and reduce diver risk. Recent advances in Behavior Cloning (BC) act have enabled robust single-task robot policies from relatively little data. While prior works explore the performance of these approaches in aquatic robotics aquabot,umiunderwater , deployment in real marine archaeology and conservation missions remains largely unexplored. BC-based policies, particularly Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, have shown remarkable generalization to novel tasks and objects, making them an appealing candidate for underwater manipulation. However, they are trained almost exclusively on terrestrial datasets featuring stable lighting and fixed-base manipulators, while underwater vehicles operating in marine environments experience unconstrained 6-DOF motion, drag, turbidity, visual distortion, occlusion, and distractors (see Fig.~ fig:method ). Whether these policies retain their generalization capabilities under such conditions and across diverse archaeological sites remains an open question. By enabling increased levels of autonomy for underwater robotic manipulation tasks, there will be scientific value not just within the field of robotics, but as well in the fields of marine archaeology, oceanography, geology, biology, and environmental conservation. This leads to a motivating question: how can the recent advances in terrestrial behavior cloning be leveraged for underwater environments? In addressing this driving question, the work presented below yields the following contributions: To our knowledge, the world's first instance of successfully implementing a multi-task VLA underwater on real hardware, where a VLA is defined as a single Vision-Language-Action model that can execute multiple tasks and be commanded to execute a specific task via language based inputs. A real-world case study of BC manipulation models deployed on an underwater Remotely Operated Vehicle (ROV) at a Mediterranean shipwreck for archaeology and conservation tasks. A thorough investigation into how different proprioception configurations and underwater sensor modalities in a model's observation and action spaces affect generalist model behavior underwater, including a new action space that leverages an underwater robot depth sensor and feedback control for stable motion in the vertical direction. Introducing the as an open source repository that enables users to collect underwater teleoperation data, train single (ACT) and multi-task models (DynamicVLA, SmolVLA), and run inference on Blue Robotics' BlueROV2 while staying compatible with BlueOS. Related Work Autonomy in Underwater Robot Systems Underwater robot systems (specifically, ROVs (Remotely Operated Vehicles) and AUVs (Autonomous Underwater Vehicles) fromrovtoauvs ) have been used for decades, largely for exploration and scientific sampling. However, most AUVs lack manipulation abilities, while many ROVs are equipped with end-effectors. ROV end-effectors are typically remotely operated by humans oceanone , while autonomous underwater manipulation has traditionally relied on classical control techniques, including PID, sliding-mode, and model predictive control autonomousmanipulation . The machine-learned approaches to developing robot manipulation control policies have largely been utilizing reinforcement learning (RL), e.g. ROVusingRL, RLunderTorque , but these works lack real-world ocean deployments. Single-Task BC in Terrestrial Contexts BC for single task policies can be described as training a model to output the appropriate signals that can accomplish a single task. The two most notable single task policy models are Action Chunking Transformers (ACT) act and Diffusion Policy diffusionpolicy (DP). When introduced in act the ACT models demonstrated the ability to accomplish highly dexterous tasks with only 100 demonstrations. These models have been augmented in several ways since then, including the addition of mobility mobileALOHA . While ACT models have not demonstrated much generalization, DP approaches have often yielded better flexibility but at the cost of needing significantly more demonstrations to achieve high success rates on a task. An advantage of single task policies over most generalist policies is the small size, (e.g. millions of model parameters as opposed to billions of model parameters), which can lead to faster training times and lower inference latency at model deployment. Generalist Policies in Terrestrial Contexts BC for generalist policies can be described as training a single model to be able to accomplish many tasks. Vision Language Action models (VLAs), a broad class of generalist models that take images and text-based language commands as inputs and output robot actions, have become increasingly popular for their robustness. Some of the first VLAs included RT-1 rt1 , RT-2 rt2 , and RT-X rtx , as well as OpenVLA openvla . Later, pizero from Physical Intelligence demonstrated a multi-expert system that leverages the world generalizability of both Vision Language Models (VLMs) and the action fidelity of diffusion-based policies. A key characteristic of the architecture is that it is built upon a large pre-trained VLM backbone (i.e. SigLIP + Gemma), providing cross-attention to another action expert that leverages flow matching to generate robot actions, or controls to be sent to a low-level joint control system. This dual architecture has been mimicked by other research teams such as in groot from NVIDIA. Although VLAs have shown strong performance in terrestrial settings, there is no standing literature describing how they perform in a marine environment, and no standing literature successfully implementing VLAs on an ROV. Data Collection Strategies The most popular data source for training models continues to be teleoperation, in which a robot manipulator is teleoperated by a human via a leader-follower control system gello , or VR system levr . These systems generate high-quality data because the data consists of actual robot trajectories in the identical format the models are being trained to generate. Other approaches, like capturing trajectories from videos of humans completing tasks, are typically noisy and require a difficult re-mapping of the human hand’s trajectory to a robot’s end-effector trajectory. However, much progress is being made in this area to increase the efficiency of data collection egovla . To note, the data sets generated with large scale human video data have not been collected for use in the underwater domain. When underwater data is collected, it is from human teleoperated demonstrations (e.g., umiunderwater, aquabot ). Adapting BC to Underwater Contexts BC models for robotic manipulation have enabled increasingly generalizable robotic behaviors on terrestrial tasks. Action Chunking Transformers (ACT) act learns complex manipulation from low-cost demonstrations, Diffusion Policy diffusionpolicy , SmolVLA smolvla , and pizero extend this idea via large-scale pretraining, and DynamicVLA dynamicvla improves inference efficiency for dynamic tasks by overlapping inference and execution across action chunks. Other works adapt BC beyond their training distribution: AirVLA pimakeitfly modifies pizero actions via a physics-aware, embodiment-specific module, UMI-Underwater umiunderwater adapts land-trained diffusion policies underwater with a depth-based affordance predictor and land-data collected from a hand-held device meant to replicate a robot’s end-effector umi , and AquaBot aquabot shows learning-based policies can improve through underwater data collection. These works demonstrate the utility of BC underwater; however, they all lack underwater demonstrations with full VLA capabilities, such as the ability to command the robot with text based instructions to execute one of many underwater tasks that the single model is capable of. Recent work in oceansim , usim , and underwatervla has attempted to leverage simulation data in the pursuit of underwater BC, given that ocean data is not accessible for many researchers. While synthetic data from simulation also provides another scalable source of underwater training data oceansim , many tasks resulting from simulation data suffer from the sim2real gap sim2realVLA , and typically fails to capture the complexity of the underwater world. Results from usim , underwatervla are notably not evaluated in the real world. Results from aquabot are derived from human teleoperated data and tested in a pool, but are limited to a single task due to the diffusion policy diffusionpolicy backbone, and cannot perceive color due to their reliance on depth instead of features. Given the standing literature, fine-tuning multi-task models using underwater data and executing these models underwater to perform complex manipulation tasks remains a critical challenge. Methodology This work presents some of the first applications of BC to underwater environments. Documented below are the different data sets collected and robot control policy model architectures trained with such data, all motivated to provide autonomous control of underwater robots for underwater tasks in underwater environments. Data Collection Robot demonstrations were collected across 3 tasks in an in-lab pool, as well as 2 tasks in an ocean setting. Pool Deployment To investigate how BC-based policies perform underwater in a controlled environment, three task families were explored (see Fig.~ fig:pool_tasks ): grab, approaching an object and grasping it with the end-effector to simulate sampling a specimen, moor, approaching a stationary post

title: MATCH: Execution-Aware Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning for Vision-and-Language Navigation in Continuous Environment
summary: Vision-and-Language Navigation in Continuous Environments (VLN-CE) requires instruction-consistent planning and reliable execution under collision constraints. Yet many hierarchical approaches optimize the planner while keeping execution fixed. We introduce MATCH, a framework that jointly learns a language-conditioned planner and a goal-conditioned primitive-action executor. An execution-aware topological graph represents start-dependent execution options and integrates executor value estimates with realized outcome memory, enabling the planner to select execution requests and refine their targets through bounded continuous offsets. A transition-aware dense macro reward balances ordered progress along the reference route against execution residual, encouraging executable requests without substituting local success for instruction following. A staged curriculum culminates in synchronized on-policy updates, with the executor learning on planner-generated requests and the planner adapting its requests to the executor's current behavior. With 0.5B parameters, MATCH achieves state-of-the-art performance on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE benchmarks. Preliminary real-robot deployments further demonstrate its practical potential.
full_text: \@maketitle \@extra@b@citeb .main [ieeetr] Vision-and-Language Navigation in Continuous Environments (VLN-CE) requires instruction-consistent planning and reliable execution under collision constraints. Yet many hierarchical approaches optimize the planner while keeping execution fixed. We introduce MATCH, a framework that jointly learns a language-conditioned planner and a goal-conditioned primitive-action executor. An execution-aware topological graph represents start-dependent execution options and integrates executor value estimates with realized outcome memory, enabling the planner to select execution requests and refine their targets through bounded continuous offsets. A transition-aware dense macro reward balances ordered progress along the reference route against execution residual, encouraging executable requests without substituting local success for instruction following. A staged curriculum culminates in synchronized on-policy updates, with the executor learning on planner-generated requests and the planner adapting its requests to the executor’s current behavior. With 0.5B parameters, MATCH achieves state-of-the-art performance on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE benchmarks. Preliminary real-robot deployments further demonstrate its practical potential. Introduction Vision-and-Language Navigation in Continuous Environments (VLN-CE)~ krantz2020beyond requires an agent to follow natural-language instructions through hundreds of collision-constrained primitive actions. Many approaches address this long-horizon problem by predicting intermediate navigation intents, such as target locations~ an2024etpnav, wei2026dualvln, ye2026revisiting , or short waypoint-based trajectories~ zhang2026navfom, xue2026omninav , which must then be translated into movement. We refer to intent selection as macro-level planning and intent realization as micro-level execution. In the hierarchical Markov decision process (HMDP) view~ parr1998hmdp , an intent is a macro action whose state transition depends on both environmental dynamics and the executor's policy. Selecting an instruction-consistent intent therefore doesn't ensure that it can be realized under collision constraints. Some methods bypass this execution challenge through teleportation~ xue2026omninav, zhang2026navfom (Fig.~ fig:teaser a), while some other methods rely on hand-designed controllers~ an2024etpnav, hnr . Even when the planner is trained on actual execution outcomes~ ye2026revisiting , the execution policy remains fixed during that training. The planner may learn to avoid a difficult doorway and select an alternative target, but the same experience does not teach how to handle that doorway more reliably (Fig.~ fig:teaser b). Our insight is to extend the learning loop beyond macro-level planning to include micro-level execution: navigation experience should help to co-optimize the planner and executor, not just improve the planner's ability to work within its limits. Hierarchical reinforcement learning (HRL)~ sutton1999hrl provides a natural framework for this joint adaptation. The planner determines the requests on which the executor learns, while the executor shapes the transitions those requests realize. The challenge is to couple these adaptations so that the executor learns on planner-generated requests and the planner selects requests that produce instruction-consistent progress under the current execution policy, rather than merely favoring easy targets. This calls for grounding macro-action learning both in the current executor and in the task contribution of its realized transitions. We address this challenge with MATCH (Macro-Action Transition Coupling for Hierarchical RL) (Fig.~ fig:teaser c), which jointly learns a language-conditioned planner and a goal-conditioned executor. We implement its decision interface within the graph-based VLN-CE architecture~ an2024etpnav , where waypoint proposals define candidate frontiers for an online topological planner. To ground the planner's requests in the executor's evolving capabilities, we develop an execution-aware topological graph. In this graph, edges from different visited nodes to the same frontier represent distinct execution options, since execution outcomes depend not only on the destination but also on the starting location. Each edge carries the executor's value estimates over a target neighborhood before execution and records the realized outcome memory afterward. The planner pairs edge selection with a bounded continuous target offset within this evaluated neighborhood, allowing it to refine an execution request rather than merely accept or reject a fixed waypoint. To learn which execution requests are useful for the task, we introduce a transition-aware dense macro reward based on their realized transitions. Each macro action receives credit for the ordered progress along the reference route, minus the execution residual---the remaining target-reaching distance---with both measured in meters. The progress term encourages the planner to advance along the route, not just choose easier targets. The residual gives the planner direct feedback on each request's execution difficulty, rather than leaving it implicit in final task outcomes. This encourages executable requests without making local success a substitute for instruction following. The executor is rewarded for progress toward assigned target. A staged curriculum followed by synchronized on-policy updates lets both policies adapt through shared navigation experience. Our main contributions are: We propose MATCH, to our knowledge the first VLN-CE framework to jointly optimize a language-conditioned planner and a primitive-action executor through HRL, with both policies learning from shared on-policy navigation rollouts. To support joint adaptation during HRL, we develop an execution-aware topological graph that uses executor value estimates and outcome memory to guide the planner's selection and refinement of execution requests. We introduce a transition-aware dense macro reward that balances ordered progress along the reference route against execution residual, encouraging executable requests that advance the route. Using a 0.5B-parameter model, MATCH achieves state-of-the-art performance on R2R-CE and RxR-CE, with real-robot deployments further validating practicality. Related Work sec:related_work Hierarchical Vision-and-Language Navigation VLN-CE~ krantz2020beyond requires instruction following through collision-constrained primitive actions rather than assuming oracle transitions between predefined viewpoints. Waypoint prediction~ hong2022bridging introduces intermediate spatial goals to connect language-conditioned planning with movement, enabling discrete-environment agents to transfer to continuous settings without predefined navigation graphs. Graph-based methods extend planning context: DUET~ chen2022duet combines fine-grained local grounding with global topological reasoning, while BEVBert~ an2022bevbert integrates metric and topological maps for spatially grounded navigation. ETPNav~ an2024etpnav couples online topological mapping and cross-modal planning with a heuristic controller that tries alternative actions when execution is blocked. DualVLN~ wei2026dualvln learns a diffusion-based executor conditioned on a supervised pixel-goal planner, but does not refine the planner through RL on executor-induced macro transitions. HSAN~ fang2026hsan combines supervised high-level planning with RL-based low-level control. Ye et al.~ ye2026revisiting optimize topological frontier selection through closed-loop macro-action RL while retaining a fixed controller. MATCH differs by applying RL to both levels, jointly optimizing a language-conditioned planner and a primitive-action executor from shared on-policy navigation rollouts. Hierarchical Learning and Execution Feedback In state-based control, goal-conditioned HRL methods jointly learn high-level subgoals and low-level policies~ zhang2020hrac, lee2022dhrl . HIRO~ nachum2018hiro corrects off-policy experience to account for changing low-level behavior, while HAC~ levy2017hac uses hindsight transitions to learn multiple policy levels in parallel. For execution grounding, SayCan~ ahn2022saycan uses value functions of pretrained skills to inform language-level decisions. For route-aware supervision and evaluation, LAW~ raychaudhuri2021law aligns corrective actions with the instructed path instead of only the destination, while nDTW~ ilharco2019ndtw measures ordered path fidelity and can serve as an RL reward. MATCH couples macro-action learning to both the executor's evolving capabilities and the task contribution of realized transitions. Its execution-aware topological graph uses current executor values and outcome memory to evaluate source--target execution options, guiding request selection and bounded continuous target refinement. Its transition-aware macro reward credits ordered route progress while penalizing execution residual, providing direct feedback on both task contribution and execution shortfall. Together, these mechanisms support joint adaptation without treating local target completion as the navigation objective. Method Hierarchical Formulation with a Learned Transition sec:formulation Task. In VLN-CE an agent must follow a natural-language instruction to its goal in an unseen 3D environment. At each step it observes a panoramic RGB-D image of 12 egocentric views and its odometry, and issues one primitive action: move forward by \,m, turn left or right by \, or stop. It succeeds if it stops within 3\,m of the goal, typically after hundreds of primitives. Hierarchy. Following~ ye2026revisiting , we cast the task as a hierarchical MDP. A waypoint predictor~ hong2022bridging predicts navigable waypoints around the agent, and the predicted waypoints are accumulated online into a topological graph ~ an2024etpnav . At macro step the planner acts on the macro state ; its macro action commits the agent to one of the predicted waypoints or to STOP, and an executor realizes it with primitive actions before the graph is updated. The macro transition is thus determined by the environment together with the executor. In~ ye2026revisiting the executor is a fixed heuristic, so this transition is fixed and only the planner learns. MATCH learns both levels jointly as a hierarchical RL agent, so the transition itself changes during training, and the planner is adapted to this in three ways: it observes the executor's expected performance before committing to a target and the actual outcome afterwards, it can adjust the target within the neighborhood it has evaluated (Sec.~ sec:graph ), and its reward is designed to account for both task progress and execution residual. (Sec.~ sec:reward ). Workflow (Fig.~ fig:overview ). At each macro step, the planner scores every active edge from a visited node to a frontier , together with STOP, and samples an edge and a continuous offset ; together they define a 2D target near the location the edge points to. If the agent does not stand at , it first returns there by replaying the primitive sequences stored on the tree edges along the path; this needs no policy, so the executor is responsible only for reaching new targets. The executor then drives toward until it declares REACHED or exhausts its decision budget (TIMEOUT). Wherever it stops, a new visited node is created, the executed edge stores the outcome, waypoints predicted from the new node extend the graph, and every new edge is annotated with the executor's value estimates for targets around it. Goal-Conditioned Executor sec:executor Interface. The executor receives no language; a sub-task is specified only by a 2D target relative to the start node. The executor acts in decisions, each of which expands to several primitives. title: Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI: Mechanisms, Evidence, and Evaluation
summary: Embodied systems can update policies, world models, skills, and executable programs from deployment experience, allowing one interaction to benefit later tasks. When a system also revises and reuses its data-acquisition, feedback, or learning procedures, experience changes the process that produces capability, introducing recursive self-improvement. This paper surveys research in physical AI through the connection between persistent capability and its improvement process. We first explain the functional distinction between learner updates and improvers, then compare policy learning, imagined experience, memory and skill accumulation, and executable harnesses. These approaches connect to revisions of curricula, rewards, and research programs in different ways. Contact validity, recovery, retention, and resource costs determine whether the resulting gains accumulate during continued deployment. An L0-L3 rubric distinguishes task-local adaptation, persistent capability gain, inherited process revision, and verified improver gain. Representative benchmarks and within-study contrasts relate these distinctions to existing results. We further propose common-data and interactive comparisons that evaluate reference and revised improvers from shared learner starts, separating the use of experience from its acquisition. This perspective connects the diverse methods, physical operating conditions, and evaluation evidence, underpinning embodied RSI. A comprehensive list of studies in this survey is available at https://github.com/nkd-lkz/physical-ai-rsi-survey.

Introduction sec:intro Robots encounter new objects, contact conditions, and task combinations after deployment. A failed attempt exposes a capability gap and can also supply experience for the next improvement. Failed grasps can inform policy updates, human corrections can become reusable skills, and recurring failures can guide further practice. Self-improvement methods incorporate this experience into continued learning so that later tasks benefit from earlier interaction. RoboCat and RECAP use robot experience to update policies, while Learning While Deploying extends the reuse of deployment experience across robot fleets. W005,W003,W004 As foundation models generate programs, interpret failures, and organize experiments, the editable parts of a robot system extend beyond its action policy to the learning process. ASPIRE and SHAPER retain changes to skills and harnesses, while ENPIRE exposes policy-development programs to agent-generated revision. This enables a further form of self-improvement: experience changes data selection, feedback construction, or training code, and the revised process produces the next update. We use mechanistic recursive self-improvement (RSI) for such system-generated process revisions that are retained and used in subsequent learning. Experience thereby changes how the system acquires new capabilities. W027,W029,W028 Current work approaches self-improvement through policy training, world models, skill libraries, harnesses, and automated experimentation. The same terminology often refers to changes at different levels. Continued practice can improve a policy, revised reward code can change its learning objective, and a more effective experimental procedure can improve subsequent learning efficiency. Connecting these approaches requires distinguishing changes in capability, changes in the learning process, and the additional gains produced by those process changes. Embodied systems must also obtain valid feedback, recover from failures, and retain existing capabilities within limited robot time and human assistance. With robot learning and deployment as the main setting, this paper connects two strands of self-improvement in physical AI: how experience becomes persistent capability, and how it changes the process that produces capability. The first covers policies and values, world models, memory and skills, and executable harnesses. The second concerns revisions to experience acquisition, feedback construction, and learning procedures. Figure~ fig:concept summarizes their relationship. The L0--L3 evidence rubric connects advances in these mechanisms to the gains established by their evaluations. This paper makes four contributions: Conceptual distinctions and evidence criteria. We distinguish task-local adaptation, persistent capability gain, inherited process revision, and verified improver gain. The L0--L3 rubric connects these claims to observable evidence for a specific system configuration and protocol. A synthesis of persistent and recursive mechanisms. We organize methods by what experience changes, what is retained, and how the retained change influences subsequent learning. This functional analysis links updates to the learner with revisions to data acquisition, feedback, learning procedures, and update control. Physical conditions and controlled evaluation. We connect contact validity, recovery, retention, and resource use to the interpretation of improvement. Common-data and interactive comparisons distinguish the use of experience from its acquisition when assessing reference and revised improvers. Evidence-based research priorities. We derive directions for grounded feedback, lasting gains, reliable recovery, and efficient improvement from the gaps between implemented mechanisms and demonstrated benefits. Related surveys provide complementary perspectives on self-evolving agents, embodied learning, and world--action models. W093,W100,W105 Embodied self-evolution has been organized around memory, tasks, world models, embodiment, and model design, including changes to optimization and evaluation procedures. W095 Code-based robot-learning surveys distinguish execution feedback, persistent memory, and program search, W096 while continual-learning research develops retention and transfer metrics alongside practical robotics constraints. lesort2020continual Recent humanoid surveys connect post-deployment mechanisms and meta-updates to safety constraints and lifetime trajectory evaluation. REC_HumanoidSelfEvo2026 General RSI surveys also cover embodied applications and controlled comparisons of original and revised improvement mechanisms under matched budgets. W092 These surveys establish the components of self-evolution. This paper connects the technical approaches through the relationship between experience, retained artifacts, and subsequent learning: how policies, models, skills, and code acquire persistent value, and when those same components participate in revising the improvement process. Decision-centered world-model evaluation similarly relates component quality to its effects on planning and policy optimization. Table~ tab:related-surveys summarizes the related perspectives. This mechanism analysis provides the basis for the evidence rubric and physical evaluation conditions developed here. REC_WorldEvalPosition2026 The remainder of the review follows this progression. Section II establishes the conceptual framework and evidence criteria. Sections III and IV examine persistent capability updates and inherited revisions to the improvement process, respectively. Section V analyzes the physical conditions for sustained improvement, and Section VI synthesizes the evidence and evaluation protocols. Section VII develops research directions from the resulting gaps, and Section VIII concludes. Foundations and Conceptual Framework sec:foundations Better performance after interaction can arise from adaptation within the current episode, capability retained across tasks, or changes to the learning process itself. We distinguish these cases through the object of change, its retention boundary, and its later use. The functional distinction between learner and improver explains the mechanism; capability gain, mechanistic recursion, and improver gain identify the empirical claims; and the L0--L3 rubric connects those claims to observable evidence requirements. These distinctions also help interpret the convergence of several research traditions, providing a common basis for comparing their approaches. Updating its grasping policy from failed trajectories changes its retained action capability. A world model can plan actions for the robot or generate experience for its training procedure. The former supports task execution directly; the latter participates in capability acquisition. An executable skill can likewise encode a grasp or an experimental schedule. Weights, memory, and code therefore do not correspond to fixed evidence levels.
