title: BudSplat: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting under a Rendering Budget
summary: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting has recently emerged as a promising alternative to per-scene optimization, enabling fast novel view synthesis by predicting Gaussian primitives directly from input images. However, it quickly faces a bottleneck of rendering efficiency while scaling from sparse to dense multi-view inputs, which offer more geometric constraints but produce a rapidly growing set of candidate Gaussians. Existing solutions cannot reliably distinguish redundant primitives, leading to many redundant primitives from repeatedly observed regions and increased rendering cost without much gain in visual quality. We propose BudSplat, a compact feed-forward 3DGS framework that learns to keep the most valuable Gaussians under a limited primitive count. BudSplat has two novel designs. The first is a detail-aware importance score that is extracted from multi-level visual tokens, providing an explicit cue for regions where pruning is likely to harm perceptual quality. The score can be injected into voxel fusion to preserve high-value local contributors during multi-view aggregation. The second is quality-aware Gaussian pruning that selects a compact set of primitives by jointly considering rendering contribution and detail importance. The quality-aware pruning enables local quota redistribution that helps avoid over-allocating primitives to large redundant regions. Experiments on RE10K, DL3DV, and ACID show that BudSplat achieves a favorable trade-off among rendering quality and efficiency.
full_text: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting has recently emerged as a promising alternative to per-scene optimization, enabling fast novel view synthesis by predicting Gaussian primitives directly from input images. However, it quickly faces a bottleneck of rendering efficiency while scaling from sparse to dense multi-view inputs, which offer more geometric constraints but produce a rapidly growing set of candidate Gaussians. Existing solutions cannot reliably distinguish redundant primitives, leading to many redundant primitives from repeatedly observed regions and increased rendering cost without much gain in visual quality. We propose BudSplat, a compact feed-forward 3DGS framework that learns to keep the most valuable Gaussians under a limited primitive count. BudSplat has two novel designs. The first is a detail-aware importance score that is extracted from multi-level visual tokens, providing an explicit cue for regions where pruning is likely to harm perceptual quality. The score can be injected into voxel fusion to preserve high-value local contributors during multi-view aggregation. The second is quality-aware Gaussian pruning that selects a compact set of primitives by jointly considering rendering contribution and detail importance. The quality-aware pruning enables local quota redistribution that helps avoid over-allocating primitives to large redundant regions. Experiments on RE10K, DL3DV, and ACID show that BudSplat achieves a favorable trade-off among rendering quality and efficiency. Introduction Novel view synthesis aims to recover a scene representation from a set of input images and render photorealistic images from unseen viewpoints. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has become a highly effective representation for this task due to its explicit Gaussian primitives and efficient splatting-based renderer, offering an attractive balance between reconstruction quality and rendering speed~ kerbl20233d . However, 3DGS relies heavily on per-scene optimization that necessitates a separate reconstruction and optimization process for each new scene, limiting its applicability to large-scale data processing, interactive applications, and practical deployment. Feed-forward 3DGS, which predicts Gaussian primitives directly from input images in a single network pass, has recently been investigated to amortize the cost of per-scene optimization. Different feed-forward designs have been explored, including pixel-aligned Gaussian prediction, cost-volume-based geometry reasoning, transformer-based large reconstruction models, voxel-aligned prediction, graph-based Gaussian aggregation, and unposed feed-forward reconstruction~ charatan2024pixelsplat,chen2024mvsplat,zhang2024gs,ziwen2025long,wang2025volsplat,zhang2024gaussian,jiang2025anysplat . More general feed-forward world models also begin to support 3D Gaussians as one of their output representations~ liu2025worldmirror . Along the above development, feed-forward 3DGS has also been moving from sparse and constrained inputs toward larger numbers of views, broader scene coverage, and weaker assumptions on camera poses. This trend exposes an underexplored bottleneck – as the number of input views increases, the main challenge gradually shifts from reconstruction ambiguity to rendering efficiency. Denser input views provide stronger geometric constraints and better scene coverage, but these benefits come at a cost of a much larger number of candidate primitives. Typical feed-forward pipelines generate Gaussians densely from pixels, image tokens, or volumetric features, and then suppress the generated Gaussians via voxelization, pooling, or other aggregation mechanisms. Although the suppression removes some redundant primitives, the final Gaussian set can still grow rapidly with the increase of input views. Since the cost of splatting is closely related to the number of visible Gaussians, such growth increases rendering pressure and weakens one of the key advantages of 3DGS as an explicit representation. A straightforward solution is to prune the predicted Gaussians, but simple pruning based on opacity or confidence is suboptimal as different Gaussians carry different rendering values. In multi-view reconstruction, regions that are observed many times often have high confidence, but they tend to produce highly redundant Gaussian primitives. In contrast, thin structures, occlusion boundaries, and high-frequency textures usually occupy only a small spatial extent, yet their reconstruction strongly affects perceptual quality of rendered images. If pruning is simply driven by opacity, confidence, or a global top- rule, the retained Gaussian set can be easily dominated by large, stable, and visually simple regions while those fine but important details are either averaged out during fusion or removed during pruning. This suggests that compact feed-forward 3DGS requires not only fewer Gaussians, but also reliable criteria for deciding which Gaussians are worth keeping. We address this issue from the perspective of rendering-budget-constrained representation learning. Instead of retaining as many predicted primitives as possible, the model should preserve the subset of Gaussians that contributes most to rendering quality under a bounded primitive count. To this end, we introduce BudSplat, a compact feed-forward 3DGS framework that propagates detail-aware importance through Gaussian generation, fusion, and pruning. BudSplat positions compactness as one part of feed-forward prediction rather than a separate post-processing step. It identifies local regions where Gaussian removal is likely to hurt perceptual quality, such as boundaries, thin geometry, and high-frequency texture. This enables importance-preserving voxel fusion that prevents valuable local contributors from being diluted by redundant observations in smooth regions, as well as quality-aware Gaussian pruning that allows selecting a compact set of primitives for rendering. On top of that, BudSplat introduces a local quota redistribution strategy that further prevents large smooth regions from monopolizing the retained primitives, ensuring sufficient representation of detail-rich regions even under a small Gaussian budget. Hence, BudSplat redefines the role of pruning in feed-forward 3DGS: pruning is not generic Gaussian reduction after dense generation but a learned allocation mechanism that decides where the limited rendered primitives should be spent. It strikes a good balance among visual fidelity, representation compactness, and rendering efficiency as the number of input views increases. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: We identify the primitive growth problem in feed-forward 3DGS and study Gaussian prediction from the perspective of rendering-budget-constrained representation learning. We propose a detail-aware compact 3DGS framework that integrates residual token-based importance estimation, importance-preserving voxel fusion, and quality-aware Gaussian pruning with local quota redistribution, enabling the model to retain primitives that are more valuable for rendering. Experiments on RealEstate10K, DL3DV, and ACID demonstrate that our method achieves a better trade-off between visual fidelity and rendering efficiency under challenging low-overlap evaluation settings. Related Work Feed-forward and generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) represents scenes with explicit anisotropic Gaussian primitives and enables efficient differentiable rendering, but it still requires per-scene optimization~ kerbl20233d . Feed-forward 3DGS amortizes this cost by predicting Gaussians directly from input images. Early methods such as pixelSplat and MVSplat generate pixel-aligned Gaussians from sparse posed views, with MVSplat further using cost-volume reasoning~ charatan2024pixelsplat,chen2024mvsplat . Later works improve geometry, hierarchy, or alignment with depth priors, hierarchical Gaussians, and voxel-aligned prediction~ xu2025depthsplat,liu2025monosplat,tang2024hisplat,wang2025volsplat . Other methods scale the paradigm through transformer-based reconstruction, long-sequence modeling, iterative refinement, whole-scene reconstruction, or unposed inputs~ zhang2024gs,ziwen2025long,kang2025ilrm,wang2024freesplat,wang2025freesplat++,ye2024no,xu2025freesplatter,jiang2025anysplat . WorldMirror further studies general feed-forward world reconstruction with 3D Gaussian outputs~ liu2025worldmirror . Despite these advances, most methods still rely on dense per-view, pixel-aligned, or voxel-aligned primitive prediction, leaving the growth of rendered Gaussians under large-view inputs insufficiently addressed. Compactness, fusion, and redundancy reduction. Many works compress optimized 3DGS scenes after reconstruction by pruning low-significance Gaussians, learning masks, reducing per-point storage, modeling inter-primitive redundancy, or combining pruning with quantization and distillation~ fan2024lightgaussian,girish2024eagles,lee2024compact,liu2024compgs,ali2024trimming . These methods demonstrate substantial redundancy in 3DGS, but mainly operate as post-reconstruction compression. In feed-forward 3DGS, FreeSplat, FreeSplat++, GGN, MuSASplat, and AnySplat reduce multi-view redundancy through feature fusion, Gaussian pooling, or differentiable voxelization~ wang2024freesplat,wang2025freesplat++,zhang2024gaussian,xu2026musasplat,jiang2025anysplat . These approaches reduce duplicated observations or improve cross-view aggregation, but they are not formulated as rendering-budget allocation methods and do not explicitly preserve local perceptual details during fusion. Our method differs from the two kinds above by treating compactness as rendering-budget allocation during feed-forward prediction, unifying detail-aware token importance, importance-preserving voxel fusion, and Gaussian-level pruning. Method Given a set of multi-view input images, our goal is to predict a compact 3D Gaussian representation that can be rendered efficiently while preserving feed-forward reconstruction quality. We build on an AnySplat-style pipeline, where a visual geometry backbone predicts dense 3D points and image-aligned features, and these dense candidates are fused into Gaussian primitives for rendering. This design is effective for unconstrained reconstruction, but becomes less scalable as the number of input views increases. More views provide stronger geometric constraints, yet also generate many redundant candidates from repeatedly observed smooth regions. In contrast, visually important regions such as thin structures, occlusion boundaries, and high-frequency textures often occupy only a small fraction of the scene. Our method makes primitive generation and pruning aware of rendering value. We first estimate patch-level detail importance from multi-layer VGGT tokens, then preserve this signal during voxel fusion, and finally select a compact Gaussian set according to a quality-aware ranking criterion. The model therefore does not simply keep the most confident primitives, but allocates the retained Gaussians to regions that are more likely to affect novel-view quality. Figure~ fig:pipeline illustrates the overall pipeline. Given multi-view RGB images, the VGGT backbone first predicts dense geometry, confidence cues, and multi-layer visual tokens. The dense geometry and image-aligned features provide an initial pool of Gaussian candidates, while the retained multi-layer tokens are passed to our detail-aware decomposition module. This module reconstructs common low-rank token components with a down-up projection structure, uses the residual as detail cues, and predicts a patch-level detail score with a lightweight detail head. Finally, the fused Gaussians are ranked by a quality-aware pruning criterion that combines opacity, detail importance, and support-based redundancy correction, followed by patch-level quota redistribution. title: What Should a Navigator Remember? Spatiotemporal Memory for Zero-Shot Vision-Language Navigation
summary: Zero-shot vision-and-language navigation (VLN) requires an agent to use past observations without navigation-specific training. We study what information an 8B-scale navigation system should retain and how it should be organized for subsequent decisions. Our agent combines instruction progress, hierarchically compressed observation history anchored to poses, and accumulated geometry in complementary task, temporal, and spatial memories. An 8B observer summarizes observations, and an 8B reasoner uses the memories to select waypoint intents or request additional views, a geometric controller executes the selected targets. A semantic information perspective motivates the distinction between retaining evidence, making it accessible to the reasoner, and acquiring further observations. On R2R-CE val-unseen, the complete system achieves the highest among the evaluated Qwen3-based zero-shot baselines. Removing temporal memory reduces SR and sharply increases average path length from 16.9 to 39.1m, removing the spatial-map and planning component reduces SR as well. Real-world experiments on a Unitree Go2 show that our zero-shot method achieves higher success rates than the post-trained baseline in both corridor and office environments, suggesting better transfer to the evaluated real-world settings. As a complementary evaluation, LAW2 uses paired instruction interventions to examine behavioral responses, instruction following ability beyond endpoint success. These results support preserving task progress, observation history, and geometry in structured memory for zero-shot navigation with smaller open models.

An 8B observer summarizes observations, and an 8B reasoner uses the memories to select waypoint intents or request additional views, a geometric controller executes the selected targets. On R2R-CE val-unseen, the complete system achieves the highest among the evaluated Qwen3-based zero-shot baselines. Removing temporal memory reduces SR and sharply increases average path length from 16.9 to 39.1\,m, removing the spatial-map and planning component reduces SR as well. Real-world experiments on a Unitree Go2 show that our zero-shot method achieves higher success rates than the post-trained baseline in both corridor and office environments, suggesting better transfer to the evaluated real-world settings. As a complementary evaluation, LAW2 uses paired instruction interventions to examine behavioral responses, instruction following ability beyond endpoint success. These results support preserving task progress, observation history, and geometry in structured memory for zero-shot navigation with smaller open models. Introduction Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) requires an embodied agent to follow a natural-language instruction through a previously unseen environment, providing a foundation for higher-level tasks such as object manipulation and human--robot interaction. Post-training methods~ guo2026awarevln, wei2026ground, wang2026lightnav fine-tune vision-language models on navigation trajectories and achieve strong success rates on R2R-CE~ krantz_vlnce_2020 . Zero-shot methods~ chen2025constraint, shi2025smartway, yuan2025opennav, li2026bridging instead reuse pretrained models without navigation-specific training. Despite their different training requirements and inference resources, both approaches must integrate visual observations, instruction progress, and execution history to make reliable navigation decisions. A central question is how navigation history should be represented for smaller open models. In our reproduced HSGM configuration~ li2026bridging , replacing GPT-5 with Qwen3-VL-8B reduces SR from 0.463 to 0.049 on R2R-CE val-unseen (Table~ tab:r2r_val_unseen ). This comparison motivates examining the demands placed on the navigation backbone. We focus on memory representation: the reasoner must connect current observations with instruction progress and earlier evidence, often across many actions. Our design preserves three complementary kinds of information: what the instruction requires and which subgoal is active, what the agent has observed and executed, and what geometry it has explored. We organize these as task memory, temporal memory with hierarchical summaries anchored to poses, and spatial memory containing an occupancy map and a committed target. The semantic communication perspective of~ lastras2026fundamental motivates retaining evidence useful for task-relevant judgments and organizing it for a computationally bounded receiver. In navigation, these judgments include whether a subgoal is complete and where to move next. We use this perspective as a design rationale. An 8B observer constructs observational summaries, while a Qwen3-VL-8B reasoner combines them with the instruction and spatial memory. Waypoint intents connect these decisions to geometric control, and a PREVIEW action allows the agent to acquire additional views. We evaluate this memory design through navigation results, component ablations, and deployment on a Unitree Go2 to experiment real world performance. We also introduce LAW2 as a complementary diagnostic benchmark: paired direction reversals, route-information removal, and paraphrases reveal how behavior responds to instruction changes with the same meaning. Our contributions are as follows. We propose a spatiotemporal memory representation for zero-shot VLN that combines instruction progress, pose-anchored observation history, and accumulated geometry. We evaluate the representation in a navigation system with an 8B observer and an 8B reasoner. Component ablations characterize the effects of temporal memory, spatial memory and active previewing with planning, an integration with CA-Nav and real-world deployment provide additional evidence of utility. We introduce LAW2 to complement navigation metrics with paired tests of directional responsiveness, dependence on route information, and sensitivity to paraphrasing. Related Work Vision-and-Language Navigation R2R~ anderson2018vision studies navigation from natural-language instructions on a discrete graph, while R2R-CE~ krantz_vlnce_2020 extends the task to continuous environments with low-level actions. REVERIE~ qi2020reverie additionally requires identifying an object referred to by the instruction. These settings require agents to connect language with visual observations and spatial decisions. Spatial representations are a central part of VLN systems. ETPNav~ an2024etpnav uses online topological mapping and obstacle-aware planning, while BEVBERT~ an2022bevbert combines global topological and local metric representations. Post-training approaches~ guo2026awarevln,wei2026ground,wang2026lightnav adapt pretrained models using navigation data. Our work studies how observation history and geometry can support navigation when the observer and reasoner are used without navigation-specific training. Agentic Navigation and Memory Agentic VLN systems combine language or vision-language models with perception, planning, and execution modules~ xin2026agentvln,huang2026sedualvln,huang2026aerr,li2026agenticnav . FreeAskWorld~ peng2026freeaskworld extends evaluation to dynamic environments and proactive tasks which needs robot to search more information when lack of task-relevant information. These settings motivate retaining information across successive decisions. Existing systems use different representations and interfaces for navigation. CA-Nav~ chen2025constraint uses a value map to score locations by their relevance to the instruction, and BSC-Nav~ ruan2026brain explores brain-inspired spatial memory. We evaluate our approach alongside zero-shot systems including SmartWay, Open-Nav, and HSGM~ shi2025smartway,yuan2025opennav,li2026bridging . Our focus is the organization of complementary evidence: task progress, compressed observation history tied to poses, and accumulated geometry. The experiments assess this representation within a complete navigation system. Spatial and Temporal Memory for Navigation Memory representations for VLN organize both observation history and spatial structure. HAMT~ chen2021history hierarchically encodes panoramic observations and their temporal relationships for multimodal action prediction. GridMM~ wang2023gridmm projects historical observations into a unified spatial grid and aggregates visual evidence according to instruction relevance. These approaches establish the importance of structured history and spatially organized evidence. Our work examines how such information can be represented explicitly for pretrained observers and reasoners used without navigation-specific training. Recent VLM-based navigation systems further explore explicit memory representations. MapNav~ zhang2025mapnav uses annotated semantic maps in place of historical frames, while HSGM~ li2026bridging organizes geometric, semantic, and decision information to support subtask reasoning and waypoint planning. HAM-VLN~ liu2026ham maintains a grounded world graph with decision-coupled semantic and reflective records, combining a recent-history window with subgoal-conditioned retrieval. These methods demonstrate that map construction, task progress, and selective history access are already important elements of navigation memory. Our design emphasizes the complementary roles of temporal records and accumulated geometry for an 8B-scale reasoner. Methodology Problem Formulation sec:problem_formulation We consider vision-and-language navigation in a partially observable environment. An agent receives a natural-language instruction at the beginning of an episode and subsequently acquires observations while executing actions. We model the interaction as a POMDP~ kaelbling1998planning , whose state includes the environment layout and the agent's physical configuration. The agent does not observe the complete state; instead, it receives observations , comprising an RGB image, depth, and a measured or estimated pose. The environment evolves according to where and are the transition and observation models. The executed action belongs to The agent maintains an internal memory that integrates the instruction with its interaction history: Here, is an internal memory representation, not necessarily an exact Bayesian belief state, and denotes the complete decision-and-control policy. The instruction is supplied once, but its retained representation remains available throughout navigation. Let denote the task requirements associated with . Successful execution requires the resulting trajectory to satisfy . Standard benchmark SR evaluates the narrower condition of stopping within a prescribed distance of the goal and does not by itself establish compliance with all route instructions. We therefore evaluate navigation performance together with instruction responsiveness. Appendix~ app:semantic_information_theory_of_embodied_ai develops the general receiver-based perspective underlying this formulation, distinguishing available information, realized computation, and task achievement through environment interaction. Design Rationale sec:design_rationale Our memory design is motivated by the semantic information perspective of lastras2026fundamental , which studies communication that enables a receiver to derive required conclusions using its existing knowledge. For navigation, this motivates retaining evidence that supports task-relevant judgments rather than reproducing the entire observation stream. We adopt this perspective as a design rationale, without transferring its communication bounds directly to memory cost or navigation performance. We distinguish evidence availability from its effective use. A navigation decision may fail because the necessary evidence has not been observed, because it was discarded during memory compression, or because the reasoner cannot reliably interpret and combine the retained information. These possibilities motivate complementary mechanisms: acquiring additional observations, retaining relevant history, and organizing that history into accessible representations. The agent is not assumed to identify these failure sources perfectly. We instantiate this rationale through task, temporal, and spatial memory. Task memory retains the instruction and its execution stage; temporal memory organizes past observations and measured motion; spatial memory accumulates geometric evidence for navigation. Hierarchical summarization and pose anchoring organize historical information for the reasoner, while a preview mechanism allows the agent to request additional views. These mechanisms support memory-conditioned decisions without guaranteeing evidence sufficiency or correct reasoning. Appendix~ sec:semantic_information formalizes the distinction between semantic sufficiency and realized computation. title: SSQA: Sibling-Selective Quadtree Attention for Hierarchical Modeling in Perception Tasks
comment: 8 pages, 6 figures, 4 tables. Published at ICRA 2026 (oral)
summary: Perception tasks for navigation in robotics, including aerial platforms such as drones and autonomous driving systems, are inherently structured. Drone-mounted cameras typically capture sky above, terrain below, and obstacles or man-made structures in between, while driving data often contains organized road layouts, lane markings, and surrounding agents. Motivated by these axis-aligned structural priors, we note that such information is typically more structured than in generic image tasks. We hypothesize that processing information in a quadtree-esque manner can not only model features effectively in a hierarchical manner, but also offers an efficient linear-time alternative to vanilla attention mechanisms, which run in quadratic time. In this paper, we propose Sibling-Selective Quadtree Attention (SSQA), which models image tokens hierarchically as a structured, full quadtree. We show analytical complexity analysis that guarantees linear-time feature modeling, in addition to empirical experiments comparing inference speeds with other popular modeling approaches, such as Mamba 2 and Quadtree Attention. Our results, benchmarked across several tasks, show that we achieve results at least as good, if not notably better, as others at a fraction of the computational costs.
full_text: Perception tasks for navigation in robotics, including aerial platforms such as drones and autonomous driving systems, are inherently structured. Drone-mounted cameras typically capture sky above, terrain below, and obstacles or man-made structures in between, while driving data often contains organized road layouts, lane markings, and surrounding agents. Motivated by these axis-aligned structural priors, we note that such information is typically more structured than in generic image tasks. We hypothesize that processing information in a quadtree-esque manner can not only model features effectively in a hierarchical manner, but also offers an efficient linear-time alternative to vanilla attention mechanisms, which run in quadratic time. In this paper, we propose Sibling-Selective Quadtree Attention (SSQA), which models image tokens hierarchically as a structured, full quadtree. We show analytical complexity analysis that guarantees linear-time feature modeling, in addition to empirical experiments comparing inference speeds with other popular modeling approaches, such as Mamba 2 and Quadtree Attention. Our results, benchmarked across several tasks, show that we achieve results at least as good, if not notably better, as others at a fraction of the computational costs. Introduction Perception tasks in computer vision face numerous sources of noise during deployment in autonomous driving and robotics under adverse weather, low-light conditions, and frequent occlusions. While state-of-the-art perception and end-to-end models perform well in the most common, normal settings, given large datasets and a high number of parameters, the capability of such systems to scale to unseen domains remains a challenge -- both in compute feasibility and in performance. Motivated by the challenge of scaling deep learning for autonomous perception, we observe that camera and remote sensing data from aerial navigation is typically more structured than generic image tasks. For example, as in a remote sensing dataset, aerial imagery often contains sky regions near the top, terrain near the bottom, and man-made structures or vegetation in between. This inherent structure can be leveraged during training as a prior to improve convergence and generalization, particularly for drone perception and navigation. Currently, state-of-the-art perception models apply variations of hierarchical attention to encode information at both low and high granularity levels~ liu2021swin,xie2021segformer . Specifically, alternatives such as Linear Transformers~ katharopoulos_et_al_2020_linear_transformers and Mamba~ mamba, mamba2 have been investigated as efficient linear alternatives to the vanilla Transformer. However, such approaches often trade modeling capacity for efficiency, and may not yield practical speedups without specialized optimization. In this paper, we propose a compute efficient, performance-preserving attention mechanism based on quadtree organization of information density within the scene, inspired by the structured nature of navigation and remote sensing data. The key difference that distinguishes our work from previous efforts in efficient transformer alternatives is the observation that optimizations in efficiency stem from priors. Our hypothesis is that some pairwise token comparisons are more useful than others, and that most task features are axis-aligned and can thus be processed hierarchically as a structured tree. In aerial robotics, perception emphasizes large-scale scene understanding, where drone-mounted cameras typically capture sky regions above, terrain below, and obstacles or man-made structures in between. In autonomous driving, systems must interpret and combine structured cues such as road layout, lane markings and surrounding moving agents to ensure safe operation. Our Sibling-Selective Quadtree Attention (SSQA) is designed to exploit this kind of inherent spatial organization, enabling efficient and robust representation learning across diverse tasks. By organizing objects or regions into a hierarchical quadtree structure, we can model an approximate priority based on spatial relevance. For instance, in aerial robotics we may wish to emphasize nearby terrain features or potential obstacles, or specific segmentation fields over the others for navigation. Similarly, in autonomous driving, closer agents such as pedestrians or vehicles demand more attention than those further away. Conveniently, quadtrees also split an image into a hierarchy of patches, which can be modeled as tokens in image transformers, making this representation well-suited for efficient perception in robotics. To formalize this idea, we propose a hierarchical attention mechanism for autonomous perception called the Sibling-Selective Quadtree Attention (SSQA). Intuitively, we organize tokens into a quadtree hierarchy, where each parent cell aggregates information from its children. Within each sibling group, A lightweight saliency-based Top- filtering adaptively selects the most informative sibling interactions. This design provides a principled form of structured sparsity: attention cost grows nearly linearly , while interpretability is retained through explicit hierarchical grouping. Crucially, global receptive fields are preserved via communication between parent agents across levels, making the model both efficient and expressive. In summary, the key contributions of this work include: We propose Sibling-Selective Quadtree Attention (SSQA), a hierarchical attention mechanism with constant-size sibling interactions and bottom--up aggregation ( sec:method ). We introduce Cross-Injection Fusion, a gated residual mechanism that injects parent evidence back to children, preserving suppressed information ( sec:pairwise ). We extend SSQA with plug-in guidance: (i) Agent-Based SSQA (Image Field) using detector/box-driven dynamic sparsity ( sec:agent_image ), and (ii) Agent-Based SSQA (Signal Field) using Fourier-based refinement that focuses computation in high-frequency regions ( sec:fourier ). We integrate SSQA into a state-of-the-art end-to-end driving model (TransFuser chitta2022transfuser ) and achieve the highest average score on the CARLA benchmark across 14 scenarios against baseline and the other top down quadtree. Related Efficient Attention in Vision Transformers The original Vision Transformer (ViT) showed that images can be tokenized into a fixed size patch grid and processed with global self-attention where each patch attends to one another, but the quadratic cost makes high-resolution tasks expensive~ dosovitskiy2020vit . DeiT~ touvron2021deit reduced data and compute via distillation and training strategies rather than architectural changes. Hierarchical backbones such as PVT~ wang2021pvt and Swin~ liu2021swin control cost via pyramids and shifted windows. For dense prediction, DPT couples a ViT backbone with multi-scale decoding to recover detail~ ranftl2021dpt . Approximate, Sparse Attention Another line of work accelerates attention by either modifying the similarity kernel (the function that scores query–key pairs) or by imposing a sparsity pattern that limits which token pairs can interact, yielding near-linear scaling with the number of tokens. Linformer uses low-rank projections~ wang2020linformer ; Performer kernelizes softmax via random features~ choromanski2020performer ; Reformer uses ``locality sensitive hashing'' (LSH) to restrict matches~ kitaev2020reformer . Longformer and BigBird impose sliding-window and global tokens with theoretical guarantees~ beltagy2020longformer,zaheer2020bigbird ; Sparse Transformers pioneered fixed strided patterns~ child2019sparse . FNet replaces attention with Fourier mixing~ lee2021fnet . These approximations trade some fidelity or flexibility for speed, which are effective for classification and dense tasks, but they may under-utilize fine spatial structures. In our work, we seek to maintain or even improve performance while optimizing modeling efficiency. Token Pruning and Merging A complementary strategy reduces the token count itself. DynamicViT prunes redundant tokens progressively and dynamically based on the input~ rao2021dynamicvit ; EViT reorganizes tokens to emphasize salient regions~ liang2022evit ; TokenLearner learns a small, content-adaptive set of tokens~ ryoo2021tokenlearner ; ToMe merges similar tokens on-the-fly~ bolya2023tome ; ATS performs content-aware sampling~ yang2022ats . These strategies reduce computations, yet still rely on global or windowed mixing among tokens. Quadtree and Hierarchical Data Structures Classical quadtrees recursively decompose space into quadrants based on informative regions~ samet1984quadtree . Quadtree Attention brings this idea into transformers by building token pyramids and restricting fine-level attention to regions selected at coarser levels, moving complexity from quadratic to linear, while retaining salient context~ tang2022quadtree . Our work follows this hierarchical principle, but differs in how selection and aggregation are organized, to be described in ~ sec:method . In short, Quadtree Attention~ tang2022quadtree processes tokens in a top-down manner, where only top- salient patches are further subdivided into smaller resolutions. As a result, depending on the hyperparameter, it is possible that sparser details may be neglected with this top-down approach. Our model addresses this by proposing an alternative bottom-up gating approach with quadtrees with soft weighting, ensuring that all features have opportunity to be represented, even those with smaller pixel area. A visualization of this comparison can be found in Figure~ fig:quadtree_diagram . Structure-Guided Attention and Matching Task-driven evidence supports geometry-aware interaction constraints. SuperGlue attends over sparse keypoints with a graph-matching head~ sarlin2020superglue , while LoFTR achieves dense, detector-free correspondence by combining global context and local refinement~ sun2021loftr . These show that imposing structure on interactions can improve accuracy and efficiency, motivating our sibling-group attention and bottom-up fusion. Positioning and Differences from Prior Work Relative to windowed/backbone hierarchies~ liu2021swin,wang2021pvt and approximate/sparse kernels~ wang2020linformer,choromanski2020performer,kitaev2020reformer,beltagy2020longformer,zaheer2020bigbird,child2019sparse,lee2021fnet , our approach organizes attention within quadtree sibling groups, where a lightweight saliency score weights the aggregation of children tokens in constant-size groups. Through aggregation of children token features, we form a compact parent token representation, which is then fused back to all siblings (bidirectional information exchange), before passing parent features upward to the next parent level. Unlike Quadtree Attention~ tang2022quadtree , which ranks across larger regions and goes deeper down into the trees, our selection is strictly local (per-sibling group) from a pre-constructed, and normally smaller tree depth compared to theirs, but with constant interaction size; our bottom-up bank and temperature-gated global fusion aggregate information across levels. With fixed sibling size, depth, and , the number of interactions per level is constant, so the overall cost scales linearly with the number of patches. Methodology sec:method We present together with a module, where “agents” correspond to objects in the scene. SSQA works on its own, and can also consume agentness signals in two complementary forms: (i) Agent-Based SSQA (Image Field) using detector cues such as bounding boxes or SAM-derived heatmaps, and (ii) Agent-Based SSQA (Signal Field) using Fourier saliency maps obtained from FFT-based high-pass filtering. title: SaiVLA-JEPA: Evaluating Future Latent Prediction in JEPA-Conditioned VLA Control
summary: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn to predict representations rather than pixels, offering a compact way to model how visual scenes evolve. We ask whether this predictive objective improves closed-loop control when a vision-language-action (VLA) policy already uses V-JEPA features. We call our JEPA-conditioned flow policy family SaiVLA-JEPA. It combines a vision-language model with a diffusion transformer action expert and receives features from a frozen V-JEPA encoder. Two lightweight auxiliary heads predict future representations during training and are omitted at inference, leaving the action sampler unchanged. We compare policies without JEPA features, with current JEPA conditioning, and with additional future supervision on 10,030 paired LIBERO-Plus episodes. Current JEPA conditioning reaches about 82.5% success versus 71.6% without JEPA, while future supervision provides no detectable aggregate gain at the evaluated training budget. We separately evaluate SaiVLA-JEPA-TCA, which adapts latent context, and SaiVLA-JEPA-TPA, which adapts selected parameters. The context-retry gain is a system-level result under a larger attempt budget; parameter adaptation shows no consistent advantage over the frozen policy and target controls. These results motivate assessing latent-prediction objectives through paired closed-loop rollouts rather than latent loss alone.

We ask whether this predictive objective improves closed-loop control when a vision-language-action (VLA) policy already uses V-JEPA features. We call our JEPA-conditioned flow policy family SaiVLA-JEPA. It combines a vision-language model with a diffusion transformer action expert and receives features from a frozen V-JEPA encoder. Two lightweight auxiliary heads predict future representations during training and are omitted at inference, leaving the action sampler unchanged. We compare policies without JEPA features, with current JEPA conditioning, and with additional future supervision on 10 , 030 paired LIBERO-Plus episodes. Current JEPA conditioning reaches about 82.5 success versus 71.6 without JEPA, while future supervision provides no detectable aggregate gain at the evaluated training budget. We separately evaluate SaiVLA-JEPA-TCA, which adapts latent context, and SaiVLA-JEPA-TPA, which adapts selected parameters. The context-retry gain is a system-level result under a larger attempt budget; parameter adaptation shows no consistent advantage over the frozen policy and target controls. Keywords: JEPA, V-JEPA, vision-language-action, flow matching, future representation prediction, test-time adaptation, LIBERO-Plus. Introduction Vision-language-action policies must preserve semantic information while producing stable, low-latency actions. We consider a VLM-conditioned flow-matching policy in which a frozen V-JEPA encoder supplies an additional visual representation to a DiT action expert bardes2024vjepa,mur2026vjepa21,black2024pi0 . The representation is useful for conditioning, but the action loss alone does not explicitly require the policy trunk to model how the scene representation changes over time. We call the shared JEPA-conditioned flow-matching policy family SaiVLA-JEPA. Within this family, CurrentJEPA denotes the matched current-feature control and FutureJEPA the variant with future-latent supervision. At test time, we study two update levels: SaiVLA-JEPA-TCA performs test-time context adaptation by inferring persistent and transient latent contexts while keeping network weights frozen, whereas SaiVLA-JEPA-TPA performs test-time parameter adaptation by updating a selected subset of network weights. We use TCA and TPA as short names after this definition; the two routes are evaluated separately rather than as consecutive stages. We study a focused intervention: add future latent prediction without changing the action parameterization, the native flow prefix, or the inference-time sampler. Figure~ fig:architecture summarizes the policy and ablation arms. The treatment predicts latents at horizons \(h \ 4,16\ \). CurrentJEPA uses current JEPA conditioning and the flow action objective without future supervision; BaseFlow removes JEPA conditioning. All three policies are trained for 25,000 steps and evaluated on the same benchmark cases. The completed paired comparison finds no detectable aggregate success-rate benefit from future supervision at this training budget. Under the final mixed-cap evaluation, BaseFlow reaches 71.63 overall and 53.12 on LIBERO-10, compared with 81.99 and 73.84 for FutureJEPA. This is a joint contrast because the policies differ in both JEPA conditioning and future supervision. The future-head estimand and its paired statistics are reported below. Hypotheses and estimand. We state the directional hypothesis that future-conditioned training improves episode success relative to current/no-future-head at fixed compute. For paired episodes \(i=1, ,N\), the primary estimand is \( = N^ -1 _i (Y_i^ -Y_i^ )\), where \(Y_i \ 0,1\ \) is the terminal success indicator under shared initial state and rollout noise. A positive point estimate is insufficient on its own: we require a confidence interval and a paired test. Both requirements are met by the primary comparison under the original all-300-step protocol: CurrentJEPA-only succeeds on 730 pairs, FutureJEPA-only succeeds on 733, the estimate is percentage points, the exact McNemar test gives , and the bootstrap 95 interval is approximately points. We interpret this as no detectable aggregate future-head gain in this single training run, not as proof that the true effect is exactly zero. Joint-embedding predictive architectures. JEPA-style methods predict representations rather than pixels, which can suppress nuisance detail while retaining task-relevant structure lecun2022path,assran2023jepa . V-JEPA and subsequent video representation work motivate using a frozen visual encoder as a reusable state abstraction bardes2024vjepa . Our setting differs in that the prediction target is consumed by a VLA policy and is trained jointly with a flow-matching action objective. It complements world-model approaches that learn latent dynamics for planning and control ha2018worldmodels,hafner2023dreamer : our predictor is evaluated as supervision for a frozen-encoder policy, not as a planner. JEPA-WAM couples a V-JEPA-space transition predictor to continuous action generation through a shared predictor lin2026jepawam . We use that line of work as architectural motivation, but report a VLM-conditioned DiT flow policy with an explicit current/no-future-head control; the two settings should not be treated as identical implementations or benchmarks. The closest concurrent work is VLAFlow xia2026vlaflow , a unified flow-matching framework for controlled comparison of VLA pre-training paradigms. Its MindWPI paradigm is directly related to ours: a frozen V-JEPA~2 encoder bardes2025vjepa2 supplies current and future frame latents at a fixed offset, and the action expert is trained to predict the future latent with an MSE objective alongside the action loss. On a heterogeneous 5 , 000-hour pre-training corpus, future latent alignment improves transfer, and its combination with language co-training (MindLWPI) yields the most stable results on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and SimplerEnv li2024simplerenv ---independent evidence that future-latent supervision can benefit VLA control. Our study differs in aim and integration. VLAFlow compares pre-training paradigms under a shared KV-cache DiT expert and a unified 14-dimensional action space, with evaluation after downstream fine-tuning; we isolate a minimal intervention at the policy stage on a single data distribution, with both the VLM and the V-JEPA encoder frozen. Architecturally, their action expert itself produces the future prediction, whereas FutureJEPA attaches two independent residual heads (offsets 4 and 16, tokenwise MSE loss) to the shared trunk while preserving the native flow prefix and masking future queries from noisy action tokens, leaving the inference path unchanged. We use episode-paired comparisons between policies with and without future supervision, rather than comparisons across pre-training data mixtures. Vision-language-action policies. OpenVLA, \( _0\), and related systems combine visual and language features with continuous, diffusion, or flow-based action decoders brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,octo2024,black2024pi0,chi2023diffusion . We retain the native flow action path to isolate the effect of future latent supervision. Representation alignment and physical grounding. Adapter-based transfer and representation alignment are attractive when the visual backbone is frozen nair2022r3m,majumdar2023vc1,karamcheti2023voltron . Our future objective is complementary to physical grounding and to PhyLatent-style invariance or counterfactual losses phylatent2026,psgjepa2026 . Combining these objectives with future prediction remains a direction for future work. Contributions. Our contributions are: We introduce training-only residual heads for future visual representations while retaining a VLM-conditioned DiT flow policy and its inference-time action sampler. We evaluate the incremental effect of future supervision with episode-paired current-feature and no-JEPA controls across the complete LIBERO-Plus benchmark. The future-head contrast is percentage points under the final mixed-cap protocol and points under the original all-300-step protocol, with no detectable aggregate benefit. We study two forms of test-time adaptation: persistent and transient context inferred from executed transitions, and updates to selected model parameters. Paired target controls distinguish lower prediction loss from better closed-loop control. Method Shared action path sec:shared-action-path Let \(z_t ^ S D_J \) denote the current JEPA token map and let \(c_t\) denote the policy conditioning, including VLM features and robot state. JEPA tokens are normalized, pooled from \(S_ in =64\) to \(S=32\), projected to the flow token width, and appended to the pretrained learned prefix. This preserves the original prefix tokens. Future queries are masked from noisy action tokens. The VLM side of the conditioning enters through a separate path from the JEPA tokens. The frozen vision-language model is run once per replan; its final-layer output hidden states are passed through a trainable LayerNorm and a trainable VLM self-attention block, and the result is supplied to the action expert as cross-attention context. Every DiT block~ peebles2023dit in the action expert then reads this single shared VLM representation through its own cross-attention sublayer (each block forms its own key and value projections), rather than receiving a per-layer bridged cache. The JEPA tokens, by contrast, enter inside the DiT self-attention sequence as the appended prefix block described above. The two streams therefore reach the trunk through distinct attention mechanisms: VLM features via per-block cross-attention, JEPA tokens via in-sequence self-attention. For each horizon \(h\), an independent linear head predicts a residual: \[ _h = g_h( (q_t)), z_ t+h =z_t+ _h. \] The variant uses \(h=4\) and \(h=16\). The auxiliary loss is \[ &= 2 ( z_ t+4 ,z_ t+4 ) + 2 ( z_ t+16 ,z_ t+16 ),\\ &= + 0.1 . \] Here \( \) is tokenwise mean-squared error. Missing future targets are masked at the sample level. For the JEPA-conditioned policies, the DiT self-attention sequence is \[ x_t = [\,c_t^ ;\; p_ ;\; P( (z_t))+e_ pos \;;\; x_ \,], \] The projected JEPA tokens are placed after the native prefix and before the noisy action tokens. The native prefix contains 32 learned tokens; the JEPA map is pooled from 64 to 32 tokens before projection. Prefix and future-latent queries cannot attend to noisy action tokens, while action queries can read the complete prefix. This mask allows the action expert to use the visual representation without exposing the future-prediction branch to the action-noise input. BaseFlow retains the learned prefix but omits JEPA conditioning. Thus CurrentJEPA versus FutureJEPA isolates the additional future-prediction objective, whereas BaseFlow versus FutureJEPA changes both conditioning and supervision. Inference Future p

title: WeVisCut: The Whole Editing Room in One Agent From Narration to Long-Form Video
summary: Producing long-form videos from narration requires interdependent decisions that remain coherent across shots. Existing agentic editors often use multi-stage workflows driven by general models, leaving the quality-cost trade-off of compact, task-adapted policies unclear. We address this gap with WeVisCut, a long-form script-to-video system that connects tool execution with policy learning. Its agent harness maintains shared production state so that tool feedback informs subsequent decisions and repairs. Because finished videos do not expose these decisions, our four-stage data pipeline combines editing inversion with verified replay to turn recovered editing intent into executable supervision. Applied to 3,750 finished videos, this pipeline yields over 130K training examples. We use this supervision to train a single 9B policy that coordinates production and recovers from failures within the same harness. Moreover, we introduce a 100-task benchmark and five metrics assessing editing quality and delivery reliability. Under a shared tool environment, WeVisCut substantially outperforms its base model and achieves comparable performance to Claude Opus 5 while using nearly 33x fewer generated tokens per successful output minute. It also outperforms task-matched native editors on our proposed metrics.
full_text: Introduction ``The whole eloquence of cinema is achieved in the editing room.'' --- Orson Welles Creating a narrated long-form video involves turning a script into a sequence of coherent shots. Planning, visual retrieval, narration synthesis, and timeline assembly are interdependent. Changing a shot's duration affects later timestamps, while unsuitable visual material may require both retrieval and planning to be revisited across the affected shot sequence. Recent agentic editors coordinate production through specialized agents and tool workflows~ zhao2026cutclaw,yan2026crayotter,zhang2026cineagents, zhou2026videoagent,mu2026script,yu2026aurora . Several systems use general models with feedback or graph refinement. Yet orchestration alone does not specify how to train a compact policy that maintains video quality at low token cost. Crayotter trains a 9B editing model using final-video preferences on manually constructed tasks~ yan2026crayottergrpb . Such a policy needs a stateful environment for execution and recovery, together with supervision grounded in that environment. Finished videos, however, omit the tool calls, intermediate artifacts, and failures needed for such supervision. The challenge is therefore to connect stateful execution, executable supervision, and policy learning. To address these challenges, we present , which integrates a script-to-video agent harness, executable data construction, and a task-adapted policy. The harness (Figure~ fig:framework ) maintains shared production state and validates tool actions. It exposes execution feedback for inspection, bounded repair, and replanning while preserving unaffected artifacts from earlier successful production steps. Within this harness, we construct executable supervision through the four-stage pipeline in Figure~ fig:data . We first recover script--shot intent through editing inversion and execute it through verified replay. When replay reveals defects, we apply observe--reflect--repair for bounded corrections that preserve successful artifacts. We then use trajectory materialization to organize the recorded executions into training examples with tool feedback and repair outcomes. From 3,750 video projects, this process yields over 130K examples. Using these examples, we train a single 9B policy across production roles in three phases (Figure~ fig:overview ). In Phase~1, we establish tool use and recovery through unified supervised fine-tuning~ zeng2023agenttuning and runtime-verified rejection-sampled fine-tuning~ yuan2023scaling . In Phase~2, we apply Guided-OPD~ to learn recovery on policy-reached states while phasing out teacher intervention. In Phase~3, we use , our role- and context-factored DAPO~ yu2025dapo , to optimize decisions by comparing runtime outcomes within matched roles and contexts. Moreover, we introduce a benchmark of 100 script-to-video tasks and five complementary metrics to evaluate editing quality and delivery reliability. These metrics relate rendered videos to their scripts and production plans, so evaluation goes beyond successful rendering alone. In a shared tool environment, our policy improves over its base model by 16.0 points in Overall Score and achieves comparable performance to Claude Opus 5 while using nearly 33 fewer generated tokens per successful output minute. Our complete system also outperforms task-matched native editors. We summarize our contributions as follows. [leftmargin=12pt,itemsep=1pt,topsep=2pt] We design a script-to-video agent harness that maintains shared production state, validates tool actions, and supports inspection, bounded repair, and final delivery. We build a four-stage data pipeline based on editing inversion and verified replay, converting finished videos into executable training examples. We train a unified 9B policy for tool use and recovery through sequential SFT, runtime-verified RFT, Guided-OPD, and within a shared production harness. We introduce a 100-task benchmark and five metrics. improves its base policy, outperforms task-matched systems, and achieves comparable quality to Claude Opus 5 at markedly lower cost. Related Work Tool agents and long-horizon post-training. Producing long-form videos requires agents to choose tools and revise plans from execution feedback. Earlier methods range from interleaved reasoning and action~ yao2023react to learned API calls ~ schick2023toolformer,qin2023toolllm,patil2023gorilla and runnable tool dialogues~ li2023apibank . To train such behavior, researchers curate interactions and synthesize instructions or tool calls~ zeng2023agenttuning,chen2024agentflan, mitra2024agentinstruct,liu2024toolace . Reflection and reusable skills also support recovery~ shinn2023reflexion,wang2023voyager . Closer to our data pipeline, AgentTrek builds verified web trajectories from tutorials~ xu2024agenttrek . Finished videos, however, do not record editing actions. We therefore infer script--shot intent and replay it with production tools to obtain executable trajectories. Long-horizon training also needs to handle policy-generated states. DAgger~ ross2011dagger collects expert labels for learner states, while generalized knowledge distillation trains on student-generated sequences ~ agarwal2023gkd . Guided-OPD mixes teacher and student turns, while TurnOPD and Step-Level OPD refine supervision at turn and step boundaries~ li2026policy,zhou2026turnopd,sun2026step . We apply Guided-OPD with truncated teacher logits. For reward optimization, GRPO and DAPO build on PPO-style updates with group-relative comparisons ~ schulman2017ppo,shao2024deepseekmath,yu2025dapo . We adapt DAPO for our multi-role policy as , comparing rewards only within matched roles and decision contexts. Video editing. Video editing systems range from user-assisted tools to autonomous agents. LAVE keeps users in the editing loop~ wang2024lave . In more automated settings, CutClaw and CineAgents handle music-synchronized editing and cinematic compilation~ zhao2026cutclaw,zhang2026cineagents . The original Crayotter uses a traceable multi-agent workflow, while VideoAgent assembles specialists dynamically~ yan2026crayotter,zhou2026videoagent . Beyond workflow design, task-specific training has also been explored. ``The Script is All You Need'' trains a ScripterAgent but uses a separate DirectorAgent ~ mu2026script . Aurora trains a planner for local edits ~ yu2026aurora . Building on the Crayotter environment, subsequent work trains a 9B policy with final-video preferences on manually constructed tasks~ yan2026crayottergrpb . In contrast, learns one role-routed policy for fixed-narration production from executable trajectories built through editing inversion, verified replay, observe--reflect--repair, and trajectory materialization. Agent and video evaluation. Evaluation of narration-driven video production needs to consider both the rendered video and the production process. VBench, VideoScore, and VMBench assess generated-video quality and motion ~ huang2024vbench,he2024videoscore,ling2025vmbench , while Goku-Bench tests instruction-based edits~ liang2026goku . Script--video timing has also been evaluated~ mu2026script . Complementary agent evaluation ranges from recorded web and mobile trajectories ~ deng2023mind2web,rawles2023android to interactive shopping, browser, and desktop environments that validate action outcomes ~ yao2022webshop,zhou2023webarena,koh2024visualwebarena, drouin2024workarena,xie2024osworld . Software-repair benchmarks use repository tests~ jimenez2024swebench , while multi-turn and tool-oriented suites measure progress, valid transitions, and task constraints ~ liu2023agentbench,ma2024agentboard,lu2024toolsandbox,yao2024taubench . We combine these perspectives in a benchmark of 100 script-to-video tasks, linking scripts, shot plans, tool trajectories, and rendered videos. Five metrics are introduced to assess script fidelity, visual--narration alignment, timeline plan realization, long-horizon consistency, and end-to-end delivery success. Agent Framework sec:agent-framework Figure~ fig:framework presents the agent framework for long-form script-to-video production. A shared policy makes editing decisions, while a stateful runtime executes tools and maintains the resulting production artifacts. Their interaction connects the narration script to a rendered video through an inspectable process that supports revision when execution reveals problems. We first define the task and policy--runtime interface, then describe the harness that implements this process. Script-to-Video Task A task input consists of a fixed narration script , target aspect ratio , feasible duration interval , optional source assets, and a versioned shared tool space . The goal is to render a video satisfying the delivery constraints without rewriting the narration. The outputs also include a typed shot plan , specifying narration coverage, visual content, and timing, and an execution trajectory recording calls and returns throughout the production process (Appendix~ app:experiments ). Production uses tools that accept typed arguments and return artifacts or execution feedback. At call , a single policy with shared parameters serves a role . The orchestrator ( ) selects tools and arguments, the generator ( ) supplies structured content, and the critic ( ) inspects artifacts and requests or verifies repairs based on recorded execution feedback. At each call, the role context combines the task input, role, a view of the production state (shot plan, artifacts, and progress), relevant call-and-return history , and tool schemas. The policy produces a complete role output , which the runtime processes under a tool contract : The contract specifies the tool, required fields, and value types. The runtime returns observation , reporting results or blockers, and the updated production state . For orchestrator calls, the role output specifies a tool action containing the selected tool and arguments (Figure~ fig:framework ). Harness Design The harness in Figure~ fig:framework implements the interaction in Equation~ eq:process through a shared tool space, persistent production state, and runtime checks. Each orchestrator turn selects one tool, which may process multiple shots and invoke generator or critic calls. Tool selection depends on the current production state, including available artifacts and blockers, rather than a predetermined sequence. Production flow and tool system. Starting from the narration script , segmentation produces production segments, and shot planning expands them into the shot plan . Shot records connect narration spans to visual queries, target durations, and spotlight assignments. Visual retrieval and text-to-speech (TTS) tools use these records to obtain shot assets and narration audio. For spotlight shots, decoration tools select verified templates~ heygen2026hyperframes and fill typed slots, allowing the policy to control presentation through structured content rather than raw layout code. Music search supplies background music (BGM) for the final mix. Timeline composition combines shot assets, narration audio, and decorations, while final rendering produces the shot videos required for stitching. Quality judging and repair tools allow the policy to revisit these intermediate products before delivery. This progression describes artifact dependencies, not an obligatory ordering of every tool call. Persistent state and selective context. These tools communicate through the production state . Global records track narration coverage, shot order, and timing, while per-shot records associate assets, audio, templates, renders, and unresolved issues with shot IDs. Planned content remains distinct from artifacts that have actually been produced. Episode memory retains these artifacts, and the event trace preserves calls, returns, and failures. title: Quantize by Doing: Task-Guided Mixed-Precision Quantization of Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces the memory footprint of vision-language-action (VLA) models, but lowering bit widths while maintaining task performance remains challenging. Existing work has used sensitivity estimates from calibration data to assign bit widths to different model components. However, using task success directly to guide mixed-precision allocation is underexplored because closed-loop evaluations are costly and the effect of quantizing one component depends on the precision of other components. To this end, we propose \textbf{QbD-VLA}, a task-guided mixed-precision quantization method that uses task success from short closed-loop evaluations to assign weight and activation bit widths while accounting for interactions between model components. Experiments covering four VLA models and all four LIBERO suites show strong task performance at average precisions of approximately 4 bits for weights and fewer than 6 bits for activations. On SIMPLER, the gain over uniform quantization is small. On a Franka Research 3 robot arm, simulation-selected allocations show no detected success-rate loss on X-VLA but fail on $π_{0.5}$. These findings support using task success to guide mixed-precision VLA quantization, while highlighting the need for real-world evaluation before deployment. Code is available at \href{https://github.com/jiuyixu25/QbD-VLA}{\texttt{github.com/jiuyixu25/QbD-VLA}}.

Introduction sec:intro Vision-language-action (VLA) models map camera images and a language instruction to robot actions with backbones of several billion parameters~ kim2024openvla,black2024pi_0,intelligence2025pi_,zheng2025x . Post-training quantization (PTQ) is the standard way to fit such a policy onto an on-robot GPU, and the practical question is a mixed-precision allocation: which groups of layers must stay at higher precision while the rest run at lower bit width. Existing methods choose the allocation from a sensitivity score computed per layer or per group on calibration data, such as Hessian-based sensitivity~ dong2019hawq,deng2023clado , a reconstruction error ~ nagel2020up,li2021brecq,frantar2022gptq , or the deviation of predicted actions on fixed inputs ~ xu2026qvla,akbari2026actquant,ranjan2026mixqvla,xu2026daptq . Such scores are cheap, but what matters for a robot policy is closed-loop task success, and the two do not agree in general~ vlaquantbench . They also score one group at a time, whereas the effect of quantizing a group depends on the precision of the others. For example, two groups of the action head cost 1.0 and 5.5 success points when quantized alone and 97.5 points together. Selecting the allocation from task success itself would capture both effects, but closed-loop evaluation is costly, and this problem remains underexplored. To fill this knowledge gap, we propose QbD-VLA, which selects weight and activation bit widths from closed-loop task success at a bounded cost. Starting from full precision, it lowers one group by one level at a time. Each candidate is evaluated in simulation with the other groups at their current bit widths, for one to three batches of one episode per task. A sequential test on the Wilson bounds of the success estimate keeps the move only if the estimate stays above a floor set compared with the full-precision policy. The allocation ends when no move passes. On four policies, QbD-VLA finds allocations with nominal weight bit widths of 4.00 to 4.16 and activation bit widths of 4.47 to 5.94. On ~ intelligence2025pi_ , OpenVLA-OFT~ kim2025fine , and X-VLA~ zheng2025x , uniform W4A4 yields 0 success, whereas the selected allocations reach 98.5 , 97.5 , and 97.0 against 99.0 , 100.0 , and 97.0 at full precision on LIBERO benchmark~ liu2023libero . At the same time, allocations chosen by action error, activation kurtosis, or reconstruction error at the same cost reach 27.5 , 0.0 , and 52.0 on . A factorial experiment shows why: lowering the action-expert MLP from A6 to A4 costs 23.5 points when three other groups are at A6 and 0.5 points when they are at A4. Across all four LIBERO suites, the allocations stay within 5 points of full precision on average. On SIMPLER~ li2024evaluating , the best allocation reaches 66.8 against 64.8 for uniform W4A6. On a Franka Research 3 robot arm, the frozen allocation succeeds on 13 of 30 layouts for X-VLA against 11 for full precision, but on none of six layouts for , where full precision succeeds on all six. Task success is therefore a practical selection criterion for mixed-precision VLA quantization at a few hundred simulation episodes, while success in simulation does not guarantee execution on hardware. Our contributions are the following: We propose QbD-VLA, which selects bit widths for VLA models from closed-loop task success, evaluates each candidate within the current mixed-precision configuration, and bounds the simulation cost with a sequential test. We conduct an evaluation on four VLA policies and all four LIBERO suites against uniform quantization, sensitivity-based allocators, a two-stage allocator, and released VLA quantization methods under the same settings. We analyze why sensitivity-based allocation fails on these policies and test the transfer of simulation-selected allocations to a real robot with two fine-tuned policies. Related Work sec:related Post-training and mixed-precision quantization. Post-training quantization lowers numerical precision through weight reconstruction or activation-aware scaling frantar2022gptq,lin2024awq,xiao2023smoothquant . Mixed-precision allocation uses layer sensitivity dong2019hawq or accuracy and hardware feedback wang2019haq to select bit widths. Additive layer-wise loss approximations omit cross-layer interactions, which CLADO explicitly models deng2023clado . All of these score candidates on calibration or validation data fixed in advance. A control policy instead observes the consequences of its own earlier actions, so a quantization error can compound over an episode. We therefore allocate bit widths from task success measured in closed-loop execution. Quantization of VLA models. VLA quantization methods allocate precision using action-space sensitivity~ xu2026qvla , contributions to action prediction~ akbari2026actquant , internal task evidence~ ranjan2026mixqvla , or motion-error sensitivity~ xu2026daptq . Other approaches address scale calibration zhang2026quantvla , rotation-based W4A4 quantization wang2026holoq , native integer execution ho2026foldquantvla , and precision adjustment using runtime error feedback~ zheng2026dyq . SQAP-VLA combines quantization with token pruning fang2025sqap , while HBVLA and BitVLA investigate binarization and ternary-weight training, respectively yan2026hbvla,wang2025bitvla . These methods report closed-loop task performance. QbD-VLA uses task success to accept candidate group-level weight and activation allocations, with all other groups at their current bit widths. Closed-loop evaluation of quantized policies. VLAQuantBench~ vlaquantbench evaluates quantization effects in closed loop and shows that the effect of quantizing a group depends on which other groups are quantized. We follow its group definitions and develop an allocation method. A distillation case study documents disagreement between offline accuracy and execution success~ jia2026anatomy , while PIVOT-Q~ ruan2026pivotq uses selective on-policy distillation to recover post-quantization generalization. Both train the policy, whereas we only change its bit allocation. We additionally evaluate whether allocations selected in simulation transfer to policies fine-tuned for a real robot. Method sec:method QbD-VLA uses closed-loop task success to select the bit widths for quantizing the weights and activations of a pretrained VLA model. It evaluates each candidate allocation with the other components at their current bit widths, so that bit allocation accounts for interactions between components. Under a fixed per-candidate budget, evaluation episodes are allocated adaptively according to the uncertainty of each success estimate. Figure~ fig:overview gives the overview of our method. Following prior VLA quantization work~ xu2026qvla , we treat the vision encoder, the language backbone, the action head, and any separate vision-language projector as model components. For bit allocation, we keep these component boundaries and further divide the action head into layer groups following vlaquantbench . Depending on the architecture, the action-head groups cover attention projections, feed-forward layers, and normalization modulators. All quantizable layers within a group share one weight bit width and one activation bit width, so sensitive parts of the action head can keep higher precision without increasing the precision of the entire head. title: Actuator-Aware Observer Inputs for Cascade ADRC of Quadrotors Under Rotor Lag, Measurement Delay and Sensor Noise
comment: 19 pages. MATLAB and PX4 SITL evaluation. Code, controller gains, random seeds, and per-seed results: https://github.com/Quang61123/actuator-aware-cascade-adrc
summary: In sampled cascade linear active disturbance rejection control (LADRC) of quadrotors, the extended-state observer typically receives the instantaneous command, although the delayed measurement reflects an earlier, rotor-filtered acceleration. This paper proposes actuator-aware (AA) observer inputs: altitude and attitude observers use limited virtual inputs filtered by an assumed rotor model and aligned with the measurement delay, and horizontal observers use acceleration reconstructed from measured attitude. Fixed gains are selected on the discrete-time model under sensitivity and step-response requirements and stationary covariance ceilings on each channel's control variance and increment and on the noise-induced inner-loop increment of the full cascade. In paired set-point trials, PID-Budget, AA-Budget and AA-HalfGain reach mean RMSEs of 65.5, 19.2 and 16.9~mm; under a stricter common cascade ceiling, the AA designs reach 29.9 and 26.4~mm versus 72.3~mm for a PID that uses roughly double their rotor-command increment. PX4 software-in-the-loop runs reproduce these results. Behind EKF2, a noise model fitted to the estimation errors predicts the roll/pitch and yaw increments within 5\% on held-out and out-of-sample runs and the total rotor-command increment within 14\%. Redesigned for this stack under the same sensitivity and response specification and estimator-aware ceilings, AA-Budget-E reduces the set-point RMSE from 59.1~mm (PID-E) to 44.0~mm with a lower rotor-command increment in every paired set-point and lemniscate run (mean S6 rotor-command-increment reductions relative to PID-E: 45\% before and 15\% after output quantization); AA-HalfGain-E beats PID-E only on the lemniscate. The evidence is simulation-based, and the ceilings are nominal tuning constraints.
