Active disturbance rejection control, actuator dynamics, cascade control, extended state observer, quadrotor control, sensor noise, time delay. Introduction Quadrotor trajectory control couples disturbance rejection, sensor-noise sensitivity, actuator dynamics, and measurement timing mahony2012 . Active disturbance rejection control (ADRC) estimates a lumped disturbance using an extended-state observer (ESO) and compensates for it in the control law han2009,gao2003 . In a sampled cascade, however, the instantaneous commanded input may differ from the acceleration associated with a delayed measurement: rotor dynamics filter the command, and the measurement refers to an earlier plant state. Increasing observer bandwidth can then amplify both measurement noise and the residual caused by this input inconsistency. This work addresses that implementation problem with two distinct observer-input paths (Fig.~ fig:architecture ). For altitude and attitude, the controller reconstructs normalized inputs from the limited thrust and torque before rotor allocation, propagates them through a first-order actuator model, and aligns the result with the measurement time. For horizontal motion, the observer uses near-hover acceleration reconstructed from measured attitude rather than the instantaneous tilt command. The nominal model uses unity normalized input gain and separates the actual plant lag and delay from the internal observer assumptions. These choices do not reconstruct post-allocation rotor clipping or adapt the assumed delay during variable-latency tests. Observer-input consistency is combined with fixed-gain activity-aware tuning. The sampled linear covariance model includes the closed attitude loop, its observer, actuator lag, and measurement buffers. It predicts tracking error, noise-induced virtual-control variance, and sample-to-sample increments. During horizontal gain selection, an additional inner-control increment ceiling includes the propagation of position and velocity noise through tilt commands. Sensitivity, overshoot and settling-time requirements constrain the same candidate search; the design target is , followed by a separate final audit against . Actuator models in observers, delay alignment and half-gain tuning each have precedents; the contribution lies in two design concepts. First, observer-input consistency in a sampled cascade with rotor lag and measurement delay: a commanded observer input adds the structural residual to the disturbance estimate, which raises the sensitivity peak with observer bandwidth at fixed controller bandwidth (Section~ sec:nominal ) and, in the redesigned ablation, allows the response and sensitivity requirements to be met, within the stated finite search, only at the lowest observer/controller ratios, where the best commanded-input design found for has 9.2 times the mean RMSE of AA-Budget (Section~ sec:abl ). Second, the outer-to-inner noise path becomes an explicit design constraint: the cascade-level increment is predicted on the full cascade model, agrees with nonlinear hover measurements, and enables a comparison under a common strict cascade-increment ceiling (Section~ sec:cascade ); with a shaping filter for the estimation error, the same constraint is computed for estimator-fed loops (Section~ sec:estaware ). The main contributions are: Two actuator-aware observer-input paths for sampled cascade LADRC, delay-aligned actuator-model inputs (altitude/attitude) and measured-attitude inputs (horizontal), with ablations of both input paths. A fixed-gain covariance design whose channel-level and cascade-level activity ceilings are computed for white or estimator-coloured measurement noise, validated on code-generated controllers inside PX4. A paired nonlinear simulation assessment including a comparison under a common strict cascade-increment ceiling, noise and latency stress, and fixed-gain rotor-lag mismatch, repeated in PX4 software-in-the-loop with the controllers code-generated into the autopilot, including a redesign for the estimator-fed loop under the same sensitivity and response specification and estimator-aware increment ceilings. Related Work sec:related Observer-based robust control. Disturbance-observer and adaptive-control methods for quadrotor disturbance rejection are reviewed in wang2024survey . Within the ADRC/ESO family, representative developments include cascade LADRC position control with PID attitude stabilization ramirez2024 , GPI-observer-based ADRC for morphing quadrotors he2023gpi , reduced-order ESO-based nonlinear PID control xu2025roeso , and geometric ADRC on zeng2025so3 . Related nonlinear-observer approaches include fixed-time extended observers combined with adaptive sliding-mode control under turbulent wind miranda2023fxeso , fixed-time disturbance observers with backstepping under input saturation and actuator failure huang2025fxtbs , high-order sliding-mode disturbance observers incorporating first-order-plus-dead-time actuator dynamics xu2024hosmdo , fixed-time disturbance-observer-based MPC xu2024fxtdompc , high-gain disturbance observers izadi2023hgdo , and neural-network disturbance observers with command filtering li2025nndo . Their analyses hold under their stated modeling and disturbance assumptions and do not directly cover Gaussian sensor noise, measurement-timing effects on the observer input, or rotor-lag mismatch in a sampled nonlinear cascade. Tuning of ADRC and PID. Bandwidth parameterization reduces LADRC tuning to gao2003 , and stability with uncertain dynamics was studied in zheng2007 . Quadrotor studies automate tuning with Kriging surrogates zhou2024kriging , crayfish optimization with fuzzy adaptation li2025ladrccoa , particle-swarm tuning with event triggering li2025etftadrc , TD3 reinforcement learning cai2026td3adrc , and multi-objective PID optimization vaiuso2025mopid . Their costs emphasize tracking and transients, in some cases with input-smoothness, power or acoustic terms cai2026td3adrc,vaiuso2025mopid ; these objectives differ from the stationary sensor-noise covariance constraints on virtual-control variance, increments and the outer-to-inner noise path used here. Noise-aware observers. The trade-off between observer responsiveness and measurement-noise sensitivity has been addressed through error-dependent observer bandwidth adaptation liu2020beso,cui2025vbeso , half-gain tuning of discrete-time ESOs herbst2025halfgain , and scalable-bandwidth linear ESOs combined with internal model control for quadrotor attitude regulation wei_scalable_leso . These approaches modify the observer bandwidth or gain structure; the present work instead specifies the input and noise paths of a sampled cascade model and combines them with fixed-gain covariance constraints (Section~ sec:proposed ). Two studies are closest in ingredients. Zhang et al.~ zhang2022meso place an actuator model inside the ESO, and Herbst and Hempel~ herbst2025halfgain derive half-gain tuning for discrete-time ESOs and validate it experimentally. The present work uses both ingredients and claims neither as new: the actuator-aware input is related to the model-based ESO, and the half-gain observer is adapted from~ herbst2025halfgain . What differs is the alignment of the modelled actuator output with the time base of the delayed measurement in a sampled cascade, the measured-attitude input of the horizontal observers, and the selection of fixed gains under cascade-level and estimator-aware increment ceilings, which neither study addresses. Their reported results are not directly comparable, because plants and objectives differ. Table~ tab:lit summarizes selected features. title: Event2Reward: Learning Robotic Rewards from Progress Relations
summary: Learning task progress from robot demonstrations provides a practical way to construct dense shaping rewards for robotic reinforcement learning. A common approach uses normalized demonstration time as progress labels, implicitly assuming monotonically increasing task progress. During policy exploration, however, actual task progress can stall or even regress. Such models may mistake regressions for progress, assigning positive shaping rewards to actions that cause progress loss. Real suboptimal and failed executions offer corrective experience, but assigning absolute progress values to their states is difficult. Our key observation is that stalls, regressions, and recoveries establish local relative progress relations even when absolute progress is unknown. We introduce Event2Reward, which uses normalized temporal labels to anchor the progress scale and these within-trajectory relations to constrain local changes, combining absolute and relative progress supervision. Its progress predictions serve as potentials for reward shaping. We curate an event-annotated dataset from approximately 100K raw real-robot execution records, covering successful, suboptimal, and failed executions, without requiring framewise absolute progress labels. Under the same training budgets, Event2Reward improves average policy success by 18.16 percentage points over a baseline using only sparse task rewards across 40 tasks in four LIBERO suites. On real robots, average success after 30 minutes of wall-clock training reaches 60.0% on three precise insertion tasks and 90.0% on three object manipulation tasks, exceeding the sparse-reward baseline under the same budget by 36.7 and 23.3 percentage points, respectively. Ablation studies further show that absolute progress supervision and relative progress relations are complementary, with joint supervision yielding better downstream policy learning.
full_text: Introduction sec:introduction Reinforcement learning (RL) enables robots to improve manipulation skills through trial and error~ luo2025hilserl . However, learning on real robots often requires extensive and costly interaction. Reward shaping offers a way to accelerate policy learning by improving credit assignment with dense rewards. A common approach learns task progress from successful demonstrations, using normalized elapsed time as a proxy~ liang2026robometer,wang2026wvm . This temporal supervision encodes monotonically increasing task progress. Progress estimates can serve as potentials for reward shaping, with the shaping term computed from discounted differences between successive predictions~ ng1999policy . During policy exploration, however, robots routinely produce suboptimal and failed executions, in which progress can stall or even regress. The reward model may still predict rising progress during such non-ideal behavior, assigning positive shaping rewards even when progress stalls or regresses. Instead of improving credit assignment, such rewards credit the actions that caused the loss, hindering rather than accelerating policy improvement. A natural remedy is to train the reward model directly on suboptimal and failed executions. However, normalized time continues to assign increasing progress values during stalls and regressions, so it cannot provide valid absolute progress supervision for these executions. A common workaround repeats or reverses demonstration frames to synthesize stalls and regressions with labels known by construction~ liang2026robometer,wang2026wvm , but these edits cannot introduce failure states absent from the original demonstrations. Another workaround uses outcome labels or trajectory-level preferences, which do enable reward learning from real suboptimal and failed executions~ lee2026roboreward,liang2026robometer . These signals describe overall execution quality, whereas progress-based shaping rewards depend on progress changes between adjacent observations. Such overall judgments therefore leave the timing and direction of these changes underdetermined: a failed execution can retain partial progress, while a successful one can include regressions and recoveries. How, then, can we obtain local progress supervision from real executions without assigning an absolute progress value to every state? Our key observation is that task events in real executions can establish local progress relations even when absolute progress values are unknown. For example, consider a robot moving a cup from a table onto a shelf. If the cup slips from the gripper and falls back onto the table, how much progress remains is difficult to quantify, yet this state clearly holds less task progress than the state just before the drop. We directly supervise the progress predictions used for reward shaping with these within-trajectory progress relations, which encode the direction of change between temporally anchored states. We combine these relations with normalized temporal labels from successful demonstrations to train our reward model, Event2Reward (Figure~ fig:roboground-overview ). The temporal labels anchor the numerical scale of predicted progress, while the relations constrain the direction of local progress changes in real suboptimal and failed executions. We also contribute an event-annotated dataset curated from approximately 100K raw real-robot execution records across multiple sources, spanning successful, suboptimal, and failed executions. The annotations identify where task progress stalls, regresses, or recovers, and link these events to temporal regions and reference states. They turn observed execution events into local progress comparisons beyond terminal outcomes, without requiring framewise completion percentages. We combine two-pass VLM annotation with independent human annotation and review (Appendix~ app:annotation-procedure ). We will release the structured annotations, data splits, and tools for constructing progress comparisons, providing a reusable resource for reward learning and execution analysis. We train Event2Reward through pretraining and rollout joint training, then adapt it using a small set of target-task executions. We evaluate whether Event2Reward improves policy learning on 40 LIBERO~ liu2023libero tasks and six real-world tasks on Franka robots. The real-world experiments cover three precise insertion tasks trained with SERL~ luo2025serl,luo2025hilserl and three manipulation tasks trained with DSRL~ wagenmaker2025dsrl using a ~ black2024pi0 base policy. Across the four LIBERO suites, Event2Reward improves average policy success by 9.96--13.76 percentage points over the strongest baseline in each suite under matched interaction budgets. In real-world experiments with a matched 30-minute training budget, Event2Reward increases average success from 37.8 to 60.0 on precise insertion tasks and from 81.7 to 90.0 on manipulation tasks, compared with Robometer, the strongest learned reward baseline in each setting. Our ablations show that combining temporal labels with within-trajectory progress relations yields larger gains in downstream policy learning than combining them with trajectory-level preferences. Combining temporal and relational supervision outperforms either alone in downstream policy learning. Related Work sec:related_work Visual reward and value models. Learning rewards from visual observations reduces the need for task-specific reward engineering in robot learning. VIP~ ma2023vip learns goal-directed visual representations through value-based pretraining, and LIV~ ma2023liv extends this approach to language and image goals. For vision-language reasoning, GVL~ ma2024gvl estimates progress in context without parameter updates, while ProgressLM~ zhang2026progresslm learns to assess progress relative to visual or textual demonstrations. WVM~ wang2026wvm instead uses video world-model representations to predict distributions over progress sequences. Our work focuses on the supervision of progress estimates: how real suboptimal and failed executions can provide evidence about local progress changes. Progress supervision from demonstrations. Demonstrations provide temporal order and semantic task structure for progress supervision. Temporal order supports ranking-based objectives: Rank2Reward~ yang2024rank2reward learns rankings on expert videos and combines them with an expert--policy discriminator, while Video-Language Critic~ alakuijala2025vlc combines sequential ranking with video--text matching and uses failed executions as contrastive negatives. VLAC~ zhai2025vlac derives signed progress differences from temporal offsets. RynnValue~ huang2026rynnvalue learns absolute temporal distance to task completion and relative temporal displacement from timestamps, using temporal-order shuffling and value-isolation attention to reduce shortcut learning. Task-stage annotations provide semantic structure: SARM~ chen2025sarm aligns numerical progress targets with annotated stages, and Robo-Dopamine~ tan2025robodopamine derives signed progress differences from stage-based progress coordinates. Augmentation extends this supervision to nonmonotonic sequences. ReWiND~ zhang2025rewind reverses demonstration segments to synthesize regressions, while WVM~ wang2026wvm constructs increasing, stable, and decreasing profiles through frame preservation, repetition, and reversal. Our approach complements these signals with progress relations grounded in stalls, regressions, and recoveries in real suboptimal and failed executions. Reward learning from nonideal experience. Preference-based reward learning uses relative judgments without requiring absolute numerical ratings~ christiano2017preferences . At the observation level, RL-VLM-F~ wang2024rlvlmf asks a VLM to compare images, and venkataraman2025offlinevlm apply this approach to reward labeling for real-world offline RL. At the trajectory level, RoboReward~ lee2026roboreward combines instruction relabeling and temporal clipping of successful demonstrations with naturally successful and failed rollouts carrying episode-level completion scores. Robometer~ liang2026robometer combines normalized temporal progress labels from expert demonstrations with success prediction and trajectory preferences, allowing real failures to contribute supervision while also producing per-frame progress estimates. Beyond these judgments, execution events provide structure for datasets and evaluation. WVM's Suboptimal-Value-Bench~ wang2026wvm converts annotated hesitation and retry intervals into reference progress curves, while REBOOT~ oforiampofo2026reboot pairs precision-assembly demonstrations with phase boundaries, failure and recovery timestamps, and a phase-level evaluation protocol. We use event-grounded within-trajectory relations to supervise the progress estimates used for reward shaping. Method sec:method Event2Reward learns task progress from temporal labels and within-trajectory progress relations. After adaptation to downstream tasks, the model's scalar progress predictions serve as the potential for reward shaping. Figure~ fig:progress-supervision-overview illustrates these complementary supervision signals. Task Progress Model sec:progress-model Event2Reward is a task-conditioned model that estimates task progress from visual observations. At time , its input is , where is the task instruction, is a reference start observation, is a short visual history ending at the current observation, and is an optional goal image depicting task completion. It outputs a scalar progress estimate , with higher values indicating greater progress toward completing the instructed task. The visual history provides context for interpreting local changes: progress may remain stable during stalled execution or decrease when previously achieved task states are lost. We implement Event2Reward with a Qwen3.5-4B vision-language backbone, a progress head, and an auxiliary trend head. The progress head predicts a distribution over discretized progress values in , whose expectation gives . As detailed in Sections~ sec:event-dataset and~ sec:joint-learning , temporal labels supervise this distribution, while within-trajectory progress relations constrain its scalar expectation. The same scalar serves as the potential for downstream reward shaping. The trend head predicts whether progress increases, remains stable, or decreases within the visual history as an auxiliary training task. Input construction and prediction-head details are given in Appendix~ app:model-inputs . Progress Supervision from Robot Executions sec:event-dataset We curate an event-annotated dataset from approximately 100K raw real-robot execution records. The annotations connect observable execution events to temporal anchors and reference states, providing local progress comparisons beyond terminal success or failure. Normal successful trajectories supply normalized-time labels as a progress proxy over their task-relevant execution intervals. Trajectories containing events supply within-trajectory relations that capture stalled execution, loss of achieved task states, and recovery. For each execution event, we record its category, a reference state, and the relevant temporal interval; regression-and-recovery events additionally identify a recovery state. Together with the supporting visual observations, these temporal anchors identify the within-trajectory progress comparisons used for supervision. Annotation therefore consists of identifying task events and their temporal anchors, without assigning framewise completion percentages. Our annotation protocol organizes events by execution outcome, while their progress relations are grounded in observable task-state changes. For successful executions, we annotate progress stall, an interval with approximately unchanged task progress, and regression and recovery, a decrease in task progress followed by rec

title: Utility-WAM: Correcting Future-Induced Action Changes
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) can condition robot actions on generated visual futures, but this additional context is neither cost-free nor uniformly beneficial. We examine what a predicted future actually changes: the action delta $Δa$ between the future-conditioned and future-free execution paths of the same model. Under a shared WAM checkpoint, this delta barely shifts average benchmark success ($+0.8$ points on LIBERO, $-0.8$ on RoboTwin~2.0), while generating visual futures increases inference latency by 1.7--1.9$\times$. These aggregate metrics conceal a concentrated failure mode that we term \emph{future-induced negative transfer}: while predictive deltas benefit long-horizon tasks ($+2.4$ points on LIBERO-Long) and remain negligible on most routine manipulations, they induce severe degradation on precision tasks---with \emph{Press Stapler} and \emph{Place Can Basket} losing 54.0 and 34.0 points, recurring as top failure modes across independently trained WAM variants. We introduce \textbf{Utility-WAM} for in-place correction of future-conditioned control. Its primary learning component is a residual adapter that repairs future-induced velocity deltas under a frozen shared WAM by aligning them with ground-truth dynamic guidance and penalizing excess error beyond the future-free baseline. The adapter selectively eliminates the majority of severe task drops (reducing losses to 6.0 and 14.0 points) while preserving long-horizon foresight. To eliminate superfluous video computation, a lightweight pre-generation gate reuses counterfactual action outcomes to selectively bypass video generation on 75.5\% of RoboTwin queries, cutting latency by 38\% while improving average success to 93.3\% on RoboTwin~2.0 and 98.9\% on LIBERO. On physical bimanual manipulation across three real-world tasks, Utility-WAM succeeds in 53 of 60 trials, compared to 43 for FAST-WAM.

Introduction sec:introduction World Action Models (WAMs) couple robot control with future visual prediction, but their deployment choices differ. DreamZero~ ye2026world , Vidar~ feng2507vidar , and LingBot-VA~ li2026causal generate visual futures for action prediction; FAST-WAM~ yuan2026fast omits future video at deployment; and AdaWAM~ tang2026dreaming routes visual reasoning by execution phase. These approaches mainly ask whether or when to spend computation on visual prediction. We instead ask what a predicted future changes: the action delta it induces relative to a matched future-free path. This delta may help, hurt, or be negligible, while its video-generation cost is always paid. FAST-WAM already suggests this tension: its separately trained future-generating variants improve LIBERO but degrade RoboTwin~2.0 relative to future-free inference~ yuan2026fast . Our controlled comparison under one shared Stage-1 checkpoint reproduces this small sign reversal (Table~ tab:component_ablation ), but the averages hide where the harm lies. Following the standard definition of negative transfer as deterioration caused by an additional information source~ wang2019characterizing,zhang2023survey , we call deterioration relative to the future-free path future-induced negative transfer (Section~ sec:prelim_ntg ) and find it to be a concentrated failure mode rather than a uniform effect. We therefore treat the action delta as the central object of study. Empirically, this delta provides meaningful guidance on long-horizon tasks, remains negligible on most standard manipulations (26 of 50 RoboTwin tasks change by at most one point), but induces severe failure on precision tasks such as Press Stapler and Place Can Basket (hereafter the two severe tasks), which also recur as the most degraded tasks across FAST-WAM variants (Appendix~ app:replication ). Because pure routing cannot rectify a corrupted action vector once future conditioning is invoked, the foundational challenge is to repair future-induced action changes while preserving the predictive foresight where it genuinely helps. To address this, we introduce Utility-WAM, which decouples test-time imagination into targeted action correction and selective compute allocation. Rather than discarding future generation or distilling it into a current-only policy---which compromises long-horizon performance---Utility-WAM retains the future-conditioned path while attaching a lightweight residual adapter to a frozen shared WAM. The adapter directly repairs harmful action shifts by aligning predicted velocity deltas with beneficial corrections supported by ground-truth futures. Furthermore, because physical imagination remains computationally expensive and unneeded on routine decisions, a pre-generation gate reuses the adapter's counterfactual action outcomes to selectively bypass video generation entirely when no action benefit is expected. Our contributions are as follows: Characterizing Future-Induced Negative Transfer: We formalize test-time imagination via the action delta relative to a matched future-free reference. We demonstrate that small benchmark-average effects mask severe, reproducible performance collapse on precision tasks across diverse WAM configurations. Targeted Action Correction: We propose a residual adapter that repairs future-induced velocity deltas via ground-truth future alignment and an excess-error penalty. On RoboTwin~2.0, the adapter recovers 89 and 59 of the losses on the two severe tasks (accounting for 80 of its overall 1.7-point gain) while preserving gains on the remaining 48 tasks and long-horizon suites. title: Information-Driven Collaborative Autonomy for Heterogeneous UAV/UGV Teams
summary: This paper considers coordinating a heterogeneous team of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) traversing a domain containing an unknown number of potentially hazardous targets. The UAVs provide aerial sensing using onboard optical cameras, adapting their trajectories to ground routes and target information. We formulate the aerial search problem using ergodic control, which distributes sensing effort according to a spatial information density to balance exploration and target localization. The formulation incorporates dynamic camera field-of-view footprints and pose-dependent probabilistic detection models. Angles-only measurements are processed through Bayesian inference and marginalization over data-association hypotheses to obtain a Poisson multi-Bernoulli (PMB) approximation of the target posterior, representing both detected and undetected targets. This belief directs aerial sensing toward unexplored regions along the ground routes and viewpoints that improve target localization. Ground planning combines chance-constrained target avoidance, enforced through confidence sets, with a void-probability objective that favors routes unlikely to contain threats. We solve each team's optimization problem in a fully decentralized manner using a nested SCvx*--C-ADMM scheme, with outer sequential convex programming iterations and inner distributed consensus optimization, accounting for nonlinearities, nonseparable objectives, and continuous-time inter-agent separation constraints. A closed-loop scheme updates both fleets' trajectories as information becomes available and permits ground motion when the remaining route risk falls below a prescribed threshold. Numerical case studies examine sensing geometry and target uncertainty, compare decentralized and centralized solvers, and demonstrate full closed-loop collaboration between multiple UAVs and UGVs.

Pilipovsky joshua.y.pilipovsky@rtx.com \\ Senior Research Engineer\\ RTX Technology Research Center (RTRC)\\ East Hartford, CT 06108, USA This paper considers the problem of coordinating a heterogeneous team of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs), where the ground vehicles must traverse a domain containing an unknown number of potentially hazardous targets. The UAVs provide aerial sensing using onboard optical cameras, and their trajectories must adapt to both the ground routes and the information collected about the targets. We formulate the aerial search problem using ergodic control, which distributes sensing effort according to a spatial information density to balance exploration and target localization. The formulation incorporates dynamic camera field-of-view sensor footprints and probabilistic detection models that depend on vehicle position and attitude. Angles-only measurements are processed through Bayesian inference and marginalization over data-association hypotheses to obtain a Poisson multi-Bernoulli (PMB) approximation of the target posterior, representing both detected and undetected targets. This belief directs aerial sensing toward unexplored regions along the ground routes and viewpoints that improve target localization. Ground planning combines chance-constrained target avoidance, enforced through confidence sets, with a void-probability objective that favors routes unlikely to contain threats. We solve each team's optimization problem in a fully decentralized manner using a nested SCvx*--C-ADMM scheme, with outer sequential convex programming iterations and inner distributed consensus optimization, accounting for nonlinearities, nonseparable objectives, and continuous-time inter-agent separation constraints. A closed-loop scheme updates both fleets' trajectories as information becomes available and permits ground motion when the remaining route risk falls below a prescribed threshold. Numerical case studies examine the effects of sensing geometry and target uncertainty, compare decentralized and centralized solvers, and demonstrate full closed-loop collaboration between multiple UAVs and UGVs. Ergodic control, trajectory optimization, sequential convex programming, distributed optimization, optical sensor modeling, risk-sensitive control, random finite set theory, multi-target tracking Introduction ~ sec:intro Collaborative autonomy deals with the problem of coordinating multiple autonomous vehicles to accomplish a common objective. In a homogeneous team, the vehicles typically share similar motion and sensing capabilities, allowing coordination to be formulated around a common vehicle and sensor model. Heterogeneous teams introduce an additional level of coupling, since the capabilities of one vehicle class may be needed for another to complete its task. For example, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) can observe regions that are inaccessible to unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs), while the ground vehicles can carry the payloads needed to execute a mission. This complementary use of aerial and ground platforms has been studied in coordinated exploration and mapping~ dewan2013coordinated , collaborative localization~ butzke2016collaborative , and persistent sensing with mobile recharging~ naveed2025adaptive . In this work, we consider a UAV/UGV team in which the ground vehicles must traverse a bounded domain containing an unknown number of potentially hazardous targets. The UAVs provide aerial overwatch, using onboard optical cameras to discover, localize, and track these targets before the UGVs encounter them. The difficulty is that neither fleet can plan effectively in isolation. The value of a UAV observation depends on its relevance to the ground routes, while the admissibility of those routes depends on what the UAVs have observed. Moreover, failing to detect a target does not imply that a region is empty, since the camera has a limited field of view and a non-unit probability of detection. The planning problem must therefore account for both uncertainty in detected targets and the possibility of targets that have not yet been observed. A natural approach to the aerial search problem is ergodic control, which seeks trajectories whose time-averaged spatial statistics match a prescribed distribution over the search domain. Regions assigned greater probability mass receive proportionally more sensing effort, allowing a single objective to express both broad exploration and concentrated information gathering. The work of mathew2011metrics introduced multiscale metrics for measuring deviations from ergodicity and designing multi-agent coverage dynamics. Subsequent works formulated continuous-time ergodic trajectory optimization~ miller2013trajectory and used expected information densities to guide active sensing with nonlinear measurement models~ miller2016information . The commonly used spectral metric compares weighted Fourier coefficients of the trajectory occupation measure with those of the desired spatial distribution. Alternatively, hughes2025ergodic formulate ergodic trajectory optimization using maximum mean discrepancy between kernel mean embeddings in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, allowing coverage objectives to be specified from samples on more general domains. For a fleet of UAVs, the ergodic objective depends on the aggregate coverage of all agents and thus couples their trajectories through the team Fourier coefficients. abraham2018measurement address this coupling through consensus on the coverage statistics, obtaining decentralized ergodic control for agents with nonlinear dynamics. The sensing model introduces a second difficulty: the point occupation measure of a vehicle does not describe the ground area observed by a camera whose footprint changes with altitude and attitude. Finite sensor footprints and obstacle constraints have been incorporated into ergodic coverage by ayvali2017constrained . Here, we derive the elliptical ground footprint from the position and attitude of the camera and construct a smooth, normalized sensing kernel from this geometry. Integrating this kernel along a trajectory gives an occupation measure that describes the spatial distribution of camera coverage and depends on both the translational and rotational motion of the UAV. Its spectral coefficients enter the fleet ergodic objective, so that the trajectories are optimized with respect to the area observed by the cameras. The same camera geometry also enters a spatially varying detection probability and an angles-only measurement model with pose-dependent covariance. This connects the coverage model used in trajectory planning with the missed detections and measurement uncertainty accounted for in Bayesian inference. The search distribution must, in turn, reflect the information collected by the UAVs. Random finite set (RFS) theory provides a natural Bayesian description of this information, since both the number of targets and their states are uncertain~ mahler2007statistical . The measurements are also a finite set, containing an unknown combination of target detections and clutter, with some targets producing no measurement. Poisson multi-Bernoulli mixture (PMBM) filtering represents undetected targets by a Poisson point process and detected targets by Bernoulli components conditioned on global data-association hypotheses~ garciafernandez2018pmbm . Marginalizing the association uncertainty provides tractable multi-Bernoulli approximations~ williams2015marginal . These ideas have also been used for multi-agent planning that balances the discovery of new objects with the tracking of existing ones~ nguyen2020multiobjective . Here, we specialize the measurement update to camera-based, angles-only observations with pose-dependent detection and measurement quality, and maintain a Poisson multi-Bernoulli (PMB) approximation of the target posterior. This distinction between detected and undetected targets is particularly useful for ground planning, since avoiding known tracks alone does not account for threats in regions that have not been sufficiently explored. Planning around the estimated target positions alone neglects this uncertainty. Chance-constrained trajectory optimization instead limits the probability of violating a safety requirement~ blackmore2011chance , and confidence sets provide a geometric means of accounting for uncertain target locations. For a multi-object belief, the corresponding question is whether an entire region contains any targets. The RFS void probability, namely, the probability that a set contains no objects, has been used to impose safety constraints in sensor control~ beard2017void ; more recently, han2026risk have developed belief control barrier functions from a Poisson representation of multi-object uncertainty. We use the PMB void probability over the corridor swept by a candidate UGV route, which accounts for both the residual undetected-target intensity and the existence and location uncertainty of detected tracks. Its negative logarithm supplies a route-risk cost, while a separate threshold on the remaining fleet corridor determines when the UGVs may proceed under the current belief. As sensing reduces uncertainty or reveals a threat, the ground routes and the aerial search distribution are updated accordingly. Solving the resulting fleet trajectory problems at a centralized ground station requires aggregating all vehicle decision variables and constraints. A decentralized formulation instead allows each vehicle to solve a local problem and exchange the quantities needed to coordinate with its neighbors. Consensus alternating direction method of multipliers (C-ADMM) provides an established framework for this purpose when the local problems are convex~ boyd2011admm . For trajectory planning, rey2018decentralized combine decentralized ADMM with adaptive linearization of collision constraints for agents with linear dynamics. For nonlinear model predictive control, stomberg2026realtime develop a closely related nested scheme in which decentralized sequential quadratic programming uses ADMM to solve the coupled quadratic subproblems. In our setting, nonlinear vehicle dynamics, camera footprints, and collision constraints likewise require an outer approximation method before the fleet problem can be distributed into convex local solves. To this end, we use successive convexification (SCvx), which replaces the nonlinear optimal control problem by a sequence of convex subproblems, with virtual controls and trust regions to handle infeasible linearizations and control the approximation error~ mao2016successive . The SCvx* extension embeds these iterations in an augmented Lagrangian framework to address feasibility of the original nonlinear problem~ oguri2023scvxstar . We also adopt the continuous-time constraint formulation of elango2024ctcs , in which integrated constraint violations are represented by auxiliary dynamics, to account for inter-agent separation between discretization nodes. Within each SCvx* iteration, local copies and graph flows separate the shared collision constraints and the global ergodic coefficient sum, allowing the convex subproblem to be solved using neighbor-to-neighbor C-ADMM updates. The main contributions of this work are as follows: We formulate multi-UAV ergodic trajectory optimization with optical sensor footprints that depend on the full camera pose. Starting from a conic field of view, we derive the position, orientation, and extent of the ground footprint and construct a smooth footprint kernel that defines the team occupation measure and its Fourier coefficients. The resulting ergodic objective measures coverage of the ground area observed by the cameras throughout their motion. We connect Bayesian inference from UAV angles-only measurements to both aerial and ground plannin

title: GradSplat: Gradients Inside the Forward Pass for Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting
summary: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting predicts a scene from a few images, but our predictor is less accurate than its own Gaussians optimized per scene on those images. This gap lies mostly in the shape of the Gaussians, their scale and rotation, since optimizing the shape alone recovers almost all of it and opacity and color recover less. Gradient steps on the input views correct this shape, and the model holds these views at inference. Log-anisotropy correction changes the axis ratios of each Gaussian in log space at constant volume, and in-forward gradient refinement renders the Gaussians into the input views and applies the gradient of the photometric loss with a learned recurrent update, first to opacity and color and then to the shape. GradSplat is a feed-forward model that refines its own Gaussians by learned gradient steps inside its forward pass, with no target view. On both complete six-view RealEstate10K protocols, it has the best PSNR and SSIM among nine methods and keeps its accuracy from $6$ to $42$ input views. Without fine-tuning, it is the most accurate on DL3DV and has the best PSNR and SSIM on ScanNet++. The code will be released at https://github.com/Jingong-Chen/GradSplat/.

title: UMI-Live for In-The-Wild Bimanual Robotics Data Collection
summary: Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) devices allow human experts to demonstrate tasks for robot learning without teleoperating physical robots. Using these demonstrations as training data still requires a consistent hardware setup, calibration, and data processing. We present UMI-Live, a full-stack open-source bimanual UMI system for in-the-wild data collection. We design our custom UMI-Live hardware to integrate camera and LiDAR--inertial sensing, onboard compute, and power, without external tracking equipment or calibration within the collection environment. We implement a simple user interface for recording data while an asynchronous pipeline performs parallel SLAM reconstruction and publishes training-ready datasets. We also release software that supports dual-YAM teleoperation and VLA policy training and inference. We validate UMI-Live data quality by fine-tuning $π_{0.5}$ and MolmoAct2, achieving success rates of 10/10 and 8/10, respectively on a bimanual pick-and-place task. Furthermore, we release 40 hours of UMI-Live data across three tasks, and complete hardware designs, software, and reproduction guides at our $\href{https://umi-live.github.io/}{\text{project website}}$.
full_text: Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) devices allow human experts to demonstrate tasks for robot learning without teleoperating physical robots. Using these demonstrations as training data still requires a consistent hardware setup, calibration, and data processing. We present UMI-Live, a full-stack open-source bimanual UMI system for in-the-wild data collection. We design our custom UMI-Live hardware to integrate camera and LiDAR--inertial sensing, onboard compute, and power, without external tracking equipment or calibration within the collection environment. We implement a simple user interface for recording data while an asynchronous pipeline performs parallel SLAM reconstruction and publishes training-ready datasets. We also release software that supports dual-YAM teleoperation and VLA policy training and inference. We validate UMI-Live data quality by fine-tuning and MolmoAct2, achieving success rates of 10/10 and 8/10, respectively on a bimanual pick-and-place task. Furthermore, we release 40 hours of UMI-Live data across three tasks, and complete hardware designs, software, and reproduction guides at our project website . Introduction Much of the recent progress in robot manipulation has come from imitation learning, in which policies learn manipulation behaviors from human demonstrations, increasingly drawn from large and diverse datasets. Diffusion policies~ chi2024diffusionpolicyvisuomotorpolicy and vision-language-action (VLA) models such as RT-2, OpenVLA, , , and GR00T N1~ brohan2023rt2visionlanguageactionmodelstransfer,kim2024openvlaopensourcevisionlanguageactionmodel,black2026pi0visionlanguageactionflowmodel,intelligence2025pi_,nvidia2025gr00tn1openfoundation are all trained this way. More recently, world-action models (WAMs) jointly predict future visual observations and robot actions~ zhu2025unifiedworldmodelscoupling,kim2026cosmospolicyfinetuningvideo,ye2026worldactionmodelszeroshot , which allows them to build on large-scale video pretraining. Video alone, however, carries no robot action labels, so WAMs still learn to act from action-labeled demonstrations. These methods allow robots to perform tasks ranging from pick-and-place to dexterous manipulation, including towel and shirt folding~ black2026pi0visionlanguageactionflowmodel . Learning these skills in new environments still depends on expert demonstrations covering the relevant objects and interactions. Collecting high-quality demonstrations across diverse environments therefore continues to be a key challenge in robot learning. Action-labeled demonstrations are commonly collected by teleoperating physical robots. Large collection efforts such as DROID and ABC-130K show the value of collecting demonstrations across operators, tasks, and environments~ khazatsky2025droidlargescaleinthewildrobot,allshire2026scalablebehaviorcloningopen . Because each collection site must host the robot along with its control, perception, and safety infrastructure, expanding to new environments requires transporting this equipment or maintaining additional robot stations. The Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) removes this requirement by letting experts demonstrate tasks with handheld grippers instead of robots~ chi2024universal . UMI showed that policies trained on wrist observations and reconstructed gripper trajectories from in-the-wild demonstrations can perform challenging tasks, including bimanual ones. Subsequent UMI systems have explored different sensing, tracking, and gripper designs. However, reproducing these systems requires clear instructions for building and calibrating the hardware, together with software for processing the recordings. Some UMI configurations use stationary tracking rigs or backpack-mounted computers, which add equipment to set up or carry~ ohkawa2026yubiyieldinguniversalbidigital,zeng2025activeumiroboticmanipulationactive . Bulky gripper designs can also make dexterous manipulation of small objects difficult~ ohkawa2026yubiyieldinguniversalbidigital . Furthermore, each recording must be reconstructed and converted into a training-ready dataset. Manually managing these steps becomes tedious, and we believe that operators should be able to start the next demonstration while the software prepares completed recordings for training and physical robot evaluation. We present UMI-Live, a complete hardware and software system for in-the-wild bimanual collection and robot learning. Each UMI-Live gripper integrates camera and LiDAR--inertial sensing, onboard compute and storage, and removable power. An operator can continue recording data with the press of a single button, while an asynchronous pipeline transfers completed recordings and performs parallel reconstruction, gripper position and jaw opening estimation, validation, and dataset preparation. We also provide software for dual-YAM teleoperation, policy training, and inference. We release approximately 40 hours of demonstrations across three tasks and evaluate policies fine-tuned on mixtures containing mostly UMI demonstrations. The handheld demonstrations are collected at a different location and under different lighting conditions from those used for robot evaluation, while the smaller teleoperation component provides demonstrations from the target robot and scene. We make the following contributions. Reproducible bimanual hardware for in-the-wild collection. We present self-contained handheld grippers with integrated sensing, compute, storage, power, and operator controls, together with hardware designs and construction and calibration guides for reproducing the system. Complete software integration from recording to robot deployment. We provide software for coordinated recording, asynchronous transfer, parallel and batched processing, LeRobot dataset preparation, dual-YAM teleoperation, and policy training and inference. Operators can continue collecting while completed demonstrations are processed. A public bimanual dataset and physical robot validation. We release approximately 40 hours of demonstrations across three manipulation tasks and evaluate two VLA policies through physical rollouts. Following mixed-data fine-tuning, succeeds in up to 10/10 trials and MolmoAct2 succeeds in 8/10 trials compared with 0/10 for its released checkpoint. Related Work sec:related-work Robot demonstration collection. Teleoperation records observations and actions directly on the target embodiment. BridgeData V2, DROID, RoboMIND, ALOHA Unleashed, and ABC-130K illustrate the breadth of manipulation data that can be collected through physical robot operation~ walke2024bridgedatav2datasetrobot,khazatsky2025droidlargescaleinthewildrobot,Wu_2025,zhao2024alohaunleashedsimplerecipe,allshire2026scalablebehaviorcloningopen . These efforts cover different tasks, environments, and embodiments, but require a robot for demonstration capture. supports handheld collection independently of robot operation and provides a separate teleoperation configuration for obtaining complementary demonstrations on the target embodiment. Handheld UMI systems. The original UMI combines a handheld gripper, wrist video, gripper-state sensing, and visual--inertial trajectory reconstruction to support robot learning from portable demonstrations~ chi2024universal . FastUMI develops the hardware, tracking, and collection tools for broader deployment~ zhaxizhuoma2025fastumiscalablehardwareindependentuniversal . UMI-3D introduces LiDAR-centered reconstruction and an integrated acquisition, calibration, training, and deployment pipeline, with a reported single-arm configuration~ wang2026umi3dextendinguniversalmanipulation . uses two independently instrumented LiDAR--inertial devices as one coordinated bimanual collection system. Other systems make different choices about sensing and interaction. YUBI emphasizes finger-aligned operation and bimanual dexterity, with stationary and portable collection configurations~ ohkawa2026yubiyieldinguniversalbidigital . ActiveUMI combines a VR headset with a backpack-mounted computer to record active egocentric perception~ zeng2025activeumiroboticmanipulationactive . HiFi-UMI uses head-mounted stereo--inertial sensing, hardware synchronization, and direct relative-pose estimation to improve bimanual trajectory fidelity~ ai2026hifiumilearningdeployablemanipulation . places sensing, compute, storage, power, and recording controls on the handheld devices and connects their outputs to an automated processing system and a dual-YAM learning workflow. Collection and robot-learning software. LeRobot provides shared dataset representations and tools for policy training, evaluation, and inference~ cadene2026lerobotopensourcelibraryendtoend . RoboPocket connects portable collection to remote policy feedback and asynchronous fine-tuning~ fang2026robopocketimproverobotpolicies , and ABC provides open infrastructure spanning collection, training, and evaluation~ allshire2026scalablebehaviorcloningopen . combines bimanual LiDAR--inertial recording, asynchronous reconstruction and LeRobot dataset publication, and dual-YAM teleoperation, policy training, and inference in a reproducible setup. System Design Figure~ fig:overview shows how connects in-the-wild bimanual collection to automated processing, LeRobot datasets, and physical robot learning. We first describe the handheld hardware, including the gripper mechanism, sensing, and power design (Section~ sec:hardware ), followed by recording, trajectory reconstruction, dataset export, and parallel processing (Section~ sec:pipeline ). We then evaluate policies trained on the collected demonstrations (Section~ sec:experiments ). Hardware Design sec:hardware Design objectives. hardware consists of two handheld grippers with onboard sensing, compute, and storage for bimanual data collection. Our design focuses on modularity, usability, and user-friendliness. Figure~ fig:hardware-views shows the assembled unit from the front, side, and rear, and Figure~ fig:cad-modules shows its main components. Appendix~ app:hardware provides additional hardware details. Gripper mechanism. We improve the original UMI gripper mechanism~ chi2024universal by using bearing-supported trigger and gear pivots for smoother actuation and reduced backlash. Squeezing the trigger rotates two sector gears that engage racks on the finger mounts (Figure~ fig:hardware-details a,b). The mounts travel along a linear guide to produce opposing parallel-jaw motion. To achieve smoother gripper motion, we apply adhesive tape as shown in Figure~ fig:hardware-details . We also place ArUco tags~ garridojurado2014aruco on the moving finger mounts to measure the jaw opening. We redesign the UMI gripper finger to adapt to more tasks that involve dexterous manipulation with smaller objects. We print the gripper fingers with a rigid PLA+ base and a thin TPU contact layer (Figure~ fig:gripper-fingers ). The rigid base resists bending under grasping loads and it supports force application and precision contact with small objects such as screws. The TPU layer provides compliance at the contact surface, which helps the fingers conform to different object shapes. We demonstrate the capabilities of the redesigned grippers through human-operated tasks involving small-object grasping and insertion, match lighting, and shirt folding in Appendix~ app:manipulation-demonstrations . title: Ask to Evolve: A Unified Harness for Lifelong Embodied Navigation with Hybrid Action Space and Persistent Memory
summary: Giving embodied agents the freedom to act autonomously, initiate interactions, and understand their surroundings through experience is a step toward bringing them to life in the physical world. Realizing this vision requires action, interaction, and memory to work together, so that each encounter can inform current decisions and contribute experience for future tasks. We present EvoLife, a unified navigation harness that enables a multimodal embodied agent to choose how to move, when to ask, and what experience to carry forward. Its hybrid action space supports waypoint navigation, local discrete adjustments, pixel-based navigation, and object-directed navigation. Active interaction allows the agent to seek clarification or assistance when it encounters ambiguity or difficulty, while persistent spatial memory binds observations and dialogue to places, retaining useful experience to guide subsequent visits. We evaluate eight benchmarks across four task families: vision-language navigation, object navigation, interactive instance navigation, and continuous multi-task navigation. With an average of only 1.87 active interactions per episode, our method achieves a first-visit success rate (SR) of 100% across four 100-episode sets spanning vision-language navigation and object navigation. Complete-sequence SR reaches 98% on 50 LHPR-VLN sequences and 94% on 50 GOAT-Bench sequences. In the R2R revisit setting, success weighted by path length (SPL) increases from 82.23% to 93.31% with retained experience. Multi-day physical navigation further demonstrates exploration, proactive help-seeking, and revisiting remembered places. Together, these results advance the vision of bringing embodied agents to life through autonomous action, proactive interaction, and the accumulation and reuse of experience.
full_text: Introduction sec:introduction Lifelong embodied navigation calls for agents that can take initiative in how they act, interact, and accumulate experience. An agent should be able to choose how to pursue a goal according to its environment and task requirements, ask questions when it encounters ambiguity, seek assistance when progress becomes difficult, and carry what it learns into future tasks. These capabilities give concrete meaning to the vision of bringing embodied agents to life in the physical world. Through sustained engagement with their surroundings, agents can connect what they perceive with what they do, use interaction to develop their understanding, and build experience that remains useful beyond a single encounter. People navigating unfamiliar environments naturally ask for clarification, request directions, and seek help when needed. Embodied agents need the freedom to take the same initiative. A question can clarify an instruction, identify a useful continuation, or obtain assistance with a physical obstacle. The value of that interaction can also extend beyond the immediate task: an answer about a place, together with the observations and actions that follow, can become experience for a later visit. This motivates the central idea of Ask to Evolve : an agent actively asks to improve its understanding, acts on the resulting information, and retains useful experience to guide future behavior. Embodied navigation provides concrete settings for studying this process. Vision-language navigation connects linguistic instructions with visual observations and navigation decisions, including movement through continuous environments~ r2r2018,rxr2020,vlnce2020,dai2026dped . Interactive navigation introduces dialogue as a source of clarification and assistance~ cvdn2020,hanna2019,orion2024 , while iterative and lifelong navigation make earlier encounters relevant to subsequent tasks~ ivln2023,goat2024 . Systematic real-world evaluations have documented a substantial gap between simulated and physical navigation performance~ wang2026comprehensive,wang2025rethinking . This gap highlights the importance of coordinating perception, decision-making, and execution, together with the ability to obtain assistance and reuse experience in real environments. Existing methods offer useful foundations. Topological planners connect visual waypoints with continuous control~ etpnav2025 , and language-model navigators integrate observations, reasoning, and actions through execution interfaces~ navgpt2024,navgpt32026 . Memory-based systems retain observations and behavior, while navigation harnesses preserve maps and task records across sessions~ memoir2026,navharness2026,harnessvln2026 . These advances motivate a unified systems question: how can an embodied agent keep multiple ways of moving, actively requested assistance, and remembered experience available within the same decision loop? The connection matters because an interaction may change the next movement, revise the interpretation of a place, and contribute knowledge that is useful during a subsequent task. We introduce , a unified harness for lifelong embodied navigation with a hybrid action space, active interaction, and persistent spatial memory. Its action space supports four complementary modes: waypoint navigation toward a selected spatial location, local discrete adjustments for fine control, pixel-based navigation toward a selected image location, and object-directed navigation toward an identified target. These modes give the agent flexibility in expressing its movement intention. It can select a spatial waypoint, make a short adjustment, indicate a visible location, or approach an object, according to the task and available observations. Execution returns the actual outcome, allowing the agent to inspect its progress and choose its next action. presents the overall framework. Active interaction is part of this ongoing decision process. The agent chooses when to ask and formulates its question using the current task, observations, and relevant memory. It can request clarification when an instruction is ambiguous, ask for guidance when the continuation is uncertain, or seek practical assistance when the environment prevents progress. After receiving a response, the agent decides how to act and uses subsequent observations and execution feedback to assess the outcome. Interaction therefore gives the agent an active means of obtaining information and assistance while remaining connected to movement and the experience generated through execution. Persistent spatial memory allows these experiences to accumulate across tasks. Place records bind locations to descriptions, observations, historical images, and dialogue. Information acquired through an interaction can update a place description, support a later navigation decision, or help interpret a familiar environment under changed conditions. New observations can, in turn, prompt revisions to existing records. This continuous accumulation and refinement of spatial knowledge allows the agent's experience to evolve across successive tasks. By creating, retrieving, updating, and reusing historical memories, the agent can not only acquire new knowledge from current encounters but also leverage evolving experience to guide future decisions. We evaluate on eight navigation benchmarks across four task families: vision-language navigation~ r2r2018,rxr2020,vlnce2020 , object navigation~ hm3d2021,hm3dsem2023,ovon2024 , interactive instance navigation~ vlln2025,coin2025 , and continuous multi-task navigation~ lhpr2025,goat2024 . The main study includes six sets of 100 single-task episodes and two sets of 50 continuous sequences. With an average of only 1.87 active interactions per episode, our method achieves a success rate (SR) of 100 across four 100-episode sets spanning vision-language navigation and object navigation. Complete-sequence SR reaches 98 on LHPR-VLN and 94 on GOAT-Bench. In the R2R revisit setting, success weighted by path length (SPL) increases from 82.23 to 93.31 with retained experience. Ablation analyses further examine interaction and experience reuse, while multi-day physical experiments demonstrate exploration, proactive help-seeking, and revisiting remembered places. Our contributions are threefold: Hybrid action space. We propose , which enables an embodied agent to select among four navigation modes and adapt subsequent decisions based on execution feedback. Active interaction. We integrate proactive interaction into the navigation loop, allowing the agent to autonomously decide when to ask, generate clarification or assistance requests, and incorporate responses into navigation decisions. Persistent memory. We develop a dynamic long-term memory mechanism that associates observations, descriptions, and dialogue with spatial locations, enabling explicit memory updates and continuous experience accumulation across tasks. Together, extensive benchmark evaluations and multi-day physical experiments advance the vision of bringing embodied agents to life through autonomous action, proactive interaction, and accumulated experience that guides future encounters. Related Work sec:related Embodied Navigation Embodied navigation connects visual perception and language understanding with executable movement~ wang2024causal,wang2026magic . R2R established instruction-guided indoor navigation, RxR expanded instruction diversity through detailed multilingual descriptions, and continuous VLN extended execution beyond discrete viewpoint graphs~ r2r2018,rxr2020,vlnce2020 . Surveys and systematic real-world evaluations organize VLN through action and model paradigms and identify challenges in transferring navigation capabilities from simulation to physical environments~ wang2026comprehensive . These developments make the connection between decision-making and execution a central issue in embodied navigation. Existing approaches organize this connection in different ways. ETPNav combines online waypoint topology, cross-modal planning, and obstacle-aware execution~ etpnav2025 . NavGPT and NavGPT-3 explore explicit reasoning and interfaces connecting reasoning, action, and runtime execution~ navgpt2024,navgpt32026 . NaVid, StreamVLN, and NaVILA connect visual history and language with executable behavior~ navid2024,streamvln2025,navila2025 . P2DNav uses panoramic direction selection and downview grounding, NavJev introduces action-specific visual compression, and CLASH coordinates reactive and reflective planning~ p2dnav2026,navjev2026,clash2025 . Correctable landmark discovery and disentangled navigation reasoning provide further mechanisms for interpreting observations and selecting actions~ console2024,navcot2025,yu2026correctnav . These studies highlight the importance of how movement intentions are expressed and executed. integrates waypoint navigation, local discrete adjustments, pixel-based navigation, and object-directed navigation into a unified interface. The agent selects among these modes, inspects execution feedback, and obtains additional information through interaction and memory, connecting action selection with the evidence available for subsequent decisions. Interactive Navigation Interactive navigation enables embodied agents to obtain information and assistance through dialogue. CVDN connects navigation with dialogue history collected through interaction with an informed guide~ cvdn2020 . HANNA studies agents that actively request language and visual assistance~ hanna2019 , while ORION integrates thinking, acting, and asking to incorporate feedback into object navigation~ orion2024 . These approaches treat interaction as an action that can influence how an agent interprets its task and proceeds through the environment. Interaction is particularly useful when the available instruction or observation is insufficient to identify the intended goal. VL-LN and CoIN study dialogue for underspecified goals and target disambiguation~ vlln2025,coin2025 . GG-Nav and ProCompNav further investigate interactive navigation and goal resolution~ ggnav2026,procompnav2026 . Talk2Escape and AVERT-VLN also examine external assistance in navigation~ talk2escape2026,avertvln2026 . Across these settings, useful interaction requires the agent to decide when help is needed, formulate a relevant request, and incorporate the response into subsequent action. Questions therefore connect the agent's current uncertainty with information that supports continued navigation. integrates this initiative into the unified navigation loop. The agent can ask for clarification, request guidance, or seek assistance with an environmental difficulty, then use the response and subsequent observations to decide how to proceed. Information acquired through interaction also becomes part of persistent place records, remaining available beyond the current exchange. This connection between asking, acting, and retaining experience is central to Ask to Evolve . title: PRIME W0: Physical Priors from World Models for Embodied Manipulation
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models excel at instruction following, yet most remain feed-forward: they condition actions only on the current observation and discard both long-horizon temporal context and the hierarchical structure of VLM representations. We present PRIME W0, a hierarchical conditional flow-matching framework that closes this gap through three synergistic designs: (1)per-layer KV injection from a pretrained VLM into an Adaptive MoE action expert; (2)dynamics-aware conditioning via asynchronous world-model subgoal-image prediction and a DINOv2 historical-frame semantic bridge; and (3)Action Dynamic Manifold (ADM) flow matching with covariance-structured noise that respects robot kinematic coupling. By pretraining on large-scale internet data and fine-tuning on robot demonstrations, VLAs achieve impressive breadth across tasks and embodiments. Recent flow- and diffusion-based VLAs further improve action expressiveness by replacing autoregressive decoders with continuous generative processes, enabling multi-modal action distributions and smoother trajectories~ pi0 . The dynamics--semantics gap. Despite these advances, most VLA policies remain feed-forward: at each control step they condition action generation only on the current observation and instruction, without an explicit model of how the scene will evolve. This creates two coupled limitations. First, temporal myopia: long-horizon tasks with occlusion, contact ambiguity, or multi-phase manipulation require tracking motion trends and anticipating near-future scene layout, yet repeating the full VLM on every historical frame is prohibitively expensive. Second, semantic compression: many architectures route action decoding through a single compressed VLM representation, discarding the hierarchical semantic--spatial structure accumulated across intermediate layers that is critical for fine-grained motor control. Flow-matching action decoders exacerbate both issues. During denoising, early steps benefit from high-level task semantics while late steps require precise perceptual grounding and kinematically consistent trajectories. A policy that conditions only on the present frame and a collapsed VLM summary cannot simultaneously supply forward temporal anchors and layer-wise semantic detail. Core question. Can we build a VLA foundation model that (i)~anticipates near-future scene evolution, (ii)~exploits long-horizon visual history efficiently, and (iii)~generates actions on the low-dimensional manifold of physically feasible robot behaviour? (Physical pRIors from world Models for Embodied manipulation) addresses this question with a hierarchical conditional flow-matching framework that couples a pretrained VLM with three synergistic design layers ( ): [leftmargin=1.5em] Semantic reasoning via per-layer KV injection. Rather than collapsing the VLM into a single bottleneck vector, we extract Key/Value projections from all backbone layers and inject them into the action expert through cross-attention, preserving both high-level intent and low-level spatial grounding. Dynamics-aware conditioning. A compact world model predicts explicit subgoal RGB images from the previous observation; these are encoded as visual tokens and injected asynchronously into the VLM, supplying forward scene anchors without blocking inference on future-frame capture. In parallel, a DINOv2-based historical-frame encoder bridges past observations into the language-model embedding space as , enabling long-range temporal context without repeated VLM forwards. Manifold-constrained action generation. We replace the autoregressive action head with Action Dynamic Manifold (ADM) flow matching over an Adaptive MoE decoder. Covariance noise sampled from demonstration statistics respects kinematic coupling, while temporally gated expert routing specialises behaviour across manipulation phases. Training proceeds in four stages ( ; ): VLM pre-training; geometry-aware action tokenisation and NTP visuomotor pre-training on a mixed teleop / UMI / simulation corpus ( ); DiT flow-matching decoder assembly with frozen VLM, WM injection, and Adaptive MoE; and end-to-end SFT under a composite objective that unifies flow matching, MoE load balancing, and auxiliary VLM/WM supervision. Contributions. [leftmargin=1.5em] We propose a hierarchical conditional flow-matching framework that closes the loop between VLM semantic reasoning, asynchronous WM subgoal-image prediction, and manifold-constrained continuous control ( ). We introduce asynchronous subgoal-image injection and a historical-frame semantic bridge, enabling dynamics-aware conditioning without increasing end-to-end latency or re-running the full VLM on past frames. We develop ADM with covariance-structured flow matching and Adaptive MoE action experts, jointly realising phase-aware, kinematically grounded action generation on a learned action manifold. We demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on LIBERO and an in-house real-robot suite, together with systematic ablations confirming the contribution of each architectural component ( ).
