title: From Reasoning to Action: Consequence-Grounded Alignment for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary:
Reasoning informs decision-making by connecting intended actions with their expected consequences. Recent vision-language-action (VLA) models incorporate embodied chains of thought (ECoTs) to guide action generation. However, such guidance remains implicit, as actions are conditioned on ECoTs rather than explicitly optimized to align with them.
  We introduce CoRAct, a consequence-grounded reasoning-to-action alignment framework that explicitly aligns reasoning and action through reward-guided optimization in action noise space. CoRAct formulates two physically grounded ECoT components as verifiable signals: movement specifies intended motion, while waypoints encode expected spatial consequences. A unified Mixture-of-Transformers jointly models ECoT reasoning, action generation, and action-conditioned future prediction. For candidate actions generated from sampled noise, CoRAct computes alignment rewards based on movement consistency and agreement between predicted outcomes and specified waypoints. These rewards guide group-relative optimization of the initial noise distribution, steering action generation toward consistency with intended actions and expected consequences.
  Experiments across RoboCasa, VLABench, and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate improvements in task success, generalization, and reasoning-execution alignment over strong ECoT-based VLA baselines. CoRAct also grounds externally provided ECoTs in executable behavior, enabling zero-shot adaptation to novel scenarios by leveraging knowledge from powerful vision-language models.
  Project page and dataset: https://onlyxingxingzyx.github.io/CoRAct/
full_text: Reasoning informs decision-making by connecting intended actions with their expected consequences. Building on this principle, recent vision-language-action models incorporate embodied chains of thought (ECoTs) as an intermediate stage in action generation. However, such guidance remains implicit, as actions are conditioned on the generated ECoTs rather than explicitly optimized to align with them. To bridge this gap, we introduce the Consequence-grounded Reasoning-to-Action alignment method called CoRAct, an offline training framework that explicitly aligns reasoning and action through reward-guided optimization in action noise space. Specifically, CoRAct formulates two physically grounded ECoT components as verifiable signals: movement specifies the intended motion, whereas waypoints encode the expected spatial consequence of execution. By jointly modeling ECoT reasoning, action generation, and action-conditioned future prediction, a unified Mixture-of-Transformers explicitly couples each action with its articulated intent and predicted consequence. For action candidates generated from sampled noise, CoRAct computes alignment rewards based on motion consistency with the described movement and agreement between predicted outcomes and the specified waypoints. These rewards drive group-relative optimization of the initial noise distribution, steering action generation toward consistency with the articulated intent and expected consequence. Extensive experiments across RoboCasa, VLABench, and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate consistent gains in task success and generalization over strong ECoT-based VLA baselines. Further analyses reveal improved reasoning–execution alignment and show that our method can ground externally provided ECoTs in executable behavior, supporting zero-shot adaptation to novel scenarios by leveraging knowledge from powerful VLMs. Our project page and dataset are publicly available at https://onlyxingxingzyx.github.io/CoRAct/ . INTRODUCTION Human decision-making often involves prospective reasoning that connects intended actions with their expected consequences. Such reasoning mediates between task intent and concrete behavior by relating action formulation to anticipated outcomes. Inspired by this capability, recent vision-language-action (VLA) models increasingly integrate intermediate reasoning into action generation in the form of embodied chains of thought (ECoTs)~ zawalski25a,sunemma,zhao2025cot,huang2025motvla,shou2026halo . By structuring action generation around textual plans, visual subgoals, spatial targets, and action-level intentions, ECoTs provide an intermediate interface between task understanding and physical execution~ ma2026unifying,lu2026thinkingvla . As the paradigm evolves, embodied reasoning is increasingly integrated into the perception–action pipeline, extending beyond purely textual deliberation toward representations more closely tied to physical control. Prior efforts have improved VLA generalization through diversity-driven task generation zhang2026robogene , visual data augmentation wang2026roboaug , and unified vision-motion representation learning fan2026xr1 . While these approaches enhance generalization across diverse tasks, objects, and visual conditions, adapting to unseen semantic constraints and novel task compositions requires reasoning beyond learned action patterns. Embodied reasoning offers a complementary path toward such out-of-distribution generalization by connecting task intent with anticipated physical consequences. However, its potential remains limited if the generated actions fail to faithfully realize the articulated reasoning. Existing VLA models typically use ECoTs as conditioning context for action generation, leaving this correspondence to be learned implicitly from demonstrations rather than enforced through an explicit optimization objective~ huang2025motvla,shou2026halo,kim2026roboalign,sun2026atomvla . In embodied control, this gap has concrete consequences: a model may articulate an appropriate motion yet generate an action that deviates from it, or anticipate a plausible spatial outcome that execution fails to realize. These discrepancies reveal a missing link between coherent intermediate reasoning and physical behavior that faithfully reflects both the stated intent and the expected outcome. To bridge this gap, we introduce CoRAct, an offline training framework for consequence-grounded reasoning-to-action alignment. CoRAct explicitly optimizes the consistency between embodied reasoning and generated actions through reward-based learning in the action noise space. The key idea is to treat the motion intent and spatial expectations expressed in embodied reasoning as verifiable constraints for action generation. These signals provide concrete criteria for evaluating whether generated actions follow the articulated reasoning and whether their predicted consequences agree with the expected outcomes. By translating these consistency evaluations into alignment rewards, CoRAct establishes a direct connection between embodied reasoning and action optimization, enabling reasoning-aware improvement of robotic policies. Specifically, CoRAct extracts two physically grounded signals from ECoT reasoning: movement for describing the intended motion and waypoints for representing the expected spatial consequence. To connect these reasoning signals to action generation and future consequences, we build a unified Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) architecture that jointly models ECoT reasoning, action generation, and action-conditioned future prediction. This joint formulation associates each generated action with both its articulated intent and predicted consequence, allowing the same action candidate to be evaluated against the reasoning that motivates it and the future outcome it is expected to produce. CoRAct therefore measures whether a generated action follows the described movement and whether its predicted consequence agrees with the specified waypoint, and converts these two forms of consistency into alignment rewards. Building on these alignment signals, CoRAct optimizes action generation in the noise space. For each reasoning context, multiple action candidates are generated from sampled noise and evaluated for motion and consequence consistency. The resulting rewards drive group-relative optimization of a conditional noise predictor, guiding it toward noise samples that induce actions better aligned with both the intended motion and expected consequence. This improves the fidelity between ECoT reasoning and generated actions, strengthening reasoning-to-action alignment. We evaluate CoRAct across RoboCasa, VLABench, and real-world manipulation tasks, demonstrating consistent improvements in task success and generalization over strong ECoT-based VLA baselines. Further analyses show stronger alignment between reasoning and execution, with the benefits extending beyond reasoning generated by the policy itself. In particular, CoRAct can ground ECoTs provided by powerful VLMs in executable actions, allowing their knowledge and decision-making capabilities to guide manipulation in novel scenarios. This capability enables zero-shot adaptation through external reasoning without additional policy training, extending ECoTs from an intermediate reasoning representation to a general interface for guiding physical behavior. Overall, our main contributions are as follows: We introduce CoRAct, a consequence-grounded alignment framework that explicitly makes consistency between embodied reasoning and physical execution. Building on joint training, we derive alignment rewards from motion consistency with movement descriptions and agreement between predicted outcomes and waypoints. These rewards drive group-relative policy optimization in action noise space, steering actions toward the articulated intent and expected consequences Experiments in simulation and the real world demonstrate higher task success and stronger generalization than strong ECoT-based VLA baselines. Further experiments show that improved reasoning–action alignment enables zero-shot adaptation to novel scenarios RELATED WORKS Embodied Chain-of-Thought Reasoning. To improve generalization and interpretability in vision-language-action policies, embodied chain-of-thought (ECoT) introduces intermediate reasoning representations that connect semantic task understanding with grounded robot control. Early approaches instantiate reasoning in language: ECoT generates grounded textual traces~ zawalski25a , while EMMA-X augments them with look-ahead spatial guidance~ sunemma . Subsequent work broadens the reasoning substrate beyond text through representations including future visual subgoals~ zhao2025cot , reinforced visual planning~ huang2026thinkact , and coarse action trajectories~ zhong2026acot . Complementary work shifts reasoning from explicit generation into latent representations: ECoT-Lite studies how reasoning supervision shapes action-relevant representations~ chen25a , while LaRA-VLA~ bai2026latent and LaST ~ liu2026last internalize multimodal and spatio-temporal CoTs in continuous latent states. ERVLA shows that ECoT supervision is not uniformly beneficial: high-level semantic traces alone yield limited gains, whereas action-grounded signals provide stronger guidance for control~ sun2026revisiting . Despite this progress, most methods induce correspondence between reasoning and action implicitly through conditioning supervision, without directly verifying whether policy-generated actions comply with the model's CoT. In contrast, CoRAct turns generated ECoTs from conditioning context into verifiable supervision, explicitly training the policy to translate articulated reasoning into physical execution. Consistency between Reasoning and Execution. Consistency between articulated reasoning and physical execution is essential for reliable embodied decision-making. Prior work formulates this correspondence as explicit language–action alignment, using contrastive grounding and preference learning to align generated descriptions with visual observations and action trajectories~ Wulff_2026_CVPR . Beyond representation-level alignment, model-based approaches couple structured reasoning with low-level planning or action-conditioned future prediction~ ma2026dvlm,tan2025latent,wu2025foresight . Feedback-driven policy optimization improves robotic behavior through human-assisted action preferences xia2025apo and reliable value estimation xia2026robovaluerl . Complementary approaches leverage external semantic reasoning to guide fine-grained action correction~ xia2025phoenix . In contrast, CoRAct directly grounds a VLA's embodied reasoning in action generation, using explicit consistency rewards to align articulated intent, executed motions, and predicted consequences. Runtime verification selects among policy samples through simulated consequences or learned action verifiers~ kwok2026scaling,wu2025you,kwok25a,dai2025rover . These deployment-time methods require repeated policy sampling and external evaluation, often through an interactive simulator or a VLM-based verifier. To move this burden into training, recent work employs verifiable rewards, task-success signals, or learned critics to post-train reasoning VLAs~ ye2025vla,yin2025deepthinkvla,wang2025alpamayo,foutter2026vision . However, these objectives primarily assess textual reasoning, visual grounding, high-level trajectories, or episode-level success, rather than directly constraining correspondence between structured CoT fields and fine- grained action chunks. They do not jointly impose two sample-level constraints central to CoRAct: whether an action follows the generated CoT and whether its predicted consequence realizes the intended spatial outcome. title: How Much Should a VLA Trust Its Reasoning? Step-Level Guidance as a Measured Action-Value Function
summary: Reasoning vision-language-action (VLA) policies write a reasoning trace and then decode the action from it. A wrong trace yields a wrong action, and even a correct-looking trace can mislead the plan. Existing remedies ask whether the reasoning is right. We ask how strongly it should steer. CoC-CFG applies classifier-free guidance between the policy's context and the same context without the reasoning span. One weight per Euler step attenuates or amplifies the reasoning, and w=1 recovers the original policy. We treat the choice of this weight as a Markov decision process whose action values are measured, not bootstrapped. With the expert frozen and the noise fixed, applying a weight for one step and finishing the plan under the current controller returns that weight's value exactly. Q-adaptive guidance fits these values with small critics and improves the controller conservatively. In the Alpasim driving simulator it outperforms every fixed weight and online RL (SAC, GRPO) in open loop, and in closed loop it passes 262 of 300 scenes, against 252 for the original policy. On held-out frames of the Waymo end-to-end driving benchmark, its first three stages outperform every fixed weight, four adaptive-guidance methods, SAC and GRPO. On the hidden test set, a frozen Alpamayo 1.5 with rule-based camera and vehicle conversions and Q-adaptive guidance sets a new state of the art among published methods: 8.135159 rater feedback score, against 8.079 for the best published method.

The trace is not a caption but part of the condition: editing it moves the trajectory nguyen2026vladrivebench . The trace is often wrong. Fewer than half of a driving VLA's traces match the scene mayumu2026faithful , VLMs answer driving questions from the text rather than the image xie2025drivebench , and hallucination has statistical causes kalai2025why . title: LOGIV: Graph-Verified Execution with Causal Local Repair for Long-Horizon Robot Tasks
summary: Agentic robots must turn a high-level goal into actions while keeping the physical conditions needed for future steps valid. A completed action does not ensure that its effects will persist: a later disturbance can invalidate support that the remaining plan still assumes. We present LOGIV, a graph engineering framework for agentic robot execution that uses an explicit task graph to connect symbolic planning, observation-based verification, and embodied action. LOGIV compiles a validated plan into condition-support and resource-ordering edges, checks their physical validity during execution, and uses dependency tracing to determine what must be restored after a failure. Repair is constrained by retained unfinished actions, and the combined continuation is symbolically validated before execution resumes. The framework operates above existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) and World Action Model (WAM) policies without adding trainable components. Across 20 dual-arm tasks from RoboTwin~V2 and BiCoord with three execution backbones, LOGIV improves mean task success without injected disturbances by 10.67 and 15.33 percentage points, respectively. Under predefined perturbations, it achieves higher task completion and condition restoration than three adapted recovery baselines for every backbone on both benchmarks. On three real-robot tasks, successful trials increase from 12/30 to 17/30. These results support explicit, continuously checked task dependencies as a practical interface for reliable agentic robot execution.

Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models~ team2024octo,kim2024openvla,intelligence2025pi_ and World Action Models (WAMs)~ yuan2026fast,cai2026aha provide increasingly capable execution policies, while an agent-level controller must decide how their actions contribute to a longer task. A distinctive difficulty in physical execution is that an intermediate result can cease to hold after the action that produced it has succeeded. A support placed during bridge assembly may be displaced before the beam is installed (Fig.~ fig:teaser ). The placement remains a completed action, yet the support condition needed by the remaining plan is no longer valid. Reliable long-horizon behavior therefore requires tracking both action completion and the continuing validity of its consequences. Existing work provides important components for this execution loop. LLM- and VLM-based systems select skills, interpret feedback, and organize multistep behavior~ ouyang2025long,huang2024rekep,feng2025reflective,chen2025robohorizon,ji2026hime,peng2026cortex,zhang2026harness,huang2026roboharness . Symbolic and program-based methods make action constraints explicit~ yang2025guiding,kwon2025fast,chen2025code,chu2025llm+ , building on established work in plan monitoring and repair~ pollack1999towards,van2005plan . Graph-based agent frameworks expose subtask dependencies for reuse and repair~ zhang2026atomic ; in robotics, AgentChord augments task graphs with anticipatory recovery branches before execution~ xu2026agentchord . These advances raise a question: when observations invalidate an earlier condition, which support should the robot restore while preserving a usable unfinished plan? R 0.48 fig:teaser We approach this question through graph engineering: constructing, checking, and revising an explicit dependency graph as the interface between planning and robot execution. We present (Long-Horizon Online Graph-based Inference and Verification for Plan Repair). Its task graph records which conditions each action supplies to later actions, together with resource-ordering constraints. The key design is to separate a node's completion status from the current validity of the support it provides. When that support fails, unfinished consumers can remain in the plan while repair re-establishes their prerequisites. The retained continuation then constrains the repair goal. This gives graph structure an operational role in deciding what to check, what to preserve, and what to change. LOGIV implements this interface as a closed-loop execution and repair layer above an existing VLA or WAM policy. Before execution, it validates a high-level plan and compiles its dependencies into a task graph. During execution, visual observations and robot feedback check the selected action and the support required by pending actions. After a confirmed failure, dependency tracing identifies affected actions; repair synthesizes a continuation constrained by retained operators and expands the replacement scope when validation fails. The combined plan is checked under the symbolic model before the graph is rebuilt and execution resumes. In the bridge example, the robot restores the displaced support while retaining the remaining beam operations. This design adds no trainable components and focuses on online repair from the observed state, with the validity of the repaired continuation checked explicitly. We evaluate LOGIV on 20 simulated dual-arm tasks from RoboTwin~V2 and BiCoord using , AHA-WAM, and Light-WAM. Without injected perturbations, mean success across the three backbones increases from 71.67 to 82.33 on RoboTwin~V2 and from 42.33 to 57.67 on BiCoord. Under predefined perturbations, LOGIV achieves higher task completion and condition restoration than three adapted recovery baselines for every backbone on both benchmarks. On three real-robot tasks, successful trials increase from 12/30 to 17/30. Ablations support the role of graph structure: removing dependency checks reduces perturbed-task success from 60 to 48 , and replacing local repair with replanning all remaining actions increases repeated valid actions from 0.2 to 1.6. These results support graph engineering for the evaluated tasks. These methods motivate the use of an explicit execution layer around an existing policy. Other approaches improve the representation or use of temporal information within the model. title: CAD-WAM: Anticipating Geometry for Text-to-CAD Generation
summary: Generating editable computer-aided design (CAD) models from text requires selecting operations that produce the intended changes to the geometry constructed so far. An incorrect operation can compromise subsequent steps, making reliable multi-step generation challenging. Existing methods based on large language models (LLMs) primarily learn to predict commands, without explicit supervision of the geometric states those commands should produce. Inspired by world-action models, we introduce CAD-WAM, which couples geometry-conditioned action generation with next-state prediction. We define complete modeling operations as actions in a CAD domain-specific language (DSL) and encode surface point clouds of intermediate solids into compact latent states using a pretrained variational autoencoder. An LLM backbone generates the next action from the target description and current geometric state, while an auxiliary head on the same backbone predicts the next state to provide geometric supervision during training. We construct step-wise training trajectories from parametric CAD models in the DeepCAD dataset, pairing each trajectory with an expert-level textual description. At inference, each generated action is executed by a CAD kernel, and the resulting solid is re-encoded to inform the next decision. On the DeepCAD test set, CAD-WAM outperforms the task-specific baselines in geometric accuracy and output validity, with larger gains on models requiring more operations, and produces more accurate geometry than general-purpose LLMs prompted with the same DSL. Ablations further show that next-state supervision reduces mean Chamfer distance by 13.2\% relative to an otherwise identical model trained only to predict actions. Code is available at https://github.com/Lzy-1037/CAD-WAM.

Introduction Parametric computer-aided design (CAD) represents a model through a sequence of editable geometric operations rather than only its final shape. Generating such models from natural language can reduce the manual effort required for CAD modeling. Existing approaches generate parametric command sequences~ khan2024text2cad or fine-tune large language models (LLMs) to produce executable programs in CAD scripting languages such as CadQuery and FeatureScript~ guan2025cadcoder,pyatov2026cadfs,kolodiazhnyi2026cadrille . Reliable multi-step CAD generation requires more than producing executable commands: each operation must also realize the intended change to the geometry constructed so far. An incorrect operation can alter the solid on which subsequent operations act, causing further deviations from the target. Our experiments also reveal an uneven error distribution: several baselines achieve low median geometric error, yet some outputs deviate substantially from the target (Figure~ fig:results ). Existing methods incorporate geometric information through reinforcement learning with geometric rewards~ guan2025cadcoder,kolodiazhnyi2026cadrille or step-wise generation conditioned on the current boundary representation (B-rep)~ qi2026pointercad . These approaches use geometry to evaluate generated programs or inform the next decision, but do not explicitly supervise predictions of the next geometric state. This motivates learning each modeling step through both its symbolic action and its intended geometric outcome, connecting operation generation with the evolving shape of the CAD model. World-action models provide a natural perspective on this formulation by coupling action learning with prediction of future observations~ tian2025seer,zhu2025uwm . Future prediction can provide additional supervision during training without making action generation depend on predicted states at inference~ ye2026gigaworld . CAD offers a direct source of such supervision: executing expert programs yields the intermediate solids after each operation. These geometric outcomes can supervise the representation used for action generation, while the CAD kernel provides the actual geometry for subsequent decisions during inference. Building on this idea, we introduce CAD-WAM, which jointly learns next-action generation and next-state prediction from the target description and current geometry. We design a CAD domain-specific language (DSL) that groups a sketch, its extrusion, and the associated Boolean operation into a complete modeling action, yielding a solid after each successful execution. We pretrain SetVAE~ kim2021setvae , a variational autoencoder for point clouds, on surface point clouds of intermediate and final solids from the training split. Its encoder is then frozen to provide compact latent states that serve both as geometric inputs and as targets for next-state prediction. The Geometric State Embedding maps the current state to geometric tokens, which are processed together with textual tokens by a shared LLM backbone. The Action Head generates the next DSL action, while the State Prediction Head regresses the next latent state. Joint training allows next-state supervision to shape the shared representation used for action generation. At inference, each generated action is executed by a CAD kernel, and the resulting solid is re-encoded to condition the next decision. To train CAD-WAM, we construct step-wise trajectories from DeepCAD, a dataset of parametric CAD models~ wu2021deepcad , by converting their construction sequences into our DSL and executing them operation by operation. Each trajectory is paired with an expert-level textual description released with Pointer-CAD~ qi2026pointercad . At each step, the description and current geometric state form the input, while the next action and resulting geometric state provide supervision. We compare CAD-WAM with task-specific baselines and general-purpose LLMs on the DeepCAD test set, applying a common geometric evaluation protocol to all available outputs. CAD-WAM achieves higher geometric accuracy and lower output invalidity than the evaluated task-specific baselines, with larger gains on models requiring more operations. It also produces more accurate geometry than general-purpose LLMs prompted with the same DSL. Ablations show that the latent-state model outperforms its textual-state counterpart and that next-state supervision reduces mean Chamfer distance by 13.2 relative to an otherwise identical model trained only to predict actions. Our contributions are summarized as follows: [label= , topsep=0pt, itemsep=3pt, partopsep=0pt, parsep=0pt,leftmargin=10pt] We introduce CAD-WAM, a text-to-CAD framework that couples geometry-conditioned action generation with next-state prediction, while using kernel-executed geometry as feedback during inference. We develop an operation-level CAD DSL and a compact latent state representation, and construct step-wise training data that pair executable modeling actions with their geometric outcomes. We demonstrate improved geometric accuracy over the evaluated task-specific and general-purpose models on the DeepCAD dataset, and establish the benefit of next-state supervision through controlled ablations. Related Work CAD Generation with Language Models sec:rw_cad Learning-based CAD generation is usually formulated over the construction sequence rather than the final geometry. DeepCAD introduced this formulation together with a dataset of 178 , 238 sketch-and-extrude sequences~ wu2021deepcad , and later models improved generation and controllability over the same representation without language supervision~ xu2022skexgen,xu2023hnccad . Language models then replaced the task-specific command vocabulary by executable code: CAD-Recode reverse engineers CadQuery programs from point clouds~ rukhovich2025cadrecode , and cadrille extends this setting to point clouds, images and text with reinforcement learning~ kolodiazhnyi2026cadrille . For text-conditioned generation, models emit either command sequences~ khan2024text2cad,govindarajan2025cadmium or programs in CadQuery~ guan2025cadcoder and FeatureScript~ pyatov2026cadfs . Closest to our setting, Pointer-CAD generates a model step by step and conditions each step on the boundary representation obtained so far~ qi2026pointercad . Unlike these methods, which either ignore the intermediate geometry or merely condition on it, our work encodes it as a latent state and predicts the state that the next action produces. World Models and World-Action Models sec:rw_wm World models learn the dynamics of an environment in a latent space, so that the effect of an action can be estimated without executing it~ ha2018world,hafner2020dream . The idea has since been scaled to generative video models, which synthesize future observations conditioned on text or on latent actions~ du2023unipi,bruce2024genie . Predicting future observations is useful for control only when it informs the choice of action. World-action models therefore couple prediction with action generation, and differ in how the two are combined: the action may be inferred from a predicted future observation~ tian2025seer , actions and observations may be produced within a single generative process~ zhu2025uwm , or future prediction may serve as an auxiliary objective during training~ ye2026gigaworld . CAD-WAM draws on this idea and applies it to CAD modeling, where the transition induced by an action is deterministic and the resulting geometry can be obtained exactly with a CAD kernel. The predicted state is therefore a well-defined target, and the observed state requires no approximation. CAD-WAM Problem Formulation sec:formulation Given a natural-language description of a target CAD model, CAD-WAM constructs the model in a step-by-step manner through a sequence of state-dependent decisions. We design a CAD domain-specific language (DSL; Section~ sec:dsl ) that represents CAD operations (e.g., extrusions and Boolean operations) as executable actions. The construction process is thus expressed as an action sequence , where and denotes the action space defined by the DSL. Let denote the B-rep of the intermediate CAD model after actions. Each action updates the current geometry through a deterministic transition implemented by the CAD kernel: where denotes the CAD kernel's execution function. We represent each nonempty intermediate model by a compact geometric state. Specifically, we sample a point cloud from its surface and encode it using a SetVAE encoder ~ kim2021setvae (Section~ sec:state ): The process starts from an empty model , represented by the zero vector . CAD-WAM conditions each decision on the textual target and the current geometric state, without explicitly taking the action history as input. Given , it jointly predicts the next action and the resulting geometric state by modeling where denotes the parameters of CAD-WAM. This formulation couples action generation with prediction of the resulting geometric state, encouraging the model to anticipate the geometric consequences of the next action. CAD Domain-Specific Language sec:dsl We design a CAD DSL in which each modeling action produces a CAD solid upon successful execution, providing an explicit geometric state after each modeling step. Figure~ fig:dsl shows a construction sequence in this DSL, the JSON form of an action, and the procedure by which an action is executed. In contrast, a single command token~ wu2021deepcad or code statement~ rukhovich2025cadrecode,guan2025cadcoder does not necessarily yield a solid, which leaves the intermediate geometry difficult to represent. Actions are serialized as JSON objects with continuous parameters, and a dedicated end action terminates the construction. title: RoboSeed: Multidimensional Evaluation of Vision-Language-Action and World-Action Models: Capability, Resource Affordability, and Research Evidence
summary:
Choosing a robot action model requires evidence about task capability, adaptation cost, deployment requirements, and the reliability of reported conclusions. Success rates alone offer limited guidance to researchers with different computing budgets and goals. We propose RoboSeed, a multidimensional evaluation framework for vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action models (WAM), within a continuing program to train, evaluate, and openly release robot models with verifiable evidence for model selection.
  The framework defines five dimensions: capability, downstream training affordability, deployment affordability, locally verified research value, and reproduction evidence. It maps empirical measurements and audit criteria to 0-100 profiles using fixed normalization anchors, with balanced, training-constrained, and deployment-constrained preference settings. Interface and protocol checks establish when comparisons are appropriate. Missing measurements remain explicit, incomplete aggregate scores are withheld, and weighted input coverage identifies evidence gaps.
  We apply the framework to representative VLA and WAM models, drawing on local training, released-weight evaluation, task-level audits, and an evaluation-system study. The results reveal budget-dependent backbone choices, sensitivity to adaptation recipes, and differences between language and visual task interfaces. Reproducible scoring code and machine-readable evidence support extension to additional models. The study provides dimension-level assessments and priorities for further measurement, while incomplete serving traces and heterogeneous protocols preclude overall numerical rankings.

VLA models and WAMs offer different combinations of semantic conditioning, predictive representations and action generation. Their practical value depends on the task interface, computing budget and strength of the experimental evidence as well as the final success rate. A reported percentage leaves much of this decision unresolved. Two checkpoints with similar success can require different adaptation budgets, observation pipelines and serving resources. A strong released checkpoint can coexist with a fragile local training recipe. A compact policy may rely on task-specific visual conditions rather than accept arbitrary language instructions. Researchers therefore need an evaluation that connects task outcomes to resource requirements and the conclusions supported by the experiment. Our goal is to continuously train, evaluate, and openly release robot models for different computing budgets, while providing verifiable evidence for model selection. The report, model checkpoints, experimental results, and reproduction materials are intended to form a connected resource that community researchers can inspect, use, and extend. We plan to publish our trained checkpoints and associated experimental results on Hugging Face, with explicit links to the corresponding configurations and report versions. Public checkpoint download entries remain pending in the current snapshot. RoboSeed addresses the model-selection need by proposing a multidimensional evaluation and scoring framework for the research community. We organize model selection around a common set of criteria, make their scoring rules reproducible, and connect each judgment to its underlying measurements. Training and evaluation across VLA and WAM families supply the empirical basis for these assessments. This organization lets researchers use the same evaluation questions across different architectures while preserving native task interfaces and experimental conditions. The Proposed RoboSeed Evaluation Framework Our framework represents each candidate by five dimensions on a 0--100 scale: capability , downstream training affordability , deployment affordability , locally verified research value , and reproduction evidence . Table~ tab:framework_overview connects these dimensions to the decisions they support. The evaluation unit includes the checkpoint, training recipe, execution interface and evaluator, so a score remains tied to a concrete experimental setting. Three design choices make the profiles reusable. First, fixed normalization anchors give cost scores a declared budget interpretation and keep existing scores stable as candidates are added. Second, balanced, training-constrained and deployment-constrained weight settings expose how research priorities affect aggregate preferences. Third, explicit missing-data rules retain unavailable measurements as dashes and withhold incomplete composites; weighted input coverage identifies which observations remain to be collected. Raw metrics accompany the scores so researchers can change anchors and weights for their own budgets. The intended use is to check task and execution compatibility, enforce capability and resource requirements, and then inspect the feasible candidates' dimension profiles under declared preferences. The research-value and reproduction-evidence dimensions further identify useful hypotheses and gaps in experimental support. This provides a broader basis for community evaluation while keeping the interpretation of each dimension explicit. The weights and thresholds are a versioned decision policy; their usefulness across additional laboratories and applications remains to be tested. Contributions A multidimensional evaluation framework for community model selection. We propose five complementary scoring dimensions that bring capability, training and deployment affordability, locally established research value, and reproduction evidence into one assessment. Fixed scoring anchors, explicit audit criteria, alternative preference profiles and missing-data rules make the framework inspectable and adaptable to different research budgets. title: Learning Safe Flow Matching Robot Policies from Binary Feasibility Oracles
summary: Robot foundation models increasingly rely on flow-based action generation for general-purpose manipulation, yet the generated actions are not guaranteed to satisfy physical constraints such as joint limits and collision avoidance. This problem is especially challenging when the feasible set cannot be described analytically and is accessible only through black-box feasibility oracles. We study this practical oracle-only setting and propose an oracle-guided differentiable safeguard for safe flow-matching robot policies. The safeguard uses binary feasibility queries to correct unsafe updates in the forward pass, while extracting local boundary information to provide constraint-aware learning signals in the backward pass. Combined with discrete-time flow matching, the same safeguard is used during training and inference, enabling forward--backward aligned policy learning without explicit or differentiable constraint models. Experiments on obstacle-aware robotic manipulation demonstrate 100% constraint satisfaction while preserving task performance.
full_text: Robot foundation models increasingly rely on flow-based action generation for general-purpose manipulation, yet the generated actions are not guaranteed to satisfy physical constraints such as joint limits and collision avoidance. This problem is especially challenging when the feasible set cannot be described analytically and is accessible only through black-box feasibility oracles. We study this practical oracle-only setting and propose an oracle-guided differentiable safeguard for safe flow-matching robot policies. The safeguard uses binary feasibility queries to correct unsafe updates in the forward pass, while extracting local boundary information to provide constraint-aware learning signals in the backward pass. Combined with discrete-time flow matching, the same safeguard is used during training and inference, enabling forward--backward aligned policy learning without explicit or differentiable constraint models. Experiments on obstacle-aware robotic manipulation demonstrate 100 constraint satisfaction while preserving task performance. Introduction sec:introduction Robot foundation models, including vision-language-action (VLA) models intelligence2025pi_,bjorck2025gr00t and world-action models (WAMs) ye2026world,yuan2026fast , increasingly combine pretrained vision-language or video-generation backbones with flow-based action generation for general-purpose robot control. However, strong task generalization does not guarantee safe physical interaction: generated actions must also satisfy constraints such as joint limits and collision avoidance. Enforcing such scene-dependent constraints remains a key challenge for deploying flow-based robot policies. Existing methods either correct generated actions only at inference time or incorporate constraint enforcement into training. Inference-time correction, e.g., through control barrier functions ames2017control,yang2026safeflowmatcher,huang2025sad,hu2025vlsa , or trajectory-wise constraint guidance utkarsh2026physics,cheng2025gradient , can be applied to pretrained policies but introduces a train--test mismatch. Training-aware approaches reduce this mismatch ma2026actsafeguard,christopher2026constraint,li2026gauge , but typically require explicit constraint functions, differentiable constraint models, or known feasible-set geometry. Such information is often difficult to obtain in robotics. For example, in robotic arm obstacle avoidance, a collision checker can readily determine whether a candidate configuration is feasible, while an analytical description of the corresponding collision-free configuration space may be unavailable. This motivates an oracle-only setting, where safety is accessible solely through a binary feasibility oracle. We ask: how can a flow-matching robot policy enforce constraints and learn from them when only binary feasibility queries are available? To address this problem, we propose an oracle-guided differentiable safeguard. In the forward pass, the safeguard uses oracle queries to restrict each predicted update to the feasible region. In the backward pass, it extracts local boundary information from nearby binary queries and uses it to construct a boundary-aware surrogate gradient. Thus, the same oracle supports both feasibility enforcement and constraint-aware policy learning, without requiring an explicit or differentiable constraint model. We integrate the safeguard with discrete-time flow matching, allowing the same correction mechanism to be used during both training and inference. This yields a forward--backward aligned learning framework in which the policy is optimized under the safety intervention encountered at deployment. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We formulate safe flow-matching robot policy learning under an oracle-only constraint interface, removing the need for explicit or differentiable constraint models. We introduce an oracle-guided differentiable safeguard that combines oracle-based forward feasibility correction with boundary-aware surrogate gradients, enabling forward--backward aligned policy learning. We validate the proposed approach on an obstacle-aware robotic manipulation task, demonstrating strong constraint satisfaction while maintaining task performance. Conclusion sec:conclusion We propose an oracle-guided differentiable safeguard for safe flow-matching robot policies using only binary feasibility feedback. The oracle enforces feasibility in the forward pass and provides local boundary information for backward learning, allowing the same safeguard to be used during training and inference without explicit or differentiable constraint models. Experiments on obstacle-aware manipulation show improved safety while preserving task performance and motion quality. title: ACD-GS: Asymmetric Curvature-aware Densification for 3D Gaussian Splatting
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for real-time photorealistic novel view synthesis. However, its training-time densification remains largely heuristic, often resulting in redundant Gaussian proliferation and inaccurate geometric reconstruction. Existing methods predominantly rely on first-order screen-space gradients to trigger cloning and splitting, which fail to distinguish true geometric discontinuities from high-frequency textures or noisy residuals. To address this limitation, we propose ACD-GS, an Asymmetric Curvature-aware Densification framework for compact and geometry-aware 3D Gaussian optimization. Our key insight is that second-order depth responses provide a more reliable structural prior for density control, enabling asymmetric regulation of cloning and splitting to better capture geometric discontinuities. Building on this, we introduce a multi-view photometric consistency constraint to suppress transient single-view errors, together with a capacity-aware adaptive regulation strategy that balances densification and pruning during training. Unlike post-hoc compression or quantization-based approaches, ACD-GS directly prevents redundant Gaussian generation during training, yielding inherently compact representations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method reduces nearly 60% of Gaussian count and storage while maintaining competitive rendering fidelity, consistently outperforming existing methods across multiple datasets. Our code is available in https://waveviewer.github.io/ACD-GS/.
full_text: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for real-time photorealistic novel view synthesis. However, its training-time densification remains largely heuristic, often resulting in redundant Gaussian proliferation and inaccurate geometric reconstruction. Existing methods predominantly rely on first-order screen-space gradients to trigger cloning and splitting, which fail to distinguish true geometric discontinuities from high-frequency textures or noisy residuals. To address this limitation, we propose ACD-GS, an Asymmetric Curvature-aware Densification framework for compact and geometry-aware 3D Gaussian optimization. Our key insight is that second-order depth responses provide a more reliable structural prior for density control, enabling asymmetric regulation of cloning and splitting to better capture geometric discontinuities. Building on this, we introduce a multi-view photometric consistency constraint to suppress transient single-view errors, together with a capacity-aware adaptive regulation strategy that balances densification and pruning during training. Unlike post-hoc compression or quantization-based approaches, ACD-GS directly prevents redundant Gaussian generation during training, yielding inherently compact representations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method reduces nearly 60 of Gaussian count and storage while maintaining competitive rendering fidelity, consistently outperforming existing methods across multiple datasets. Our code is available in . Introduction 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ 3dgs has rapidly emerged as a powerful paradigm for real-time photorealistic novel view synthesis. Unlike implicit neural radiance fields, 3DGS represents a scene as an explicit collection of anisotropic Gaussian primitives and renders them through differentiable rasterization, achieving both high rendering fidelity and remarkable efficiency. Benefiting from its explicit representation and fast optimization, 3DGS has inspired extensive advances in anti-aliasing~ mipsplatting,prismgs,AnalyticSplatting , surface reconstruction~ aligngs,sugar,2dgs,gsmesh,pgsr , dynamic scene modeling~ 4DGC,4dgcpro,spacetimegs,4dgs,luiten2023dynamic , compression~ compact_3dgs,3DGSzip,hac,contextgs,hac++ , and hybrid implicit-explicit representations~ scaffoldgs,octreegs,gsembedding,splatnet,gnf,tang2026neuralgs . Despite these advances, the efficiency and scalability of 3DGS still critically depend on how Gaussian primitives are created and evolved during optimization. In standard 3DGS, densification is mainly driven by accumulated screen-space positional gradients, where Gaussians are cloned or split once the gradient magnitude exceeds predefined thresholds. While simple and effective in practice, this mechanism remains largely geometry-agnostic, as first-order gradients primarily reflect local optimization pressure rather than underlying scene structure. Consequently, regions with high-frequency textures, smoothly varying surfaces, and sharp geometric boundaries may all produce similarly large gradients despite requiring fundamentally different density-control behaviors. A flat textured wall, for example, should avoid excessive Gaussian proliferation, whereas thin structures and depth discontinuities require localized geometric refinement. This reveals an intrinsic ambiguity in gradient-driven densification, where first-order photometric signals alone are insufficient for reliable density control. This ambiguity leads to a persistent trade-off in existing densification strategies~ iadc,pixel_gs,absgs,gdags,steep_gs . Aggressive thresholds tend to trigger excessive Gaussian growth in textured regions, resulting in redundant primitives, increased storage overhead, unstable optimization, and floating artifacts near foreground-background transitions. Conversely, conservative thresholds often fail to reconstruct fine structures and sharp depth discontinuities. Recent approaches attempt to improve densification stability by incorporating pixel-aware gradients~ pixel_gs , absolute gradient magnitudes~ absgs , or gradient-direction statistics~ gdags,steep_gs . Although these methods alleviate optimization instability to some extent, they still rely primarily on first-order, single-view photometric signals and therefore remain insufficient for disentangling true geometric complexity from texture-induced residuals. As a result, existing methods struggle to simultaneously achieve compact representations, geometric fidelity, and stable optimization. These limitations motivate the need for a geometry-aware density-control prior that directly reflects scene structure rather than relying solely on photometric optimization cues. In this work, we propose ACD-GS, an Asymmetric Curvature-aware Densification framework that reformulates Gaussian densification as a geometry-aware optimization process. Our key insight is that second-order depth responses provide a more reliable structural cue for identifying geometric discontinuities than first-order screen-space gradients. Compared with gradient magnitude alone, depth curvature is more sensitive to local geometric changes such as occlusion boundaries, thin structures, and high-curvature regions, while remaining less responsive to purely planar textured areas. Based on this observation, ACD-GS introduces an asymmetric densification mechanism that explicitly decouples cloning and splitting behaviors according to curvature-aware structural priors. Specifically, cloning is suppressed near depth discontinuities to avoid ambiguous foreground-background duplication and floating artifacts, whereas splitting is promoted to refine boundary-crossing Gaussians into finer geometric primitives. To further resolve the ambiguity between geometry and appearance, we introduce a multi-view photometric error gating strategy that enforces cross-view consistency instead of relying on volatile single-view residuals. Furthermore, we design a capacity-constrained adaptive optimization scheme that dynamically regulates primitive growth and lifecycle-aware pruning throughout training. Together, these designs establish a unified geometry-aware density-control framework that enables native sparsification, where redundant Gaussian primitives are prevented during training rather than removed through post-hoc compression or quantization pipelines. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ACD-GS reduces nearly 60 of Gaussian primitives and storage while maintaining competitive rendering fidelity across multiple datasets, consistently achieving a favorable quality and compactness trade-off compared with existing methods. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We propose ACD-GS, an asymmetric curvature-aware densification framework that leverages second-order depth priors to explicitly decouple cloning and splitting behaviors for geometry-aware Gaussian evolution. We introduce a multi-view photometric error gating strategy and a capacity-constrained adaptive optimization scheme to suppress transient photometric noise, regulate primitive growth, and encourage compact yet high-fidelity representations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ACD-GS significantly reduces Gaussian count and model storage natively during training while maintaining competitive rendering quality across multiple datasets. Related Work sec:related 3D Gaussian Splatting Representation 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ 3dgs represents a scene as anisotropic Gaussian primitives and renders them through differentiable rasterization. Its explicit formulation has inspired extensions for anti-aliasing~ mipsplatting,prismgs,AnalyticSplatting , surface reconstruction~ aligngs,sugar,2dgs,gsmesh,pgsr , dynamic scenes~ 4DGC,4dgcpro,spacetimegs,4dgs,luiten2023dynamic , and appearance modeling~ HyperGaussians,hypergs,thermalgaussian,7dgs . Hybrid representations such as Scaffold-GS~ scaffoldgs , SplatNet~ splatnet , and Octree-GS~ octreegs further organize primitives with learned features or hierarchical structures, while implicit fields~ nerf,instantngp,mobilenerf,snerg provide complementary scene parameterizations. These methods mainly change representation or rendering; the number and placement of Gaussians still depend on training-time density control, which is the focus of this work. Because all of them retain a primitive-based rendering pipeline, their efficiency and fidelity are also affected by how many Gaussians remain after optimization. Gradient-Driven Density Control Standard 3DGS~ 3dgs densifies Gaussians using accumulated screen-space positional gradients. Pixel-GS~ pixel_gs accounts for pixel coverage, AbsGS~ absgs uses absolute gradients to reduce cancellation, and GDAGS~ gdags incorporates gradient-direction information; other methods add external constraints~ iadc,steep_gs . FastGS~ fastgs instead estimates Gaussian importance from multi-view reconstruction errors inside projected footprints and uses this score for both densification and pruning. ACD-GS shares the use of multi-view evidence but assigns it a different role: rendered-depth curvature modulates cloning and splitting, while center-projected RGB residuals only verify whether a candidate is consistently under-reconstructed across views. This separates structural guidance from photometric verification and avoids using a footprint error score as the direct densification criterion. 3DGS Compression Post-hoc compression reduces Gaussian storage through significance-based pruning and vector quantization~ lightgaussian,eagles,compact_3dgs,trimming_fat,OccluGaussian,PUP3D-GS , while context models and entropy coding target rate--distortion efficiency~ hac,contextgs,rdogaussian,pcgs,cat3dgs . Mini-Splatting~ mini_splatting studies compact representations under constrained primitive budgets. These approaches mainly operate after or around training and may require codebooks or fine-tuning. ACD-GS instead reduces redundant primitive generation during optimization, without a post-hoc quantization stage. Because it changes where capacity is allocated rather than how parameters are encoded, it can be combined with downstream compression; this combination is not evaluated here. This distinction also delimits the scope of our experiments, which measure training-time sparsification rather than gains from entropy coding or quantization. Method sec:method Problem Formulation and Overview sec:problem_overview 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) represents a scene as a set of anisotropic Gaussian primitives optimized through differentiable alpha blending. During training, standard 3DGS densifies visible Gaussians according to their accumulated view-space positional gradients: where is the projected 2D center of . Large photometric gradients may be caused by flat textures, smooth slopes, or true depth discontinuities, although these cases require different density-control behaviors. This ambiguity often leads to redundant primitives on planar or textured regions, while sharp boundaries and thin structures may remain under-refined. title: TouchBridge: Tactile-Conditioned Human-to-Robot Transfer for Dexterous Manipulation
summary: Human demonstrations offer an efficient and scalable source of data for dexterous robot manipulation, but differences in sensing and hand morphology complicate the transfer of contact-rich interactions. We present TouchBridge, a hardware--software co-designed framework for human-to-robot data transformation. A wearable human demonstration interface and a corresponding robot interface establish cross-embodiment correspondence in visual and fingertip tactile sensing. We introduce Tac-Retarget, a tactile-conditioned retargeting method that uses measured contact to align fingertip contact patches and preserve their spatial relations within and across hands. Unlike object-aware or simulation-based transfer pipelines, Tac-Retarget requires no object mesh, object-pose estimate, or physics simulation for retargeting, enabling direct and scalable conversion of human demonstrations into robot-domain training data. Combined with visual synthesis and camera-anchored action conversion, TouchBridge produces robot-domain demonstrations for fine-tuning a pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) model. Across four real-world contact-rich tasks, policies fine-tuned solely on TouchBridge-converted human demonstrations achieve a 72.5% average success rate, compared with 77.5% using an equal number of teleoperated robot demonstrations, while human demonstration collection is 7.0x faster. Under the same policy and training setup, Tac-Retarget outperforms DexPilot and UniDex by 25.0 and 42.5 percentage points, respectively.
full_text: We introduce TouchBridge, a tactile-conditioned human-to-robot transformation framework. TouchBridge-Cap records human demonstrations with sensing configurations aligned to the robot interface. Building on this correspondence, Tac-Retarget converts human demonstrations into robot-domain training data while preserving the demonstrated contact locations and spatial relations. Policies fine-tuned on these data achieve success rates close to those achieved by policies trained on teleoperated robot demonstrations, while human demonstrations can be collected substantially faster. fig:teaser Human demonstrations offer an efficient and scalable source of data for dexterous robot manipulation, but differences in sensing and hand morphology complicate the transfer of contact-rich interactions. Under the same policy and training setup, Tac-Retarget outperforms DexPilot and UniDex by 25.0 and 42.5 percentage points, respectively. INTRODUCTION Building foundation models for contact-rich dexterous manipulation requires large-scale demonstrations that capture not only hand motion, but also physical interaction with the environment. Collecting such data directly on dexterous robots, however, is slow and demands substantial operator effort. Human demonstrations provide a natural and potentially scalable source of manipulation experience, and have increasingly been used for large-scale pretraining~ zhang2026unidex,zheng2026egoscale and direct human-to-robot transfer~ wang2026humanego,guzey2026dexterity . Realizing this potential, however, requires transforming human experience into robot-executable training data both faithfully and efficiently. This transformation faces two key challenges. First, kinematic correspondence alone does not preserve physical interaction. Conventional retargeting methods typically match hand poses, fingertip positions, or hand-centric vectors~ handa2020dexpilot,qin2023anyteleop,zhang2026unidex . While effective for free-space motion, these objectives do not explicitly capture contact. As a result, fixed human-derived fingertip targets can displace a contacting finger from its support region, distort relations among simultaneous contacts, or break contact altogether. For contact-rich manipulation, kinematically plausible motion may therefore still be physically ineffective. Second, preserving physical interaction should not come at the cost of data scalability. Object-aware approaches incorporate hand--object geometry or physics-based constraints~ huang2025fungrasp,lin2025dexflow,wu2026toporetarget,fan2026robopaint , while other human-to-robot pipelines refine transferred trajectories or policies through simulation and reinforcement learning~ li2025maniptrans, kedia2026simtoolreal . Such methods can improve physical consistency, but require object meshes, object-pose estimation, environment reconstruction, or simulation-based rollout and refinement. These object- and task-specific requirements introduce substantial modeling and engineering overhead, making them difficult to scale with increasingly large and diverse human datasets. Our key observation is that physical contact itself provides a natural correspondence across embodiments. Tactile sensing directly reveals which fingertips are in contact, where contact occurs, and how strongly different regions are loaded. Because these signals are measured directly during human demonstrations, they provide interaction constraints without requiring explicit object reconstruction or simulation-based refinement. Tactile sensing therefore addresses both challenges simultaneously: it augments kinematic retargeting with physical interaction information while preserving a direct human-to-robot data conversion pathway. Building on this idea, we present TouchBridge, a hardware–software co-designed framework for scalable conversion of human demonstrations of contact-rich dexterous manipulation into robot-domain data. At the hardware level, we develop TouchBridge-Cap, a wearable capture interface that records RGB observations, hand motion, and fingertip tactile measurements. The corresponding robot interface approximately matches the wrist-camera-to-hand geometry, fingertip sensor placement, and tactile sensing layout of TouchBridge-Cap, establishing cross-embodiment correspondence in visual and tactile observations. At the software level, TouchBridge transforms these human demonstrations into robot-domain observations and actions for policy learning without task-specific robot demonstrations or object-specific environment modeling. At the core of TouchBridge is Tac-Retarget, a tactile-conditioned retargeting method that uses measured contact to guide motion transfer across embodiments. Tac-Retarget combines contact-patch alignment, which aligns tactile contact regions between human and robot fingertips, with a contact-activated graph, which preserves spatial relations among simultaneous contacts within and across hands. Together, these objectives transfer not only fingertip motion but also the geometry and spatial structure of demonstrated contacts. The optimization operates directly on measured human kinematics and tactile responses, requiring no object mesh, object-pose estimate, or physics simulation. Combined with robot-domain visual synthesis and camera-anchored action construction, the resulting pipeline converts raw human demonstrations into robot-domain training sequences. We evaluate TouchBridge on four contact-rich real-world manipulation tasks: bulb screwing, sauce application, fragile-object grasping, and page flipping. Under the same policy and training setup, demonstrations converted using Tac-Retarget yield an average real-robot policy success rate of , outperforming DexPilot~ handa2020dexpilot and UniDex~ zhang2026unidex by and percentage points, respectively, while also achieving lower contact error. Policies fine-tuned solely on TouchBridge-converted human demonstrations achieve a average success rate, close to the obtained using an equal number of teleoperated robot demonstrations, while human demonstrations are collected faster. These results show that TouchBridge retains much of the utility of robot-collected demonstrations while substantially reducing the cost of acquiring training data, providing a practical path toward scaling robot learning from human experience. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We present TouchBridge, a hardware--software co-designed framework that transforms contact-rich human demonstrations into robot-domain training sequences. Through aligned visual and fingertip tactile sensing across human and robot interfaces, TouchBridge enables policy learning for contact-rich dexterous manipulation without task-specific teleoperated robot demonstrations. We introduce Tac-Retarget, a tactile-conditioned retargeting method that uses measured contact-patch alignment and a contact-activated graph to preserve physical interaction across embodiments. Compared with kinematic retargeting, Tac-Retarget substantially improves both contact preservation and downstream real-robot policy success. TouchBridge converts human demonstrations without object meshes, object-pose estimates, or simulation-based rollout refinement. Together, the faster demonstration collection and policy performance close to that obtained from robot-collected data make the framework well suited for scaling robot learning from human demonstrations. Related Work Learning from Human Demonstrations Human demonstrations provide a scalable alternative to collecting task data on physical robots. UniDex~ zhang2026unidex and EgoScale~ zheng2026egoscale use large-scale human-derived data to pretrain transferable dexterous policies. These works primarily emphasize scaling human-derived data, with less emphasis on the fidelity of the converted demonstrations, particularly the preservation of contact interactions across embodiments. EgoMimic~ kareer2025egomimic and MotionTrans~ yuan2026motiontrans co-train manipulation policies on human and robot demonstrations. Many other methods use simulation to ground human demonstrations in the robot embodiment. ManipTrans~ li2025maniptrans refines retargeted hand-object trajectories through residual reinforcement learning. SimToolReal~ kedia2026simtoolreal trains an object-centric policy in simulation and uses object trajectories from human videos as deployment goals. Both involve additional effort in environment construction and robot--object interaction modeling. A further line of work develops interfaces and transformation pipelines for learning directly from human demonstrations. DexUMI~ xu2025dexumi combines wearable exoskeletons and visual conversion to bridge the human--robot embodiment gap, with the exoskeleton mechanically designed to match the target hand's kinematics. Adapting to new robot hands generally requires hardware redesign, which is particularly challenging for high-DoF hands. Moreover, the wearable mechanism is typically tailored to a limited range of human hand sizes, reducing user adaptability and potentially compromising wearer comfort during demonstration collection. HumanEgo~ wang2026humanego enables task-level transfer without robot training data, but has only been demonstrated with parallel-jaw grippers. AINA~ guzey2026dexterity extends robot-data-free transfer to multi-fingered hands using visually estimated hand--object geometry and fingertip motion, without explicit tactile contact constraints. Our method instead uses measured tactile signals to preserve contact patches and their spatial relations during motion retargeting without simulation refinement, while using a glove-based capture interface that requires no mechanical correspondence with the target hand's joint structure. This enables policies fine-tuned solely on converted human demonstrations to be deployed on the real robot without task-specific robot demonstrations. Dexterous Retargeting Dexterous retargeting maps human hand motion to robot hands with different kinematic structures. DexPilot~ handa2020dexpilot and AnyTeleop~ qin2023anyteleop optimize hand-centric task-space or keypoint-vector correspondences. TopoRetarget~ wu2026toporetarget preserves local interaction topology using an object mesh and pose trajectory.
