title: Continuous-Action World Models: Learning Cross-Embodiment Spatiotemporal Dynamics Priors
summary: We introduce Continuous-Action World Models (CoAWM), a framework for learning cross-embodiment spatiotemporal dynamics priors that support robot action generation across embodiments and execution frequencies. At its core is a shared latent function space that captures the spatial and temporal structure of robot actions. We learn this space through two stages. First, function pretraining brings trajectories from different embodiments and sampling frequencies into a common representation, learning shared dynamics priors through action reconstruction and consistency across temporal sampling views. By accommodating heterogeneous robot trajectories, this stage broadens the range of data sources available for pretraining and facilitates scaling to larger and more diverse datasets. Second, we connect the pretrained function space to a world-model backbone, enabling observations, language instructions, and the current robot state to condition the prediction of a latent action function. A single decoder takes any query time and returns the corresponding end-effector action. By separating shared dynamics priors from task-conditioned action selection and temporal sampling, our approach provides a unified foundation for transferring robot experience across embodiments and control frequencies.
full_text: We introduce Continuous-Action World Models (CoAWM), a framework for learning cross-embodiment spatiotemporal dynamics priors that support robot action generation across embodiments and execution frequencies. At its core is a shared latent function space that captures the spatial and temporal structure of robot actions. We learn this space through two stages. First, function pretraining brings trajectories from different embodiments and sampling frequencies into a common representation, learning shared dynamics priors through action reconstruction and consistency across temporal sampling views. By accommodating heterogeneous robot trajectories, this stage broadens the range of data sources available for pretraining and facilitates scaling to larger and more diverse datasets. Second, we connect the pretrained function space to a world-model backbone, enabling observations, language instructions, and the current robot state to condition the prediction of a latent action function. A single decoder takes any query time and returns the corresponding end-effector action. By separating shared dynamics priors from task-conditioned action selection and temporal sampling, our approach provides a unified foundation for transferring robot experience across embodiments and control frequencies. Introduction Robots with different bodies can perform similar tasks, yet their experience is recorded through different action interfaces and control frequencies~ oxe2023,ghosh2024octo,black2024pi0 . A reaching motion may be demonstrated by one manipulator and executed by another, with different command sequences governing a related physical behavior. This diversity raises a central question for robot world models: how can experience collected across embodiments be used to learn shared spatiotemporal dynamics priors that guide action generation? Answering this question would broaden the sources of experience available to a model, allowing robot learning to benefit from data beyond a single embodiment or collection setup. The challenge is not simply to combine more trajectories. Robot datasets differ in what their actions specify, how those actions are grounded in the robot's state, and when commands are issued. The same sequence index can correspond to different physical times, while numerically similar commands can have different meanings across action interfaces. A common storage format alone does not resolve these differences. To learn from heterogeneous experience, a model needs a representation that captures reusable spatial and temporal structure while retaining the information required to interpret and execute an action on a particular robot. For a world model, this representation must also connect shared experience to action selection in the current scene and task. Our key insight is to learn the evolution of an action as a function, rather than treating its sampled commands as the fundamental object of representation. A latent action function encodes how a motion unfolds in space and time; individual commands are obtained by querying that function (Fig.~ fig:insight ). This provides a common learning space for trajectories sampled at different frequencies. More importantly, it separates two complementary learning problems: acquiring dynamics priors from heterogeneous trajectories, and selecting an action using the current interaction context. The former can draw on a broader pool of robot experience, while the latter connects these priors to the observation-conditioned capabilities of a world model. We introduce Continuous-Action World Models (CoAWM) to realize this idea through two stages (Fig.~ fig:interface ). First, we pretrain a shared latent function space using trajectories from different embodiments and sampling frequencies. A function encoder and decoder learn spatiotemporal dynamics priors through action reconstruction and consistency across temporal sampling views. This pretraining stage expands the range of trajectory sources that can contribute to representation learning, providing a path toward larger and more diverse training datasets. Second, we connect the pretrained function space to a world-model backbone. Visual observations, language instructions, and the current robot state condition a prediction head that produces a latent action function, which a shared decoder converts into end-effector actions through time queries. CoAWM thus connects cross-embodiment prior learning with task-conditioned action generation, while allowing the execution frequency to be specified through the query times. Related Work Continuous Action and Function Representations Action representations determine how a policy organizes motion over time. ACT predicts action chunks~ zhao2023act , Diffusion Policy generates action sequences through denoising~ chi2023diffusionpolicy , and FAST compresses temporal structure into frequency-domain tokens~ pertsch2025fast . Continuous action representations capture how motion evolves over time and allow actions to be queried at different execution times. Dynamical Movement Primitives encode motor behavior through attractor dynamics and learned forcing terms~ ijspeert2013dmp , Probabilistic Movement Primitives model distributions over trajectories~ paraschos2013promp , and ProDMPs connect these dynamic and probabilistic formulations~ li2022prodmp . These foundations establish motion trajectories as structured objects from which reusable action priors can be learned. Recent visuomotor policies explore different function families and decoding mechanisms. FLASH represents trajectories with a Legendre basis and history-anchored flow~ bai2026flash , while B-spline Policy uses control points and knots to parameterize actions~ han2026bspline . Neural Implicit Action Fields learn modulated continuous-time action functions and supervise their temporal derivatives~ liu2026niaf . Periodic-activation implicit networks provide a general foundation for coordinate-queryable neural functions and their derivatives~ sitzmann2020siren . These efforts to represent actions motivate us to learn shared spatiotemporal dynamics priors through a continuous function representation. A latent function representation captures how motion evolves over time. A decoder takes this representation and a time query to produce the corresponding action. Querying the same representation at different times yields action sequences at different temporal resolutions. FunDiff combines function encoding, latent diffusion, and continuous decoding for physical-field generation~ wang2026fundiff . Function-Space Diffusion for Motion Planning models trajectory distributions using temporally correlated noise and boundary-compatible operators~ chang2026fsdmp . CAT learns a fixed-size set of continuous trajectory latents over a physical-time window and uses frequency-aware positional encoding with a causal action decoder to accommodate different control rates~ yang2026cat . These works establish important precedents for learning continuous representations and transferring between temporal resolutions. CoAWM focuses on learning shared spatiotemporal dynamics priors from heterogeneous robot trajectories and connecting the resulting function space to world-model-conditioned action generation. Cross-Embodiment Learning and Action Priors Cross-embodiment learning expands the experience available for robot policy training. Open X-Embodiment brings together robot datasets and studies cross-robot policies~ oxe2023 . Octo develops generalist pretraining and adaptation to new observation and action spaces~ ghosh2024octo , and combines a vision-language model with flow-based action generation for general robot control~ black2024pi0 . These approaches make heterogeneous data a practical resource for learning behavior across tasks and robot systems. A central representation question is which structure can be shared while maintaining a meaningful connection to each robot's executable actions. Latent-action learning addresses this question by separating reusable action knowledge from specific command spaces. LAPA learns latent actions from video before adapting them to robot control~ ye2024lapa , and UniVLA learns task-centric latent actions for embodiment transfer~ bu2025univla . LAC-WM learns shared latent actions from visual transitions with auxiliary motion reconstruction for cross-embodiment world modeling, and reports benefits from increasing the diversity of pretraining embodiments~ huang2026lacwm . These results motivate shared action priors for both control and prediction. CoAWM approaches this problem through action trajectories: a function autoencoder learns their spatial and temporal structure, and an observation-conditioned head connects the pretrained function space to a world-model backbone. Its pretraining interface is designed to accommodate trajectories from multiple embodiments and sampling frequencies, broadening the sources of data available for learning dynamics priors. World Models for Action Generation and Execution World models connect experience to predictions that support action selection. V-JEPA 2 adapts self-supervised video representations for action-conditioned prediction and planning~ assran2025vjepa2 . LAWM learns latent actions through future-frame modeling~ tharwat2025lawm , while Learning Latent Action World Models In The Wild investigates continuous-valued latent actions for prediction and controllable interaction~ garrido2026wild . villa-X combines latent-action modeling with visual and proprioceptive forward dynamics and robot-action prediction~ chen2025villax . Alongside LAC-WM~ huang2026lacwm , these approaches highlight the role of an action representation in linking predicted transitions to executable behavior. LaWAM conditions action generation on predicted latent visual subgoals and explicitly supports physical-time alignment and mixed-frequency training~ chen2026lawam . Its mixed-frequency setting retains native-rate action sequences with variable lengths and uses physical-time encoding to align them. AHA-WAM separates a slow video planner from a fast action executor through observation-guided context routing and horizon-adaptive offset training~ cai2026ahawam . AW-0 extends world-action modeling with joint code, video, and action generation~ liu2026aw0 . CoAWM learns a shared latent function space through cross-embodiment pretraining and connects it to world model and action generation. Given visual observations, language instructions, and the current robot state, the model predicts a latent function in this pretrained space. The decoder then takes time queries to produce executable actions. This design makes the pretrained dynamics priors directly available to action generation and allows a single predicted function to produce action sequences at different execution frequencies. Execution introduces complementary questions about continuity, latency, and commitment. Real-Time Chunking overlaps prediction and execution through inference-time inpainting~ black2025rtc , Legato learns native continuation for action-chunking flow policies~ liu2026legato , and REMAC uses masked action chunking to address real-time execution~ wang2026remac . Mixture of Horizons combines action predictions over multiple horizons~ jing2025moh ; PACE uses kinematic phases to select execution boundaries~ nie2026pace , and DVAC adapts the executed prefix using denoising variance~ feng2026dvac . Reliable Action-Chunk Extension models when to switch according to predicted subskill transitions~ yu2026raceextension , whereas Reachability-aware Accelerated Chunk Execution retimes predicted state paths under physical constraints~ kim2026racetimeoptimal . These methods concern how a plan is committed, continued, or retimed during execution. CoAWM complements these execution mechanisms by separating the latent action function, the times at which it is queried, and the physical timing of the represented motion. Met

title: Optimal Path Planning with Localization constraints
summary: This paper studies UAV path planning in areas where GPS signals are not present. Because these drones can easily get lost when they don't have GPS, they must rely on dead reckoning and occasionally pass near cellular towers, which act as landmarks to reset and fix their position. The goal is to find the shortest path from a start to a goal location while keeping the estimation uncertainty within a given bound. To solve this problem, we propose a localization-constrained A* planner that treats uncertainty as a hard constraint during search. The robot state and covariance are propagated using an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF), and only paths that satisfy the covariance limit are considered. We also show that the proposed method does not affect heuristic used in A* and remains admissible and consistent, ensuring optimality among all feasible paths. Extensive Monte Carlo simulations and PyBullet quadrotor test show that the proposed method finds shorter and more reliable paths compared to RRT* and PRM, while always satisfying the uncertainty constraint.

Extensive Monte Carlo simulations and PyBullet quadrotor test show that the proposed method finds shorter and more reliable paths compared to RRT* and PRM, while always satisfying the uncertainty constraint. GPS-Denied Navigation Path Planning Uncertainty Aware Navigation INTRODUCTION The use of autonomous unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) has expanded rapidly, driven by affordable platforms and sensors. Applications ranging from search and rescue operations in disaster zones to autonomous delivery in remote areas often encounter GPS-denied conditions due to signal interference, multipath effects, or insufficient satellite visibility. In such scenarios, robots must navigate using alternative localization methods, typically combining their local sensors, such as inertial measurement units (IMUs) and external aids like observations of nearby landmarks, to localize and navigate without GPS. The navigation is challenging not only because of obstacle avoidance, but also because localization uncertainty grows as the robot moves without absolute position updates due to sensor noise and external disturbances like wind. Most classical path-planning algorithms focus on geometric optimality measures like distance or time, but they generally assume that the robot’s pose is known exactly or with negligible error like in c1,c2,c9 . This can lead to paths that are optimal in geometry but pass through regions with poor sensing, causing the estimation uncertainty to increase beyond acceptable limits. When this happens, the robot may be forced to replan or may fail to complete the mission. Therefore, planning methods that explicitly account for localization uncertainty during path generation are essential for reliable operation in GPS-denied settings. At the same time, UAVs have limited battery life, so they cannot afford to take very long paths. A longer path may help reduce localization error by passing through areas with better sensing, but it also increases flight time and energy use. This creates a trade-off: short paths are energy-efficient but risky for localization, while safer paths may be too long. So, we need to find paths that are both short and keep the localization error within acceptable limits. In this context, consider a scenario given in figure fig:problem-introduction , where a robot needs to reach a goal where GPS may not be available all the time. A geometrically direct path (shown in blue), typical of classical geometry-based planners can get lost and risk mission success due to localization uncertainty (shown in dotted blue). Alternative paths that exploit landmark sensing regions are shown in green and yellow. Sampling-based planners may instead produce a longer landmark-assisted path (shown in yellow) that remains feasible but increases flight time and energy consumption. Our method selects the shortest localization-feasible path (shown in green), while also satisfying the covariance bounds. \ We address the problem of path planning in GPS-denied environments with sparse localization zones. The environment is assumed to be known, and sensor models are available to predict the effect of motion and observations on the robot’s state estimate. Our goal is to compute paths that explicitly bound state-estimation error while remaining as short as possible, ensuring both localization safety and mission efficiency. In the literature, work on cooperative localization like ~ 1668252,8049492,7120118,9250516 and path planning~ Song,9037111,9384209 have largely been studied independently. Localization in GPS-denied environments has been a significant challenge in the field of autonomous systems. The early work focused solely on improving navigation estimation accuracy, e.g.,~ ding2007 ,~ hide2003 . Many of these approaches have often relied on filtering techniques and probabilistic roadmaps to mitigate localization errors. While effective, these methods typically rely on sampling and do not provide optimality guarantees. A related work ~ c4 studies path planning with localization constraints using a graph built from a probabilistic roadmap (PRM). This helps deal with uncertainty, but since it is based on sampling, it does not guarantee the best optimal solution. The authors improve their method by creating a larger graph to handle multiple objectives. However, their approach assumes the robot can move freely in any direction (holonomic motion). In contrast, our method considers more realistic motion constraints (non-holonomic) by generating smooth, continuous paths between points using a carrot-following controller. Another related work ~ c3 proposes a time-optimal path planner that keeps the localization uncertainty within limits using Particle Swarm Optimization and a carrot-following controller. They use cellular towers as landmarks for UAV localization. However, the method only finds a near-optimal solution and does not guarantee optimality. In ~ SundarKaarthik2019Ppfu , the authors take a different approach by placing landmarks optimally in the environment to satisfy localization constraints. Their method computes both the robot’s path and the best locations to place these landmarks. In contrast, our work assumes that landmarks (such as cellular towers) are fixed and sparse, which better reflects real-world urban environments. Planning under uncertainty has also been addressed through belief-space planning, where the belief over the system state is treated as the planning state. Approaches such as platt2010belief formulate navigation in partially observable environments as a POMDP and compute policies over belief dynamics. Their method requires reliable belief updates and explicit belief transitions, which may be violated in GPS-denied settings with intermittent or weak observations. Similarly, 10770054 studies decision-making under uncertainty by formulating navigation and selective localization as a constrained POMDP and learning policies that balance localization frequency against mission risk. This approach, while powerful for when to localize, still relies on maintaining a belief over states and solving a complex POMDP or reinforcement learning problem over that belief, which can be computationally expensive. In addition to planning-based approaches, another line of work focuses on improving localization through better state estimation techniques. Moving-horizon estimation (MHE) has been suggested as an alternative to EKF to increase the accuracy of nonlinear estimation problems by~ RAWLINGS20061529 ,~ WANG20141581 , and~ 10.1007/s10846-016-0408-2 . For instance ~ 8901098 proposed an approach combining NMPC and pose-graph-MHE for 3D formation control of micro aerial vehicles with relative sensing capability. The use of Nonlinear Model Predictive Control (NMPC) for cooperative localization in multi-agent systems has also been explored in~ 8797888 , where they proposed a joint cooperative path planning algorithm and localization for GPS-denied areas. Their approach combines NMPC for optimal path generation and a Moving Horizon Estimator (MHE) for state estimation, reducing the computational burden of traditional Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) methods. Although effective, NMPC-based methods typically incur high computational costs and lack the deterministic completeness and optimality guarantees provided by search-based planners. The key contributions of this paper are: We propose a path planning method for robots in GPS-denied environments that uses cellular towers as localization landmarks. The planner minimizes travel distance while explicitly constraining state-estimation uncertainty arising from dead reckoning. Non-holonomic A* planning is used to compute feasible paths with A* guarantees. title: Improving Fine-Grained Manipulation through Demonstration Expansion and Execution Design
summary: Fine-grained manipulation requires a robot policy to follow instructions, remain robust to visual variations, and translate predicted actions into precise robot control. We present Demonstration Expansion and Execution Design (DEED), a framework for adapting a pretrained vision-language-action policy to the five MetaFine tasks through structured demonstration expansion and execution design. DEED generates demonstrations for different instructions from the same initial scene and renders each physical trajectory under different camera positions and lighting conditions while preserving its original states and action targets. A hierarchical sampling strategy balances instructions, trajectories, and visual conditions during supervised adaptation. At deployment, DEED converts predicted action chunks into robot commands using inverse kinematics, gripper mappings selected for each task, and closed-loop replanning. DEED achieves an official Overall score of 85.55%. Fixed-policy evaluations show that performance varies with execution horizon, denoising budget, and gripper mapping.

We present Demonstration Expansion and Execution Design (DEED), a framework for adapting a pretrained vision-language-action policy to the five MetaFine tasks through structured demonstration expansion and execution design. DEED generates demonstrations for different instructions from the same initial scene and renders each physical trajectory under different camera positions and lighting conditions while preserving its original states and action targets. A hierarchical sampling strategy balances instructions, trajectories, and visual conditions during supervised adaptation. Introduction Language-conditioned manipulation requires a robot to identify the object, part, or motion specified by an instruction and translate it into precise spatial control~ shridhar2022cliport,mees2021calvin . Recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies combine pretrained visual-language representations with robot action learning and have demonstrated broad transfer across tasks and robot embodiments~ brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,black2024pi0,octo2024,openx2023 . However, fine-grained manipulation remains challenging because it jointly requires instruction-sensitive target selection, robustness to visual variations, and accurate conversion from predicted actions to robot control. MetaFine~ xu2026beyond,benchmark evaluates these capabilities through five tasks covering part-level grasping, directional motion, switch toggling, object sorting, and letter insertion. Its evaluation considers three dimensions: perception under camera and illumination changes, understanding of instruction-conditioned behavior, and controlled behavior during task execution. Directly fine-tuning a pretrained VLA policy on the provided demonstrations leaves three practical gaps. First, observing different instructions only in different scenes can lead to scene-instruction confounding. Second, limited camera and illumination conditions provide insufficient visual coverage. Third, predicted action chunks may fail when the execution horizon, inverse kinematics conversion, or gripper semantics do not match the simulator interface. Addressing these gaps requires adapting both the demonstration distribution and the execution pipeline. To address these gaps, DEED expands demonstrations across instructions and visual conditions, balances training exposure through hierarchical sampling, and adapts closed-loop execution to each task (Figure~ fig:pipeline ). Our contributions are: (1) A demonstration expansion strategy that varies instructions within the same scene and visual conditions for the same physical trajectory, supported by hierarchical sampling. (2) A task-aware execution pipeline that converts predicted action chunks into robot control through inverse kinematics, task-specific gripper mappings, and receding-horizon replanning. (3) A five-task evaluation achieving an official Overall score of 85.55 , together with fixed-policy studies of key execution choices. title: A Two-Wheeled Quadrotor with All-Clockwise Tilted Rotors for Level-Attitude Surface Locomotnion
summary: Conventional wheel-equipped quadrotor UAVs must tilt their bodies to generate lateral forces, limiting their ability to maintain a desired attitude during lateral motion. This paper proposes a wheeled quadrotor with all-clockwise tilted rotors that uses surface contact as a constraint to generate propulsion along the contact surface without tilting the vehicle. We analyze feasible forces and system controllability under surface contact and optimize the vehicle design considering different rotor-spin configurations. The optimization results show that a configuration in which all four rotors spin clockwise can generate a larger tangential force than the conventional alternating-spin configuration. This approach enables both aerial and contact-based locomotion without additional rotor-tilting actuators or mechanisms. Simulation results demonstrate both hovering in free space and horizontal locomotion on a floor while maintaining a level attitude.

title: BURGER: Benchmarking and Understanding Robotic Generalization via Embodied Drawing
summary: How effectively can vision-language-action (VLA) models learn diverse language-conditioned behaviors as training data scales? Investigating this question requires large and varied robot datasets, whose collection on physical robots remains costly. We introduce BURGER, a language-conditioned robotic drawing benchmark with a scalable, prompt-driven pipeline for generating continuous drawing trajectories, both in simulation and the real world. In BURGER, an agent starts from the same blank canvas and controls a robot arm to draw the object or spatial composition specified by language, while each instruction allows an open-ended variety of valid drawings and stroke orders. Using 28,200 simulated demonstrations spanning 282 drawing tasks, we evaluate five representative VLA models across data scales, language grounding, and multimodal behavior. BURGER supports fine-grained analysis of language grounding, spatial composition, and action generation, revealing distinct failure patterns across VLA models. Our experiments suggest that some VLA models can benefit from greater task diversity and demonstration scale, capture multimodal drawing behaviors, and generalize to unseen compositions of familiar objects. Finally, we deploy a trained policy on a Franka Panda arm, demonstrating the ability to draw reactively under human intervention. Project homepage and code can be found at https://siyingzhao.github.io/BURGER/.

Introduction sec:introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) models integrate visual perception, language understanding, and action generation into policies for robotic control ~ zitkovich2023rt,kim2024openvla,black2026pi0visionlanguageactionflowmodel,black2025pi05 . As VLA models increasingly benefit from larger and more diverse datasets, an important question is whether current architectures are ready to effectively exploit large-scale language-conditioned robot trajectories. Investigating this question requires robot datasets with controllable scale and diversity, together with evaluations that distinguish different aspects of model behavior~ mees2022calvin,zhang2025vlabench,wang2025vlatest . However, collecting diverse demonstrations on physical robots remains costly~ khazatsky2024droid,o2024open , which motivates a more scalable setting for such studies. Robotic drawing provides a complementary data regime with several practical advantages for such studies. Starting from the same blank canvas, the agent cannot infer the requested drawing from the initial observation alone, eliminating a potential visual shortcut~ xing2025shortcut . Language prompts can be systematically increased in semantic complexity by composing objects, attributes, and spatial relations. The same instruction can admit many valid trajectories that differ in stroke order, starting point, and drawing direction, this intrinsic multimodality forces model to understand the concept, rather than memorizing the action sequence. The resulting canvases and execution trajectories make semantic, spatial, and action-execution failures directly inspectable, supporting fine-grained diagnosis of model behavior. Drawing therefore provides a scalable setting for testing whether VLA architectures can learn complex language-conditioned and multimodal robot trajectories before scaling up costly real-world data collection. Motivated by these properties, we introduce , a scalable benchmark and data-generation pipeline for language-conditioned robotic drawing, shown in Fig.~ fig:teaser . Our pipeline generates target sketches from natural-language prompts and converts them into robot end-effector trajectories executable in simulation and on a real robot. Using this pipeline, we construct 132 single-object tasks and 150 compositional tasks, with 100 demonstrations per task. The dataset spans diverse objects, spatial compositions, and trajectory realizations. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:data_comparison , drawing trajectories in ~exhibit substantially greater diversity in the plane for a given instruction than manipulation trajectories in LIBERO~ liu2023libero . We introduce a DINOv3-based metric for scalable evaluation of generated drawings and validate its agreement with human judgments in a single-object user study. We use ~to examine how representative VLA models learn from larger datasets, capture trajectory diversity, and generalize to new compositions. The flow-matching models generally improve as either the number of demonstrations per task or the number of training tasks increases, suggesting that some existing approaches can benefit from scaling robotic drawing data. The -family models~ black2026pi0visionlanguageactionflowmodel, black2025pi05 can autonomously produce recognizable drawings after fine-tuning. Beyond visual recognizability, retains multiple modes of the drawing trajectory distribution, as shown in Fig.~ fig:data_comparison . We further observe that evaluated policies can generate unseen spatial compositions of familiar objects, but struggle to draw object categories absent from training. Inspecting the resulting drawings and trajectories reveals semantic, spatial, and geometric failure patterns that are difficult to distinguish through task-success metrics alone. We further demonstrate successful real-robot drawing after fine-tuning on 100 real-robot demonstrations alone, as well as sim-to-real transfer of a policy co-trained on 13,200 simulated ~demonstrations. Although robotic drawing simplifies the contact-rich interaction and object dynamics involved in manipulation, it retains important demands on language grounding and action generation. Following a drawing instruction requires translating object descriptions and spatial relations into long-horizon continuous actions, while the range of valid drawings and stroke sequences provides a setting for evaluating multimodal behavior modeling. These capabilities are also central to language-conditioned manipulation, making ~a distinctive lens for examining the readiness and limitations of current VLA architectures in learning from larger and more diverse training datasets. Related Work sec:related_work Vision-language-action (VLA) models map visual observations and language instructions to robot actions. Recent VLAs broadly follow autoregressive or continuous generative paradigms. Autoregressive models, such as OpenVLA~ kim2024openvla , predict actions sequentially, with recent variants improving action representations, chunking, and parallel decoding~ kim2025fine, pertsch2025fast, song2025pdvla, wang2025vqvla, liu2025faster . Continuous generative models produce action chunks using flow matching or diffusion~ lipman2023flowmatching : and use flow matching~ black2026pi0visionlanguageactionflowmodel, black2025pi05 , while RDT-1B and GR00T N1 adopt diffusion-based generation liu2025rdt, bjorck2025gr00tn1 . Hybrid methods such as DiffusionVLA~ wen2025diffusionvla combine autoregressive reasoning with diffusion-based action generation. ~evaluates these paradigms under multimodal, long-horizon, and semantically rich drawing data. Benchmarking of VLA systems has moved beyond measuring binary task success rates toward more diagnostic evaluation. Recent benchmarks evaluate VLA abilities in long-horizon reasoning, spatial and semantic grounding, robustness to scene or language perturbations, structured behavioral metrics, and memory-dependent manipulation~ zhang2025vlabench, wang2025vlatest, wang2025roboeval, dai2026robomme, chen2026rmbench . These efforts show that similar success rates can hide different failure modes in grounding, planning, robustness, or temporal consistency. ~ follows this capability-oriented evaluation direction, but uses language-conditioned drawing as the diagnostic domain. Unlike goal-oriented manipulation, drawing admits many valid stroke orders, geometries, and trajectories for the same prompt. This makes the more dedicated abilities directly observable from the generated canvas and rollout trajectory. Data scaling in VLA learning has been studied in robot imitation learning and generalist policy training. Prior work analyzes how data quantity and data composition affect manipulation-policy generalization, including object and environment diversity, camera viewpoints, spatial arrangements, and dataset fragmentation lin2025datascaling, saxena2025whatmatters, xing2025shortcut . ~ considers a related scaling question in a controlled language-conditioned drawing domain. Robotic drawing and painting have been studied primarily as a control and planning problem. For example, Lee et al.~ lee2022scratch formulate robotic sketching as a deep decoupled hierarchical reinforcement learning problem, where separate policies learn stroke-based rendering and motor control from scratch. FRIDA~ schaldenbrand2022frida develops a collaborative robot painting system with a differentiable real2sim2real planning environment, enabling a robot to generate paintings from high-level human inputs such as language descriptions or reference images. More recently, IMPASTO~ wang2026impasto studies robotic oil-painting reproduction by integrating learned pixel dynamics models with model-based planning. These works advance robotic drawing by improving stroke planning, motor control, and real-world execution. In contrast, our work studies sketching as a language-conditioned VLA benchmark. Method sec:method Task Formulation sec:task At time , a policy receives a language instruction , a canvas observation , and robot proprioception , and predicts an end-effector command (or an action chunk, depending on the model). The task is to produce the requested object or spatial composition through sequential drawing actions. The policy is not given a target sketch at inference. Canvas observations change as strokes accumulate, while pen-lifting transitions separate disconnected strokes. The benchmark therefore involves both drawing geometry and decisions about when to move without marking the canvas. The same SVG drawing task is executed in SAPIEN, MuJoCo, and Isaac Sim using corresponding robot-control interfaces. fig:simulators sec:main_paper_pipline Figure~ fig:teaser summarizes our prompt-to-trajectory pipeline. We record RGB observations, robot proprioception, and actions as observation-action pairs, then convert the trajectories to the robot-dataset format. title: Gym-Anything for Robotics: Scaling physical simulations with digital agents
summary: Realistic, fast robotics simulations could enable large-scale training of embodied AI models that transfer to the real world. However, despite decades of progress, available simulations cover only a narrow range of real-world tasks and physical phenomena. The core bottleneck is that creating better simulations requires significant expert effort and therefore does not scale. To address this, we introduce Gym-Anything for Robotics, a framework in which coding agents create realistic robotics simulations. Our core insight is that simulation creation is a coding agent task, so improvements in coding agents translate directly into richer and more faithful simulations. We select simulations based on U.S. GDP data to cover economically valuable physical work, define what makes a good simulation and a good task, and develop an adversarial creation-audit loop that checks each simulation and task against these definitions. Using this pipeline, we build RoboWorld, a set of 25 simulations with 25 test and 175 training RL environments of varying difficulty. Even the best frontier models fail on every RoboWorld test task, achieving an average reward of only 0.06. Building on RoboWorld, we introduce several new ways for frontier models to improve, including in-context learning across repeated attempts, a privileged teacher that reads the simulator state and teaches a student in context, self-assisted learning from the model's own privileged experience, and code policies that generate demonstrations across varied scenes to train vision-language-action models (VLAs) such as $π_{0.5}$. Each of these substantially improves performance. We release our pipeline, RL environments, and benchmark to facilitate future research. Code and data are available at https://gym-anything.github.io/robotics

Each of these substantially improves performance. We release our pipeline, RL environments, and benchmark to facilitate future research. Code and data are available at . Introduction Simulation is one of the most promising paths to training embodied AI at scale. Unlike the real world, a simulator can run thousands of episodes in parallel, reset instantly, expose the full ground-truth state, and provide rewards without human supervision~ todorov2012mujoco,makoviychuk2021isaac,tao2025maniskill3 . For these advantages to matter, however, simulations must faithfully represent the real world. Although the field has developed various hand-built environments~ james2020rlbench,yu2020metaworld,liu2023libero,li2023behavior1k,nasiriany2024robocasa , a key bottleneck is that building additional, more realistic simulations requires significant time and expert effort. Indeed, despite decades of human progress, today's simulations cover a narrow range of real-world tasks and physical phenomena (Tables~ tab:benchmarks and~ tab:prior-sims ), often with limited visual fidelity. Simulation as a path to embodied AI is hindered by the challenge of building diverse, realistic simulations at scale. Our core insight is that simulation creation can be framed as a coding agent task. Building a simulation means writing code, including assembling assets into scenes, configuring physics, defining tasks, and implementing rewards. Recently, coding agents have become increasingly capable of a wide range of coding-related work~ jimenez2024swebench,yang2024sweagent,wang2025openhands,wang2024gensim,wang2024robogen . We hypothesize that frontier agents are already capable of building diverse robotics simulations with high visual fidelity and realistic physics. Moreover, framing simulation creation as a coding agent task allows future improvements in coding agents to translate into better simulations, thereby providing a means for scalable, realistic simulation creation that is expected to improve over time. Building on these insights, we introduce Gym-Anything for Robotics, a framework in which coding agents create realistic robotics simulations of real-world physical work (Figure~ fig:overview ). Building simulators for real physical work requires modeling a wide variety of materials and physical phenomena. For instance, a realistic titration requires the solution to form drops, mix, and turn pink rather than red at the endpoint. To organize the coverage of such phenomena in our simulation environments, we ground the selection of simulations in U.S.\ GDP data~ aggarwal2026gymanything,gdpval2025 . In brief, we consider each occupation, decompose the physical portion of the occupation's tasks into atomic physical actions, and weight the actions by economic value. We then select simulations that cover the most valuable physical actions and any robotic and physics capabilities that these actions require. A coding agent then builds each simulation in code, assembles scenes from real assets, and configures the robot and physics ( 3). However, simulations built by coding agents frequently contain errors that make them unrealistic. For instance, a liquid simulation may not handle surface tension or inter-particle interactions correctly, or objects may pass through walls. Therefore, we develop an agentic creation-audit loop~ aggarwal2026gymanything for detecting issues in the simulations and fixing them. Specifically, we define criteria for what constitutes a good simulation, including realism, solvability, speed, and robustness to exploits, and then run a creation agent and four audit agents in an adversarial loop. The creation agent must produce evidence that its simulation is good, such as renders, physical measurements, and assisted demonstrations. The four audit agents, including an adversarial agent that tries to break the simulation, then check the evidence and report issues for the creation agent to fix. Furthermore, for each simulation, we use coding agents to create multiple tasks and control their difficulty ( 4). This is important since tasks that are all too easy or all too hard provide little signal for evaluating or improving models~ shao2024deepseekmath,yu2025dapo . As with simulation creation, generated tasks may have issues such as being unsolvable or having incorrect rewards. We therefore define what makes a good task, and hand-curate checklists for six independent audit agents, which check each task against this definition, including solvability and reward correctness. We further ensure that each task's reward measures both progress and the final outcome, computed from the physical state of the simulation. For instance, a cleanup task can credit each object placed in its correct location rather than only a fully cleaned scene. Finally, every task can be run with different robots, from single arms to bimanual arms and humanoids, and under variations of object poses, appearance, and physics, which change the scene but not the task itself. We use Gym-Anything for Robotics to construct RoboWorld, a collection of 25 simulations spanning domains such as manufacturing, construction, food service, laboratories, and logistics, with 25 test and 175 training RL environments of varying difficulty. RoboWorld is far from solved: even the best frontier models score 0 on the full benchmark, while on an easier subset, the best model reaches 32 . Beyond benchmarking, we introduce several new ways for models to learn on RoboWorld ( 5). To do so, we exploit privileged access to the full ground-truth state, which is readily available in our simulations and a benefit of the simulation paradigm. We first show that models can improve on RoboWorld tasks through in-context learning, and that in-context learning is accelerated by access to the privileged simulation state. Since privileged state is unavailable at test time on a real robot, we develop three ways to leverage it as a learning signal, including (1) a teacher-student setup where the teacher has privileged access and teaches a student model through qualitative hints alone, (2) a ``self-learning'' setup where a model learns from its own privileged experience, and (3) a setup in which privileged code policies train the vision-language-action model (VLA) ~ black2025pi05 , which observes only camera images and robot proprioception. In summary, we contribute (1) Gym-Anything for Robotics, a modular framework and multi-agent pipeline for automatically building high-quality robotics simulations, together with our definitions of what makes a good robotics simulation and a good task; (2) RoboWorld, 25 GDP-grounded simulations with 25 test and 175 training RL environments, each supporting swappable robots and variations of object poses, appearance, and physics; (3) an evaluation showing that frontier models perform poorly on RoboWorld, with no model scoring above 0 on the full benchmark; and (4) several new ways for models to learn in simulation, showing that frontier models improve through in-context learning and do so faster with privileged state, that a frontier model with privileged state can teach a student model without it, even through verbal hints, that a model can learn from its own privileged experience, and that code policies can train VLAs such as . Methodology sec:method In this section, we introduce the problem setup and the GDP-grounded selection of simulations. In sec:creation , we describe our multi-agent strategy for creating simulations, and in sec:tasks , how we create tasks of controlled difficulty for each simulation. Problem Setup sec:setup Simulation. We refer to a simulation as a scene implemented in code, consisting of objects with physical models (such as rigid, articulated, deformable, or liquid), a robot, cameras, and a physics engine that advances the physical state of the scene (Figure~ fig:setup ). Each simulation specifies a default robot, which can be swapped for other robots from a shared catalog, from single arms to bimanual arms and humanoids. Each simulation further supports variations of object poses, appearance, and physics, which change the scene in which a task is performed but not the task itself. For instance, our welding simulation is a robotic welding cell, in which a UR10e arm carrying a welding torch and an FR3 arm with a gripper work at a fixture table holding a steel plate and a bracket. Three cameras observe the cell, and the physics engine melts and solidifies the steel under the welding arc. The same cell can also be run with five other robot setups, from a single FR3 arm to a Unitree G1 humanoid, and its 10 , 000 variations shift the plate, change how far the wire sticks out of the torch, and add a draft that can blow the shielding gas away from the weld. Task. A task consists of a simulation with initial state , a natural-language instruction , and a verification function that maps the physical states of an episode to a binary success label and a reward . The reward measures both progress and outcome, and every successful completion receives . For instance, in one welding task, has the bracket tacked to the plate, asks to ``weld a continuous 1/4~in fillet along the near side in the horizontal position, end to end, and fill the crater,'' and inspects the solidified weld under the AWS D1.1 welding code, checking that it is continuous and fused, reaches the specified size, and stays within the limits on undercut and porosity. If the weld fails, is proportional to the share of the required weld that is sound. Since swapping the robot or applying a variation changes only and , this task can be run with any of the six robots and from any of the 10 , 000 variations. Interaction. At each step , the agent receives an observation , consisting of images from the robot's cameras and robot feedback such as joint positions, and issues a robot command , such as a joint target, an end-effector motion, or a gripper command. title: SwapBot: Tool-Centric Robot Manipulation via Interchangeable End-Effectors and Tactile Sensing
summary: Robot manipulation in everyday environments inherently involves substantial tool usage. Seemingly simple household tasks, such as cooking pan-fried tofu, require forceful cutting, delicate brushing, and precise placement using different tools under contact-rich interaction. Thus, the ability to autonomously swap and use task-appropriate tools is important for tool-centric manipulation. We introduce SwapBot, a modular, tool-centric end effector system featuring low-cost adapters that quickly convert common household tools into robot end effectors. Rather than pursuing a single universal gripper, SwapBot adopts a unified design principle that combines a fixed robot-side coupling interface with low-cost, tool-side adapters, enabling compatibility with diverse tools, including articulated ones, and multiple robot platforms. Each adapter integrates compact tactile sensors, supports fast autonomous swapping, and interfaces with an intuitive teleoperation system for efficient demonstration collection. User studies show that, during teleoperation, SwapBot reduces task completion time and operator workload. Using collected demonstrations on the robot, we train imitation learning policies to successfully perform tool-centric tasks like cooking tofu, stirring salad, flipping meat. Our ablation study shows that using tactile-augmented demonstrations improves policy performance across contact-rich skills, increasing success rates by 15 to 25 percentage points over RGB-only policies. These results highlight modular, tactile-equipped tools as a practical and extensible pathway toward robust and capable robot manipulation. Project website https://personalrobotics.github.io/SwapBot.

Introduction Robotic manipulation is advancing toward increasingly human-level capabilities; however, seemingly simple tasks, such as cooking pan-fried tofu, remain challenging for robots to perform. Performed with different tools under contact-rich interaction, these tasks require precise but forceful control (cutting), delicate interaction with deformable objects (brushing), and dexterous motion (grasping and placing). Such tool-centric manipulation is challenging under the current end-effector design, which falls into two broad categories. First, anthropomorphic hands mimic human dexterity~ shaw2023leap, shadowhand , but their mechanical complexity imposes a high cost in maintenance, sensing, and control, hindering scalable data collection and policy learning. Second, parallel jaw grippers, though practical and demonstrating impressive versatility~ zhao2024aloha, black2024pi_0, khazatsky2024droid , struggle to perform tasks requiring nuanced physical interactions, such as cutting or spreading. These capability vs controllability tradeoffs create significant barriers to more capable and scalable tool-centric robot manipulation. Humans accomplish complex manipulation tasks by using tools, e.g., knives, brushes, or screwdrivers, as extensions of their bodies. Robotists have explored tool use using dexterous hands ~ chen2025vegetable, yin2025dexteritygen or parallel grippers~ lin2022planning, shi2023robocook . However, existing methods either inherit the complexity of manipulating anthropomorphic hands, struggling to maintain tool stability under load, or, critically, lack tactile sensing~ zhao2023learning at the tool-object interface, hindering effective control and learning for contact-rich tasks. To balance robot manipulators' capability and controllability, we propose to equip robots with the ability to swap modular tools through a tool changer. Industrial tool changers, such as those used in CNC machining or on UR5 robots, demonstrate the practicality of extending robotic capabilities through automatic tool exchange. However, these costly systems are typically customized for specific robots and cannot easily accommodate actively articulated tools - e.g., tongs and scissors. Moreover, they lack integration with tactile sensing, limiting their ability to support contact-rich manipulation tasks. Instead, our approach turns accessible household items into robot tools and equips each tool with compact, custom tactile sensors, enabling robots to both select the appropriate tool for each subtask and sense contact at the tool–object interface. Drawing inspiration from surgical robots that interchange end-effectors such as scissors, cauterizers, and forceps, our system thus enables scalable household manipulation through tool diversity, not anatomical mimicry. We present , a modular, low-cost, tool-centric manipulation system with integrated tactile sensors, as shown in Fig.~ fig:Overview . It features: (1)a unified adaptation interface for diverse tools and robots, (2) fast and autonomous tool swapping protocol, (3) integrated tactile sensing, and (4) intuitive teleoperation for demonstration data collection. Our system employs inexpensive, 3D-printed interfaces (\ 35 60 10), rapid swapping of tools, robot-agnostic, enabling compatibility with common manipulators, and flexible for both passive and articulated tools. To achieve these goals, we design our tool-swapping adapter and coupling system to enable a fully accessible fabrication workflow and straightforward assembly using basic hand tools, such as an Allen wrench. As shown in Figure fig:System (left), we 3D-print tool adapters and inserts to enable the quick instrumentation and mounting of common household tools. The adapter both attaches the tool securely and houses the tactile sensors stably. For tools with moderate handle sizes, the same adapter can be reused, while soft silicone fills the remaining gap to accommodate variations in handle shape and size. Only substantially thinner tools require a smaller 3D-printed adapter, while the robot-side coupling interface remains unchanged. Though many everyday tools include their own actuation mechanisms, equipping each with dedicated motors for automatic control would be complex and expensive. Instead, we shift all power and control functionalities to the robot side, ensuring a simpler and lower-cost tool implementation. To transmit torque, we add a bearing system on top of the adapter cover that transfers motion from the robot’s end joint. For robots without a final joint, we supplement with a single servo motor to ensure compatibility across Franka, UR, and other common platforms (Fig. fig:multi-robot ). To support rapid tool exchange, we implement a self-aligning electromagnetic coupling that mates a robot-side hub with tool-side adapters. This design supports both passive tools (e.g., knives, brushes) and articulated tools (e.g., tongs, chopsticks) through a pass-through mechanism. A kinematically guided gear ensures reliable engagement and release under small alignment errors, while the electromagnet provides sufficient holding force for secure tool attachment during forceful manipulation. In practice, our system completes a swap in about 10~s by guiding the robot to a docking station, releasing the current tool, and attaching a new one. This approach shifts capability from a single complex hand to a library of instrumented tools while retaining the ability to compose skills across tools. We summarize key design specifications in Tab.~ tab:specs . Compact Tactile Sensing: Instrumented Tools sec:2b We design compact, tool-specific piezoresistive tactile sensors that provide task-relevant contact information for teleoperation and policy learning. By tailoring the sensor layout to each tool, we capture force information without adding bulk or compromising usability. The piezoresistive tactile sensors consist of a three-layer structure, shown in Fig.~ fig:System (center), where a force-sensitive material layer (Velostat) is sandwiched between top and bottom electrodes (conductive fabric) for signal transmission. These sensors ~ sundaram2019learning convert real-time normal force pressure information into an electrical signal via the drop of resistance. The electrodes are made from copper-nickel conductive fabric, laser-cut to precise dimensions for optimal fit considering the sensitivity they need for tasks. To accommodate the limited surface area of tools, we implement the sensors in a matrix layout, where sensing nodes are formed at the intersections of orthogonal electrode rows and columns. This configuration enables an n n sensor array using only 2n electrodes. Our approach is low-cost, relies on only off-the-shelf materials, and supports easy customization through digital fabrication. We show the design and placement of tactile sensors for each tool in Fig.~ fig:System (center). For tools with larger surfaces, we place sensors on both the handle and the blade or tip (e.g., tongs, spoons, knives). For smaller or thinner tools, such as chopsticks, brushes, and forks, it is impractical to mount sensors directly on the blade or tip. In these cases, we instrument only the handle, providing indirect measurements of tool–object interaction. This strategy ensures that tactile information is captured where feasible while keeping the modules compact and lightweight. For blade or tip instrumentation, we mount the fabricated tactile sensors directly onto the tool surface. To accommodate handles of varying sizes, instead of attaching sensors directly, we install them between the TPU layer and the PLA adapter cover and fill the gap between the handle and TPU shell with soft silicone. This approach allows the sensors to comply with different handle shapes, stabilizes the installation process, and ensures consistent reflection of sensor readings during interaction. Teleoperation Interface: High-Quality Demonstration Collection sec:2c We design the teleoperation interface to maximize operator intuitiveness and data quality, both of which are critical for downstream policy learning. Our interface maps the intuitive leader device's 6-DoF pose and actuation commands directly to the corresponding tool on the robot side. By using similar tools on both sides, e.g., chopsticks to control chopsticks or a knife to control a knife, operators interact with familiar household tools, making control feel natural. This reduces the re-targeting effort common in teleoperation and lets operators focus on task execution rather than compensating for mismatched dynamics. For each leader tool, we estimate the 6-DoF pose using an Intel RealSense T265 tracking camera, and use the result to drive the robot during teleoperation. For articulated tools, we infer the actuation command from the relative motion measured by two IMUs, providing accurate correspondence between human and robot tool motion. During demonstration data collection, all data streams are synchronized at 20~Hz, including multi-view RGB images, tactile signals, robot joint states, actions, and task labels. This ensures that multimodal inputs remain temporally aligned for learning. We also provide visual overlays that display the live contact forces and tactile maps to help operators anticipate and refine contact-rich interactions. As we will show in Fig.~ fig:UserStudy , tactile information is visualized on-screen to indicate contact information. This immediate feedback provides operators with additional information about contact, improving both control precision and the quality of collected demonstrations. title: FutureWorld: A Plug-and-Play Causal Next-State Predictor for Interactive Video World Exploration
summary: Interactive video world models aim to follow user actions while maintaining scene consistency over extended interactions. History-based methods reuse generated latents to preserve scene content, but three limitations of this reuse contribute to error recirculation. 1) The latent generated at each interaction is retained as history, potentially containing blurred details, geometric distortions, or semantic drift. 2) Although retrieved historical content matches the current scene, it can still contain errors that are carried into the next chunk. 3) New outputs then become history for later interactions, potentially reinforcing the same errors through repeated reuse. To limit this cycle, we aim to predict the future scene state from the current generated latent and the next action before generating the next interaction's video chunk. This future-state prior provides guidance for the next chunk, with the aim of reducing the errors carried forward from history. To this end, we propose a plug-and-play Causal Next-Chunk Predictor (C-NCP) with cross-model adaptability and prediction-guided modulation. We integrate C-NCP into four base generators and evaluate the augmented models across three benchmarks for interactive long-video generation and action-conditioned world modeling. Extensive experiments demonstrate reduced error accumulation and improved long-horizon consistency across diverse generation settings. The project page is at https://GuangYuanKK.github.io/futureworld.

We integrate C-NCP into four base generators and evaluate the augmented models across three benchmarks for interactive long-video generation and action-conditioned world modeling. Extensive experiments demonstrate reduced error accumulation and improved long-horizon consistency across diverse generation settings. The project page is at . Introduction sec:introduction Interactive video world models~ li2026magicworld,sun2025worldplay,robbyant2026lingbotworld,wu2026infiniteworld,wang2026matrixgame3,zhu2026sanawm,zhao2026minwm,dreamx2026world,alayaworld2026alayaworld,chen2026reworld,zhao2026quantwm,ji2025sonic generate visual environments that evolve under user action control. Sustained interaction requires each new chunk to follow the next action while preserving the scene's structure and semantics. As interactions continue, local generation defects can affect subsequent chunks, making error propagation a central obstacle to long-horizon consistency. To maintain scene consistency, history-based approaches~ sun2025worldplay,wang2026matrixgame3,li2025hunyuan,zhu2025memorize,yu2025context,zhao2026relax,yu2025videossm,kim2026memrope,yin2026framemorrow repeatedly retrieve and reuse generated content. However, this reuse can lead to error recirculation. Defects from earlier generations enter new outputs, which are then added to history and reused in later interactions, as illustrated in . Three limitations of history reuse contribute to this cycle. First, the latent generated at each interaction is retained as history, potentially containing visual defects such as blurred details, geometric distortions, or semantic drift. Second, although a retrieved history view matches the current scene, it can still contain errors. Reusing such a view can therefore propagate these errors to the next chunk. Third, the new output is then added to history and reused in later interactions, potentially reinforcing the same errors. To limit this cycle, the generator needs guidance for the next chunk that does not rely solely on reusing potentially flawed history. Based on this analysis, our motivation is to predict the future state from the current generated latent and the next action, providing an explicit future-state prior before generating the video chunk for the next interaction. Supervision from real video transitions teaches the predictor how scenes change under action control. It uses these learned transitions to re-estimate the upcoming state, rather than only selecting content already present in history. The resulting future-state prior guides the next generation, with the aim of reducing errors carried forward from earlier outputs. To turn this prior into effective guidance, we need to meet the following two requirements. (1) Adaptability. To make future-state prediction usable across different interactive video generators, the predictor must adapt to their latent representations. Different models use VAE latents with different dimensions and distributions, so the predictor needs a way to accommodate these differences. (2) Modulation. The future-state prior must also help guide the generation of the next chunk. Direct concatenation places the predicted latent alongside the generator's main latent, but the generator must still learn how to use this extra input when producing the next chunk. Modulation instead uses the future-state prior to adjust the main latent directly, while keeping its tensor shape unchanged. These considerations lead to our central research question. How can we predict a future state from the current generated latent and the next action, and use it to guide subsequent generation and limit error propagation across interactions? To address this question, we propose the plug-and-play Causal Next-Chunk Predictor (C-NCP), which estimates the complete next latent chunk from the current interaction's generated latent and the next interaction's action control. We use Bayesian decision theory ~ sarkka2013bayesian to formulate this prediction task as learning a future-state estimate that minimizes expected prediction loss given the current latent and next action. To enable adaptation, VAE-specific input adapters map each model's latents into a shared representation for the causal spatiotemporal predictor, while output heads map its predictions back to the corresponding model's latent space. To enable modulation, we use the future-state prior to adjust the generator's main latent through residual feature modulation based on adaptive instance normalization~ huang2017adain . After each interaction, the newly generated latent becomes the input to the next prediction, so the future-state prior is updated as interaction continues. Our main contributions are summarized as follows. We introduce a future-state-guided correction paradigm for error recirculation in interactive video generation. Rather than only selecting content from generated history, this approach learns to re-estimate the state expected under the next action. The resulting prior guides each new chunk before it becomes part of history. We develop the plug-and-play Causal Next-Chunk Predictor with cross-model adaptability and prediction-guided modulation. VAE-specific adapters let the predictor work with different latent representations, while residual modulation uses its future-state prior to adjust the generator's main latent. We integrate our C-NCP into four base generators and evaluate the augmented models across three benchmarks for interactive long-video generation and action-conditioned world modeling. Extensive experiments demonstrate reduced error accumulation and improved long-horizon consistency across diverse generation settings. Related Work sec:related Interactive Video World Models. Interactive video world models~ li2026magicworld,sun2025worldplay,robbyant2026lingbotworld,wu2026infiniteworld,wang2026matrixgame3,zhu2026sanawm,zhao2026minwm,dreamx2026world,alayaworld2026alayaworld,chen2026reworld extend visual generation to environments that evolve under action control. Early token-based systems such as iVideoGPT~ wu2024ivideogpt model observations, actions, and rewards within an autoregressive sequence. Matrix-Game 2.0~ he2025matrixgame2 and LingBot-World~ robbyant2026lingbotworld develop real-time streaming generation across diverse environments, while SANA-WM~ zhu2026sanawm combines hybrid linear attention and long-video refinement for efficient minute-scale generation. Recent work also addresses the mismatch between clean training contexts and generated histories. Matrix-Game 3.0~ wang2026matrixgame3 reuses prediction errors to expose the model to imperfect conditioning, and DreamX-World~ dreamx2026world combines residual recycling with training on self-generated long-horizon contexts. These approaches improve the generator's ability to continue from its own outputs rather than assuming error-free history. However, remaining defects in generated history can still affect subsequent chunks. Our plug-and-play Causal Next-Chunk Predictor provides an explicit future-state prior before the next interaction's video chunk is generated. It learns from real video transitions, and VAE-specific adapters accommodate different latent representations so that the predictor can be integrated into different base generators. History Modeling for Video Generation. History modeling preserves scene context through retrieval and compact memory. Spatial-memory world models~ wu2025spatialmemory reconstruct static 3D scenes for rendering along target trajectories, while WorldPlay~ sun2025worldplay reconstructs relevant historical context. WorldKV~ yi2026worldkv retrieves viewpoint-matched chunks and compresses redundant tokens; Matrix-Game 3.5~ qian2026matrixgame35 uses geometry-aware patch memory; and ReWorld~ chen2026reworld combines a bounded KV cache with a pose-indexed landmark bank. Compression and adaptive selection further reduce context costs. FramePack~ zhang2025framepack uses frame-dependent compression and anti-drifting sampling, while TinyHistory~ zhang2025tinyhistory learns compact history embeddings through frame-query pretraining and content-consistency learning. Infinite-World~ wu2026infiniteworld uses pose-free hierarchical memory, and CaR~ peng2026car combines context compression with attention-based implicit retrieval. OmniMem~ zhao2026omnimem sparsely retrieves KV blocks from historical caches. Future Forcing~ luo2026futureforcing uses future-query proxies to guide KV retention and merging. Retrieval and compression help preserve scene content, but the generated latents they reuse can still contain visual defects. When these defects enter new outputs and those outputs become history, repeated reuse can cause error recirculation. To address this problem, our predictor learns how scenes change under action control from real video transitions and predicts the next latent state from the current generated latent and the next action. The resulting future-state prior guides the generator's main latent through modulation, aiming to reduce the errors passed into subsequent chunks.
